title: Ford Wants To Somehow Sell 100000 Ford Fathom EVs In Its First Year - Jalopnik
description:
Ford is shooting for the stars with its yet-to-be-revealed Fathom electric pickup truck.
Of course, Tesla sold 357,000 Model Ys and 190,000 Model 3s, but that's besides the point.
I mean, across three different brands, General Motors managed to only sell 170,000 EVs in 2025.
[...] Ford executives say the Fathom's $30,000 price range will help it succeed where other EVs—which often cost $50,000 or more—didn't.
I don't know if 100,000 sales is in the cards, but the Fathom does seem to be pretty damn cool for under 30 grand.
text:
Good morning! It's Thursday, September 3, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Ford has designs on 100,000 Fathom EV sales in year one, Uber is laying off 3,300 employees in its biggest cuts since Covid, The Blue Oval must pay $2.3 million to settle a racial harassment case at its Buffalo Stamping facility and longer working weeks probably won't fix Volkswagen's issues.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Ford is shooting for the stars with its yet-to-be-revealed Fathom electric pickup truck. The automaker has apparently set a sales goal so lofty that it's only really been met by Tesla in the U.S.: selling over 100,000 vehicles in its first year. That is a hell of a tall order, even for a vehicle that is supposed to start at $29,945 when it goes on sale next year. I mean, the F-150 Lightning and Mustang Mach-E have never sniffed even a fraction of that type of sales success.

If it were to actually meet those targets, the Fathom (a good name) would immediately become one of the best-selling EVs in the U.S. Outside of Tesla, no other automaker has sold over 100,000 units of a single model in the U.S. in a year. Of course, Tesla sold 357,000 Model Ys and 190,000 Model 3s, but that's besides the point. I mean, across three different brands, General Motors managed to only sell 170,000 EVs in 2025. From The Wall Street Journal:

Expectations are high. Ford's earlier EVs, including an electric version of its F-150 pickup, often sold well in their respective segments but never achieved the high volumes of its gas and hybrid cars. Behind the scenes, they racked up billions of dollars in losses. Ford halted production of the electric F-150 Lightning late last year.

Ford says it has learned many lessons since then. Chief Executive Jim Farley has said those vehicles had more parts and costs than are necessary for EVs. The Fathom is designed with fewer components and will be assembled through a manufacturing process that has been overhauled to keep costs in check. He has called the truck Ford's new "Model T moment."

The projected sales target for 2027 illustrates the big bet Ford is making on an all-electric vehicle in a country where EV enthusiasm has waned, following policy changes by the Trump administration and Congress.

[...]

Ford executives say the Fathom's $30,000 price range will help it succeed where other EVs—which often cost $50,000 or more—didn't. The automaker also says its new assembly line for the EV will lower costs and increase efficiency.

[...]

Andrew Frick, president of Ford's electric- and gas-vehicle divisions, said in a recent interview that the company believes it will attract gas-powered and hybrid-vehicle owners to the Fathom.

There isn't a ton known about the Fathom right now — which is sort of hard to fathom for a car that's this important and this close to launch. But it'll apparently have more passenger room than the Toyota RAV4, Apple Maps built into the vehicle's navigation system and Ford's excellent BlueCruise Level 2 hands-free driver assist system. It'll also have in-bed power outlets, a possible mid-gate and a NACS charging plug.

I don't know if 100,000 sales is in the cards, but the Fathom does seem to be pretty damn cool for under 30 grand.

Uber is set to lay off nearly 3,300 employees, marking its largest job cuts since Covid, and the ride-share company says it's all being done in an effort to navigate the rise of robotaxis cutting in on its business. The cuts are meant to flatten management layers, and that will theoretically reduce organizational complexity that was built up while it experienced a period of rapid growth.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in a note to employees earlier this week that this complexity was providing a hurdle to decision-making. That must be really hard for him. From Reuters:

Unlike several tech executives, Khosrowshahi did not blame the cuts ​on AI even as a push to adopt the technology and the efficiencies it can unlock have driven large cuts in the industry this ​year, with tracking website layoffs.fyi putting the overall number at over 123,000 across nearly 390 companies.

"A leaner organization ⁠will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating. It will also generate savings that we intend ​to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years," Khosrowshahi said.

[...]

Some of the concern stems from reports of growing tension between Uber and Waymo, the biggest U.S. robotaxi operator, which runs ​its cars through Uber's app in Austin and Atlanta.

Waymo has also been expanding into new markets without Uber, while rivals such as Tesla double down on ‌robotaxis, feeding ⁠fears that a growing fleet of driverless cars could erode Uber's lucrative role as the middleman between vehicles and riders.

To defend its position, Uber plans to put more than $10 billion into robotaxis in the coming years, backing the companies developing autonomous-driving systems and positioning itself as a go-to marketplace for driverless rides.

[...]

As part of Wednesday's overhaul, Uber will reduce the number of employees positioned seven or more reporting layers below the ​CEO by 20% and cut the number of teams with only one or two direct reports ​by nearly half. It ⁠will also combine some teams and concentrate much of its staff presence around key hubs.

Uber is also limiting fully remote roles to about 1% of staff (boo), while also maintaining its three-day in-office policy. All in all, about 10% of its 34,000-strong workforce are losing their jobs.

Ford has agreed to pay $2.3 million and will do extensive anti-discrimination training as part of a settlement for a 2021 charge, investigated by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, that alleged racial and national origin harassment claims at its stamping plant in Buffalo, New York, that employees about 800 people and makes body panels for various vehicles. Here's what the EEOC found. From the Detroit Free Press:

In a media release, the federal agency said its investigation found reasonable cause to believe that Ford personnel at the plant subjected numerous employees to harassment and discrimination based on race and national origin.

The EEOC said during its investigation it found graffiti targeting Black employees and employees of various national origins, including Native American and Hispanic workers, scrawled in several employee areas throughout the plant, including bathrooms and break rooms.

[...]

"We appreciate Ford's cooperation throughout this process and the proactive steps taken to improve conditions at the facility during the investigation. Their willingness to engage constructively demonstrates a genuine commitment to fostering a workplace free of discrimination," Arlean Nieto, acting director of the EEOC's New York District, said in a statement.

Bryce Currie, chief manufacturing officer for Ford, visited the plant to meet with all shifts and outline the steps the automaker was taking.

"As soon as concerns were brought forward, we took action to improve accountability, strengthen employee support, and upgrade the workplace environment," Currie told the employees, according to a transcript of his speech at the plant that Ford provided exclusively to the Detroit Free Press. "Under new plant leadership, we enhanced on-site (human resource) resources and invested more than $3.5 million in facility and security improvements. Those investments included installing 326 high-definition cameras throughout the plant, applying specialized anti-graffiti coatings in restrooms, and implementing a strict rapid-response process to report and remove offensive material."

Now, Ford will pay $2.3 million in cash to eligible claimants, and it has agreed to post information explaining the anti-graffiti protocol, conduct regular training at the plant and report any discrimination complaints or graffiti at the facility over the next three years to the EEOC. It also took voluntary steps to upgrade surveillance, coat the restrooms with graffiti-repellent materials and is in the process of developing a "rigorous" graffiti reporting and removal protocol.

Tensions are rising between Volkswagen's management and the unions that build its cars as the automaker looks for ways to right itself. Now, attention is turning to the industry's 35-hour work week — the full-time standard for many production workers in Germany's metalworking industry that has stood since the '80s. From Reuters:

In Saxony, where Volkswagen's Zwickau plant is ​threatened with closure, state premier Michael Kretschmer said a 40-hour week should be seriously considered, and praised Mercedes-Benz, where management is ​pushing unions to agree to longer working hours for the same pay.

Kretschmer and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a fellow conservative, have both warned that the 35-hour week harms German competitiveness, although any change to labour contracts must be negotiated between unions and employers.

According ​to Oliver Wyman's Harbour Report, Germany has some of the highest automotive labour costs in the world, at about $3,307 ​per vehicle versus $955 in Spain and $597 in China. The authors say this is down to strong unions and labour regulations.

Using an example hourly labour cost of €65, auto industry analyst Ferdinand Dudenhoeffer calculates that increasing the standard working week to 40 hours for the same pay could reduce labour costs by some 13%, helping German auto plants maintain or even increase current production.

However, ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski said five more contractual working hours a week would not ​close the structural gap with ​low-cost industrial locations like China.

Volkswagen ⁠also has a demand problem, and this is not solved by working more, according to unions and some industry observers.

With Volkswagen currently in the process of removing around half a ​million vehicles' worth of excess annual capacity from its European network and considering the ​closure of four ⁠German plants, if anything workers would need to work less, they argue.

As you might have guessed, the unions aren't exactly on board with this idea. IG Metall has pushed back strongly. There is some precedent for cooperation, however. In 1994, an agreement was struck in between VW management and their unions that reduced pay in exchange for a 28.8-hour, four-day work week. It bought the automaker time to restructure and introduce leaner production methods, helping it ride out a sales slump that could have killed tens of thousands of jobs. Perhaps something like this is on the horizon once again.

The average price of a gallon of gas is on the rise once again, but that's not what we're concerned about today. As WTI Crude Oil futures and Brent Crude prices remain elevated — sitting at $92 and $97, respectively, at the time of publication — the price of diesel has quietly skyrocketed in recent weeks, far outpacing the price of gasoline. Today, the average price for a gallon of diesel is $5.78 — meaning it jumped a whopping 10 cents overnight. It's now just 3 cents away from breaking the all-time record high that was set back on June 19, 2022. Not good!

Anyway, here's where national average prices stand right now, according to AAA:

AAA

In terms of regular gas prices, those are up pretty significantly, too. The average price of a gallon of gas rose another 2 cents overnight to $4.14, according to AAA. After over a month of prices hovering around $4.10, this is certainly a bit of a cause for concern, and I wouldn't be too surprised if we start heading back toward the 2026 high of $4.56 we saw back in May.

text:
A plan by the Environmental Protection Agency could make it harder for the public to learn about and comment on proposed AI data centers that have sparked backlash in communities across the United States and transformed the midterm election landscape.

The EPA proposal would eliminate a federal requirement that states notify the public and seek comment before issuing air pollution permits for data centers and other industrial facilities. States could still offer opportunities for public comment, but the EPA would no longer mandate them as a condition for states to grant permits.

Critics say the move could thwart local residents from learning about proposed data centers or making their voices heard before projects are approved and construction begins. The move comes during a widespread backlash as tech giants build hundreds of massive server warehouses to fuel artificial intelligence and cloud computing.

“By eliminating the long-standing federal requirement for public notice, this proposal continues efforts by the Trump administration to turn its back on the fundamental EPA principle of transparency,” said Mike Koerber, a former deputy director of EPA’s air quality office.

If made final, the plan could create “an unlevel playing field where citizens in one state are kept completely in the dark about new data centers and heavy industrial emissions in their backyards, while neighboring states maintain oversight,” he said.

Under the EPA plan, states with weak or no requirements for public comment could speed permits for data centers, power plants and other pollution sources without consulting the public or even informing communities where the facilities are located, Koerber and other critics said.

Communities deserve a chance to weigh in, advocates say

“Data centers and other industrial sources should not be able to get their air pollution permits in secret,” said Keri Powell, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center, an advocacy organization that leads a coalition of nearly 200 environmental, health and community groups that filed comments with the EPA opposing the plan. “Communities deserve a chance to weigh in" before potentially harmful projects are approved.

An EPA spokesperson called that a false narrative.

“In our proposal we are saying that states get to pick how they want their permitting process to go for minor sources” of air pollution, spokesperson Carolyn Holran said.

The EPA proposal does not specifically identify data centers, she said, noting that the plan also would apply to laundromats, car repair shops and even landfills and steel mills that are considered “minor” pollution sources under the federal Clean Air Act.

The proposal does not demand that states make particular changes to their programs, nor does it alter federal emission standards or weaken environmental protections, Holran said. “Rather, the proposal simply aligns the national program with the Clean Air Act language to ensure that states are in the lead regarding their programs."

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, who has made U.S. leadership in AI a top agency priority, said in a statement that the plan is aimed at “cutting unnecessary and burdensome red tape, unleashing American energy and advancing cooperative federalism” with states. The EPA is expected to make the rule final next year.

President Donald Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both parties criticize them and many communities try to block them. Trump said on social media this week that U.S. communities that don’t have data centers will “end up being backwards and poor.”

Trump says data centers are crucial in the AI race against China

Trump has acknowledged that data centers need “a little public relations help” and has pushed tech companies to generate their own electricity to shield consumers from higher utility bills. The Republican president calls data centers critical to winning the AI race against China.

Environmental groups and other critics say the EPA proposal ignores the reality that many states, particularly in the South and Midwest, don't require public notice or hearings beyond those set by federal agencies. The federal plan would leave many communities in the dark before data centers show up in their backyards, they said.

“It’s beyond cruel for Trump’s EPA to silence front-line communities who bear the brunt of unhealthy air,” said Brandon Jones-Cobb, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, another environmental group.

The EPA “has already turned its back on science, cut enforcement against industrial polluters and eliminated life-saving air pollution measures," he said. “Now it wants to shut the public out of decisions to build or expand facilities that expose communities to dangerous air pollution, including data centers.”

Powell, whose organization focuses on six Southern states from Virginia to Alabama, said many states “only do what is required by federal law” when it comes to public notice of land-use projects and other environmental concerns.

"We rely on a minimum federal requirement to ensure we have environmental protections and a voice,'' she said in an interview, calling regulation of data centers a crucial issue in a region where the energy-hungry behemoths are proliferating. Virginia and Georgia are both among states with the highest concentration of current and proposed data centers.

Americans worry data centers could cause pollution, job losses

About 4 in 10 U.S. adults say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the environmental impacts of AI, according to a poll last year from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago. Americans are more likely to think that over the next decade, artificial intelligence will do more to hurt than help the environment, the economy and society as a whole, the poll found.

Besides powering AI and cloud computing, data centers are often sources of nitrogen oxide, which helps form ozone, as well as carbon monoxide and other air pollutants. Local communities also have expressed concerns about excessive water use and noise from data centers.

Many Americans worry that AI could increase economic disparities and cause widespread job losses.

Data center advocates stress that local taxes paid by the centers can help fund public schools, reducing the financial burden on homeowners.

Jane Williams, executive director of California Communities Against Toxics, said even if data centers ultimately are approved, "every community should be able to participate robustly in governmental decisions that can pollute our air.''

Rolling back the EPA rule “pulls a dark cloud, filled with soot and toxic chemicals, over communities’ right to know what polluting facilities are planned in their community,” she said.

authors: Lucy Valeski, Ken Ruinard, USA Today Network

text:
South Carolina utility regulators won’t review a natural gas plant being built for a data center, a unanimous decision some say could encourage future developers to come to build in the state.

The decision could lead to more data center developers coming to South Carolina without enough oversight, said Frank Holleman, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center.

“But as a practical matter, it’s putting out a welcome mat in South Carolina for large data centers who want to build power plants, and without any review at the state level of the impact of these plants on neighboring communities, the environment, our energy system.”

The Trump administration, political candidates and some state lawmakers have advocated for data centers to build their own power, rather than rely on public utilities, to avoid costing ratepayers.

Private power sources may create other issues, though, including air pollution, leading to questions over who in the state should oversee its developments. The Public Service Commission is tasked with reviewing new power generation and whether its necessity outweighs potential downsides of the project, like harm to the environment.

But for a Spartanburg data center’s 450 megawatt natural gas plant, built by Valara Holdings, the Public Service Commission decided it did not have a say, since the power would be generated by and for the developer alone.

The $2.8 billion data center development project is being built at 4000 Pine Street. It includes four proposed buildings, a power yard, internal roadways, a site access road, 45 natural gas-fuel generators, 11 natural gas turbines and electrical equipment houses, according to a permit description and applications.

A group of local residents in Spartanburg County and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy wanted the Public Service Commission to require Valara Holdings to seek and receive permission from the state regulators to continue.

Doing so would inform residents and regulators about the large project and “protect the public, air, and environment of the surrounding communities, Spartanburg County, and South Carolina,” attorneys from the Southern Environmental Law Center wrote in filings.

The PSC unanimously determined it did not need to investigate the natural gas plant because the power would be produced for and by a private company, matching the argument made by Valara’s attorneys. Valara Holdings is a subsidiary of NorthMark, and a spokesperson said in an email the company was pleased the PSC agreed with their position. A final order from the PSC is still pending.

The Office of Regulatory Staff, the state’s utility watchdog, disagreed. The “siting act is not limited solely to public utilities or to entities generating electricity for public use,” the state’s watchdog wrote in a letter to the PSC in July. While determining whether to grant any project a certificate, the Public Service Commission looks at its necessity against potential consequences, like negative impacts to the environment.

“The whole Siting Act, at least the way I view it, is it gives the commission this holistic view of what’s the impact on the state,” said Office of Regulatory Staff deputy director Ben Mustian during a hearing last month.

The Public Service Commission also decided only the Office of Regulatory Staff could “compel compliance” of the state’s siting law by hauling a private company to state court. That means environmental or citizen groups alone could not ask the PSC to rule on data center development, according to the PSC’s passed motion.

A spokesperson for ORS said the office would review the legality of future projects on a “case-by-case basis.”

“Once the Commission issues its formal order in this matter, ORS will review the decision and its potential impact on future generation projects,” ORS spokesperson Hank Page wrote in an email. “ORS also would look at those projects on a case-by-case basis to determine whether those projects will be constructed in compliance with the law, and whether to bring any enforcement actions likely would be dependent upon the specific facts associated with each individual project.”

State law requires the PSC to grant a “certificate of environmental compatibility and public convenience and necessity” to a “major utility facility,” or electric generation plants 75 megawatts or greater. But the PSC determined their authority did not extend to Valara, a private company.

Holleman said because the natural gas plants can have an impact on the environment and surrounding communities, a statewide entity should determine where the infrastructure is sited. Holleman represented the Spartanburg residents.

“That’s why it’s called a siting act,” Holleman said. “And [it’s] not just left to the desires of an equity firm from New York or somebody from Chicago or Europe or Asia or wherever who decides they want to buy property and put a facility, a data center, and a big power plant somewhere.”

But in an editorial published by the Post and Courier, state Rep. Brandon Newton, R-Lancaster, a House Republican leader, argued the siting law was not intended for private businesses generating power for themselves. Newton did not respond to a call requesting more information about his position.

The Valara Holdings data center, and the Public Service Commission’s decision over whether to scrutinize the project, garnered significant public interest and concern. 46 individuals or couples, all unaffiliated with an organization and many with a Spartanburg address, filed letters of protest on the petition’s docket. During a meeting on the issue, Commissioner Justin Williams said the last time so many people were present in the Columbia hearing room was “the merger and abandonment hearing for Dominion Energy and SCE&G back in 2018.”

The public outcry isn’t unique to Spartanburg County. Residents and local governments across South Carolina and the country have pushed back against rapid data center development, often citing concerns that the infrastructure needed to power AI and other digital services could use too much water, raise power bills or lead to noise pollution in rural communities.

This week, President Donald Trump criticized communities protesting data center development, saying “you will only have yourselves to blame” if the U.S. “kills the Golden Goose.”

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote on TruthSocial. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

Other Valara data center permits

The Spartanburg data center and its natural gas generation has applied for other permits, including two environmental and development, which also offer chances for public participation.

Valara has applied for synthetic minor air construction permits with the Department of Environmental Services, one of which has been approved, and land development permits with Spartanburg County. It’s expected to ask for another air quality permit once construction is completed, according to a draft application.

The generators and turbines will emit pollutants, including particulate matter, carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxide, according to a state Department of Environmental Services fact sheet.

Valara also asked for two minor permits for their project rather than a major development permit, which opponents of the project say helps the data center evade public participation. The land development permits are the subject of a pending lawsuit brought by the same group of Spartanburg County residents.

South Carolina lacks any statewide standards for data centers. Lawmakers put up several bills placing guardrails on data centers, but they did not gain traction this year. A one-year water reporting requirement for data centers passed in the state’s budget.

name: EPA
title: Truck drivers flag flaws in EPA emission fix - Land Line Media
description:
The Environmental Protection Agency published a proposed rule in July to revise a 2023 truck-emission rule.
The Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association welcomed the removal of limp mode but warns that other changes favor manufacturers at the expense of truck drivers.
In comments to the EPA, OOIDA noted that its members face various issues affecting their business.
The Association says shorter warranties are “simply a cost-cutting measure” at the expense of small-business truck drivers.
One major issue for truck drivers is the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) system.
text:
The federal government is quickly revising truck-emission rules set for later this year, but truck drivers say parts of the facelift are more like lipstick on a pig.

The Environmental Protection Agency published a proposed rule in July to revise a 2023 truck-emission rule. While there are numerous changes involved, a few caught the attention of truck drivers:

Replacing “limp mode” with audible and visual warnings

Cutting manufacturer warranties for emission issues

Delaying longer useful life of a truck engine

Reactions were mixed. The Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association welcomed the removal of limp mode but warns that other changes favor manufacturers at the expense of truck drivers.

Who pays for repairs?

OOIDA’s biggest concern is the reduction of warranties that protect owner-operators from faulty equipment.

Under the 2023 truck-emission rule, emission-related warranties were to extend from 5 years/100,000 miles to 10 years/450,000 miles for model year 2027 and newer trucks. The proposed rule keeps the 5-year/100,000-mile requirement.

In comments to the EPA, OOIDA noted that its members face various issues affecting their business. These include expensive visits to dealers, lost productivity, poor efficiency and towing costs.

“Any emissions rule should ensure that drivers and carriers who are purchasing new equipment are getting a fair deal and will not be constantly sidelined from their profession due to costly and repeated breakdowns,” OOIDA President Todd Spencer wrote in comments.

In explaining the warranty reduction, the EPA says it will ensure robust truck emission control technologies. However, OOIDA argues this will discourage manufacturers from making reliable equipment. The Association says shorter warranties are “simply a cost-cutting measure” at the expense of small-business truck drivers.

“A 100,000-mile warranty may be suitable for fleets with hundreds or thousands of trucks that are constantly purchasing new vehicles, but does not provide the necessary protection for small-business truckers that are making a long-term investment in their equipment,” OOIDA wrote. “Larger fleets also have the luxury of dedicated personnel, documentation systems and warranty-management processes to identify eligible repairs and recover warranty costs.”

Truck drivers are not guinea pigs

OOIDA also raised concerns about how long equipment must remain compliant, also known as “useful life.”

The 2023 truck-emission rule would extend the useful life of model year 2027 and newer trucks from 435,000 miles to 650,000 miles. Regulatory useful life is the period during which an engine must continue meeting applicable truck-emission standards.

EPA now proposes keeping the 435,000-mile requirement through model year 2029 and implementing the longer period beginning in model year 2030.

Extending useful life aims to make engines more durable over time and to hold manufacturers accountable. In reverting to shorter useful life, the EPA says it gives manufacturers “more time to evaluate their new technologies in the real world and more confidence in the in-use durability over the longer useful life periods.”

OOIDA believes this approach turns truck drivers into test drivers.

“Under this reasoning, OEMs can sit back and see if their engines perform while truckers will be left on the side of the road if and when the engines fail during this ‘real world’ testing phase,” the Association stated in comments.

No derate a win for truckers

Not all changes the EPA proposes are negative.

One major issue for truck drivers is the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) system. If sensors detect DEF issues, trucks can be forced to crawl.

Instead of going into limp mode, drivers will hear a 90-second warning for bad, low or no DEF. A visual alert will inform the driver of the problem. Trucks will continue operating normally, although manufacturers could still derate engines to prevent catastrophic damage.

OOIDA fully supports these changes.

“An audible warning system would allow drivers to properly address DEF problems in a safe manner without having to drastically reduce speeds, miss deliveries or be sidelined for days/weeks at a time,” OOIDA said.

What’s next?

With the comment period over, a revised truck-emission final rule could be coming, but time is running out.

According to the docket, more than 13,500 comments were received, which EPA will have to review. Before publishing a final rule, the agency will have to send a draft to the White House Office of Management and Budget for review.

name: Louisiana American Energy
title: Op-Ed: On Labor Day, remember who builds this country and what fuels their work | Opinion
authors: Jim Welty and Jeff Nobers, Jim Welty, Jeff Nobers
description:
Our Commonwealth is the nation’s second-largest natural gas producer, sitting atop one of the world’s most prolific shale formations.
Meanwhile, the Northeast Supply Enhancement pipeline project is moving forward to deliver more Pennsylvania natural gas to consumers across the Northeast.
Taken together, these projects tell a story that goes well beyond natural gas.
The relationship between the natural gas industry and the skilled trades matters because our interests are fundamentally aligned.
We are rebuilding our energy infrastructure and strengthening domestic supply chains.
text:
Labor Day is a celebration of the people who build America.

They are the workers who wake before dawn, put on a hard hat and steel-toed boots, and head to a job site. They build the roads we drive on, the buildings where we work, the power plants that keep the lights on and the pipelines that deliver the energy that makes modern life possible.

But workers need something to build.

Right now, America has a tremendous opportunity to put both its resources and its workers to work. After years of delays and uncertainty surrounding critical infrastructure, the country is confronting the need to build more power generation, pipelines, manufacturing capacity and other infrastructure needed to support a growing economy. At the same time, Americans want good-paying jobs that allow families to build a future here at home.

Pennsylvania sits at the center of that moment.

Our Commonwealth is the nation’s second-largest natural gas producer, sitting atop one of the world’s most prolific shale formations. That resource is becoming the foundation for a new wave of American construction, manufacturing and power generation.

Importantly, it’s also creating opportunities for the people who build these projects.

Consider Homer City, once Pennsylvania’s largest coal-fired power plant. Today, that site is being transformed into a massive natural gas-powered energy and technology campus. More than 1,300 skilled workers are now on site, with the project expected to support more than 10,000 direct jobs over the course of the construction.

Those numbers represent paychecks. They represent apprentices getting hours and hands on training. They represent union members putting their skills to work. They represent families supported by a project that will help power the next generation of American industry.

And Homer City is far from alone.

In Beaver County, plans to transform the former Bruce Mansfield coal plant site into a natural gas power facility is expected to generate thousands of construction jobs and hundreds of permanent positions.

Meanwhile, the Northeast Supply Enhancement pipeline project is moving forward to deliver more Pennsylvania natural gas to consumers across the Northeast. The project is expected to create roughly 2,000 jobs – a majority of which will be performed by union tradespeople.

Taken together, these projects tell a story that goes well beyond natural gas. They tell the story of an America that is beginning to build again.

Electricity demand is growing rapidly as advanced technology and manufacturing transform our economy. And we cannot afford to become dependent on foreign energy or allow critical infrastructure to fall behind.

The answer is not choosing between energy and workers. The answer is putting American energy and American workers on the same team.

Pennsylvania has an extraordinary advantage. We have the natural gas. We have the industrial sites. We have the infrastructure. And we have a highly skilled workforce with generations of experience building the energy systems that power this country.

What we need is the opportunity to put those resources to work.

The relationship between the natural gas industry and the skilled trades matters because our interests are fundamentally aligned.

And beyond the jobs, there is another benefit for Pennsylvania families: abundant natural gas helps keep energy affordable. Pennsylvania households and businesses have saved billions of dollars because of the availability of domestic natural gas.

So this Labor Day, let’s honor the people who show up to work, and support the their opportunity to work for decades to come.

America is bringing manufacturing home. We are investing in artificial intelligence and advanced technology. We are rebuilding our energy infrastructure and strengthening domestic supply chains.

We are fortunate to have the best workers in the world, let’s make sure we give them the opportunity to put their skills and know how to work building it.

Jim Welty is President of the Marcellus Shale Coalition. Jeff Nobers is Executive Director of the Builders Guild of Western Pennsylvania and Pittsburgh Works Together.

Cllr Marc Macrae, Chair of Moray Council's Economic Development and Infrastructure Committee, said: “This is a very welcome investment in Moray's future.

text:
The funding will support two key projects that form part of Moray's wider Just Transition programme.

A total of £900,000 has been awarded for Buckie Harbour Redevelopment enabling works, helping to progress plans that could strengthen Moray's role in the marine and offshore energy sector. The funding will support technical studies, design development, environmental assessments and business case preparation required for the harbour's future expansion.

A further £300,000 has been awarded towards the Green Energy Parks project, which is being led by Crown Estate Scotland with Moray Council as a partner. The project will explore opportunities at strategic sites including Mosstodloch and Dallachy Airfield, helping to unlock future investment, job creation and clean energy development.

The successful funding bid was developed by Moray Council in collaboration with partner organisations as part of a long-term programme of projects designed to ensure Moray benefits from Scotland's transition to net zero.

Cllr Marc Macrae, Chair of Moray Council's Economic Development and Infrastructure Committee, said: “This is a very welcome investment in Moray's future. The funding will help us develop projects with the potential to create economic opportunities, support jobs and strengthen our communities as we move towards a low-carbon economy.

“Buckie Harbour is a strategically important asset for Moray, while the Green Energy Parks project has the potential to attract future investment and support growth in emerging industries. This award is recognition of the strength of the partnership working that has taken place across Moray and demonstrates our commitment to ensuring the area benefits from a just transition.”

Annie Breadon, Crown Estate Scotland, Interim Director of Corporate Operations, commented: “We believe that strategic sites across Moray have the potential – as Green Energy Parks – to become valuable contributors to the regional economy, supporting skilled employment, renewable energy and sustainable communities in the future.

“In order to reach that potential, they will need new infrastructure investment around them – and these funds will help to unlock it.”

text:
New Hampshire residents need to pay very close attention to this—especially to what is already happening in Claremont.

Jabil/Mikros Technologies is directly involved in the AI data-center industry right here in New Hampshire. This isn't speculation. Jabil announced its 2024 acquisition under the headline: “Jabil Acquires Mikros Technologies to Support Demand for Liquid Cooling in AI Data Centers.” Jabil said the acquisition would help “enable the growth of AI infrastructure.”

Mikros now describes its role within Jabil as extending from chip-level cooling through rack- and facility-scale data-center deployments, with new-product development occurring at its New Hampshire R&D operation.

Then on August 26, Drew Matter appeared before the Claremont City Council and presented Mikros/Jabil technology involving DATA CENTERS, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, HIGH-PERFORMANCE COMPUTING and HYPERSCALE applications. The presentation included high-powered data-center network-switch cooling and microchannel liquid-cooling technology using water.

Drew also discussed Creare and Mikros's origins, Gov. Kelly Ayotte and her visit to Mikros, and the data-center conversation.

So my question remains:

Why was an AI/data-center infrastructure company giving this presentation to Claremont's governing body?

Who requested it? What communications preceded it? What expansion is contemplated? Have there been discussions involving Eversource, electrical capacity, water/wastewater, Ashley's Landing, River Road, infrastructure, land or economic incentives?

Casella Waste Systems, Inc., headquartered in Rutland, Vermont, provides resource management expertise and services to residential, commercial, municipal, institutional and industrial customers, primarily in the areas of solid waste collection and disposal, transfer, recycling and organics services in the eastern United States.
About Waga Energy Waga Energy produces competitively priced Renewable Natural Gas (RNG, also known as biomethane) by upgrading landfill gas using a patented purification technology called WAGABOX®.
To date, Waga Energy has 19 RNG production units under construction worldwide.
Each project initiated by Waga Energy contributes to the fight against global warming and helps the energy transition.
Waga Energy is listed on Euronext Paris (FR0012532810 – EPA: WAGA).
text:
Vermont Business Magazine Vermont-based Casella Waste Systems, Inc, a regional solid waste, recycling and resource management services company in the Eastern United States, and Waga Energy, a global expert in the production of Renewable Natural Gas from landfills, announced the start of operations of the RNG production facility at the McKean Landfill in Mount Jewett, Pennsylvania.

The McKean facility is the third to come online this year, following the successful commissioning of facilities at the Chemung County Landfill(link is external) and the Hyland Landfill(link is external). Together, the three projects complete the partnership agreement signed in 2023(link is external).

“Bringing this facility online at our McKean landfill is another important step in our efforts to recover more value from the materials we manage,” said Ned Coletta, President and CEO of Casella Waste Systems, Inc. “Our partnership with Waga Energy has always been focused on collaborating to leverage each other’s strengths, and it’s extremely gratifying to see the third facility come online and producing as anticipated.”

The facility uses Waga Energy's patented WAGABOX® technology to upgrade landfill gas into pipeline-quality RNG. With 2,000 SCFM of installed processing capacity, McKean can generate up to 407,000 MMBtu (120 GWh) of renewable gas annually. Production will ramp up progressively as landfill gas volumes increase at the site.

“The commissioning of the McKean WAGABOX unit is a strong testament to the commitment and execution capabilities of the Casella and Waga Energy teams,” said Guénaël Prince, Chief Executive Officer of Waga Energy Inc. “This project also demonstrates the strength of a partnership model that creates long-term value for both partners by transforming landfill gas into a reliable source of renewable energy.”

The RNG produced on-site is injected directly into the National Fuel Gas network, supplying the region with a renewable alternative to fossil natural gas. The project is expected to avoid 31,000 tons of CO₂-equivalent emissions each year, according to U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards.

Under the terms of the agreement, Waga Energy fully funded the construction of each facility and will own and operate each of them for 20 years, while Casella and Waga Energy share the revenue generated from RNG sales.

About Casella Waste Systems, Inc.

Casella Waste Systems, Inc., headquartered in Rutland, Vermont, provides resource management expertise and services to residential, commercial, municipal, institutional and industrial customers, primarily in the areas of solid waste collection and disposal, transfer, recycling and organics services in the eastern United States. For more information, visit www.casella.com(link is external).

About Waga Energy

Waga Energy produces competitively priced Renewable Natural Gas (RNG, also known as biomethane) by upgrading landfill gas using a patented purification technology called WAGABOX®. The RNG produced is injected directly into the gas grids that supply individuals and businesses, providing a substitute for natural fossil gas. Waga Energy currently operates 36 RNG production units in France, Spain, Canada and the USA, representing an installed capacity of more than 6.5 million MMBtu (1.9 TWh) per year. To date, Waga Energy has 19 RNG production units under construction worldwide. Each project initiated by Waga Energy contributes to the fight against global warming and helps the energy transition. Waga Energy is listed on Euronext Paris (FR0012532810 – EPA: WAGA).

name: American Energy
title: How low should it go? Maryland regulators weigh energy efficiency program cuts
description:
Maryland’s electric utilities submitted proposals Tuesday to reduce the size of EmPOWER Maryland, the state’s signature energy efficiency program, changes that could save residential customers up to $9 a month on their electric bills starting in January.
Now, regulators at the Maryland Public Service Commission are deciding how dramatically to cut the EmPOWER program.
Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative customers, meanwhile, would see a monthly decrease of 22 cents or $1.53.
BGE’s lower-budget scenario would end a few EmPOWER initiatives, including an appliance recycling program and a budget for experimental energy efficiency pilot programs, said Jessica Yu, a senior manager of BGE’s energy efficiency portfolio.
But a coalition of advocates, the Maryland Energy Efficiency Advocates, have appealed that decision, arguing that the two models approved by the commission wouldn’t meet the legislature’s goal.
text:
Maryland’s electric utilities submitted proposals Tuesday to reduce the size of EmPOWER Maryland, the state’s signature energy efficiency program, changes that could save residential customers up to $9 a month on their electric bills starting in January.

The proposals follow a temporary reduction of the program by lawmakers earlier this year to offset high electric bills, amid pressure on the grid from data centers, retiring power plants and more.

Now, regulators at the Maryland Public Service Commission are deciding how dramatically to cut the EmPOWER program. The commission in July asked asked each utility that offers EmPOWER to submit two options: a more aggressive cut to the program and a less aggressive one.

At Exelon, which owns Baltimore Gas & Electric, Pepco and Delmarva Power, officials said they’re hoping to see the commission approve the deeper set of cuts.

“Given where our customers are in terms of their bills, I think the most important thing that we can do is offer some relief — and we think that’s in line with the legislative intent,” said Lindsay North, director of strategy at Pepco and Delmarva Power.

But those cuts would come as Maryland’s Exelon utilities are proposing rate increases that may make any EmPOWER savings less noticeable.

Baltimore Gas & Electric in July put forward what it called a “bare bones” rate increase request that would raise the average residential customers’ monthly bill by $8, if approved by the PSC. Regulators recently cut a Pepco rate increase request in half, but Pepco customers will see, on average, a $3.94 increase in their monthly bills, the commission ssid.

And consumer advocates and environmental groups have warned that short-term cuts to the EmPOWER program would increase bills in the long run, as homes and businesses that are less energy efficient place greater strain on the electric grid. That would add costs to consumers and ultimately require new infrastructure such as substations and power plants.

“It’s really just shifting those costs into the future,” said Mike Specian, a senior research manager at the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy. “Because if you’re not going to pay for energy efficiency now, you’re going to have to pay for additional generation later.”

Utility proposals differ

Under the plans submitted Tuesday, Potomac Edison’s residential customers in Western Maryland could see the biggest EmPOWER Maryland surcharge drop on their monthly bills. Its two proposals would cut either $8.79 or $8.06 per month compared to this year. (Some of that decline is because the company over-collected EmPOWER funds in 2026, said spokesman Will Boye.)

Delmarva Power’s residential customers could see a similar decline — either $7.86 or $8.39 a month — according to its plan. At BGE and Pepco, the monthly decrease would be more like $6 to $7.50.

Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative customers, meanwhile, would see a monthly decrease of 22 cents or $1.53. In total, the EmPOWER program would cost those customers $14 to $16 each month in 2027.

North, of Pepco and Delmarva Power, said she’s hoping customers don’t feel the effects of a shrunken program. She said the goal was to trim programs that customers are using less, and keep the most popular programs, offering similar-sized rebates as in years’ past — but fewer in number.

“I don’t know that our customers are going to notice that much of a difference,” North said. “It’ll be the same impactful EmPOWER where they [can] participate in the majority of programs that they know, or their neighbors have done.”

EmPOWER, which began in 2009, offers consumers free and reduced price energy efficiency services, including home energy audits, insulation and weatherization, HVAC upgrades, smart thermostats and more.

Under their plans for 2027, the Exelon companies plan to continue offering free “quick home energy checks,” which are considered a “gateway” to EmPOWER programs, wherein an energy efficiency professional visits a customer’s home and identifies possible improvements, installing LED light bulbs and weather stripping along the way.

But fewer rebates will be available. Homeowners seeking rebates for new HVAC equipment and other upgrades could encounter exhausted budgets if they apply too late, North said.

“The contractor who is running or helping to support that program would know when those budgets are getting close to being spent, and so they’d probably encourage the customer to get those applications in and sign up sooner so that they get those rebates and those incentive dollars before the budgets run out,” North said.

Some EmPOWER programs could end entirely. BGE’s lower-budget scenario would end a few EmPOWER initiatives, including an appliance recycling program and a budget for experimental energy efficiency pilot programs, said Jessica Yu, a senior manager of BGE’s energy efficiency portfolio.

The company believes the temporary cuts won’t be “too detrimental” to the state’s long-term energy demand.

“Like the appliance recycling program — that’s not really impacting peak demand,” Yu said. “We are taking the resources and budget that were used towards that program and actually shifting it towards the programs that provide the biggest reduction in peak demand.”

BGE has also proposed adding new resources for customers, including a dedicated staff member to help people who in multifamily dwellings, such as apartments and condos, access EmPOWER programming where eligible. The company also plans to better target marketing dollars for EmPOWER, Yu said, sending information to customers most likely to use it.

“In the past, because of how ambitious the goals were and because they were climbing at the degree that they were climbing at, it required us to basically have to throw everything at the wall to get as much GHG [greenhouse gas] savings as possible. Now that there’s a little bit more breathing room, we’re really able to focus and optimize our portfolio,” Yu said.

Maryland geothermal energy program faces delays amid cost concerns

Disputes over emissions goals

When the General Assembly decided to cut EmPOWER in this year’s Utility RELIEF Act, they did so by trimming the greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals associated with the program. The goals will decline in 2027, and then begin increasing again in 2029, reaching today’s goals by 2033.

But the legislature also allowed utilities to count solar energy in their territories toward their goals, effectively reducing the size of the EmPOWER program further — and adding some complexity to the calculations.

The utilities proposed a formula that would cut EmPOWER more drastically, said Specian, of ACEEE.

“The utilities took advantage of the RELIEF Act,” Specian said. “In my opinion, they used it as an excuse to try to lower the size of the program even further. But in doing so, it violates the law.”

ACEEE proposed its own formula, as did the PSC staff. Amid the disagreement, the commission asked the utilities to produce two plans for their EmPOWER budgets — one following the utility model and the other from the commission.

But a coalition of advocates, the Maryland Energy Efficiency Advocates, have appealed that decision, arguing that the two models approved by the commission wouldn’t meet the legislature’s goal. The advocates argue that the utility model would result in nearly $40 million less net benefit to utility customers, and the model from the commission’s staff would result in $13 million less net benefit.

The commission is accepting comment on the rehearing request, and has not made a decision.

name: EPA
title: EPA proposal could leave public in the dark on data center plans - KCRA
description:
Critics say the move could thwart local residents from learning about proposed data centers or making their voices heard before projects are approved and construction begins.
The Republican president calls data centers critical to winning the AI race against China.
The federal plan would leave many communities in the dark before data centers show up in their backyards, they said.
The EPA “has already turned its back on science, cut enforcement against industrial polluters and eliminated lifesaving air pollution measures," he said.
Virginia and Georgia are both among states with the highest concentration of current and proposed data centers.
text:
WASHINGTON —

A plan by the Environmental Protection Agency could make it harder for the public to learn about and comment on proposed artificial intelligence data centers that have sparked backlash in communities across the United States and transformed the midterm election landscape.

Related video above: Nearly half of U.S. children live in counties with failing air quality, report says

The EPA proposal would eliminate a federal requirement that states notify the public and seek comment before issuing air pollution permits for data centers and other industrial facilities. States could still offer opportunities for public comment, but the EPA would no longer mandate them as a condition for states to grant permits.

Critics say the move could thwart local residents from learning about proposed data centers or making their voices heard before projects are approved and construction begins. The move comes during a widespread backlash as tech giants build hundreds of massive server warehouses to fuel artificial intelligence and cloud computing.

“By eliminating the long-standing federal requirement for public notice, this proposal continues efforts by the Trump administration to turn its back on the fundamental EPA principle of transparency,” said Mike Koerber, a former deputy director of EPA’s air quality office.

If made final, the plan could create “an unlevel playing field where citizens in one state are kept completely in the dark about new data centers and heavy industrial emissions in their backyards, while neighboring states maintain oversight,” he said.

Under the EPA plan, states with weak or no requirements for public comment could speed permits for data centers, power plants and other pollution sources without consulting the public or even informing communities where the facilities are located, Koerber and other critics said.

Communities deserve a chance to weigh in, advocates say

“Data centers and other industrial sources should not be able to get their air pollution permits in secret,” said Keri Powell, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center, an advocacy organization that leads a coalition of nearly 200 environmental, health and community groups that filed comments with the EPA opposing the plan. “Communities deserve a chance to weigh in" before potentially harmful projects are approved.

An EPA spokesperson called that a false narrative.

“In our proposal we are saying that states get to pick how they want their permitting process to go for minor sources” of air pollution, spokesperson Carolyn Holran said.

The EPA proposal does not specifically identify data centers, she said, noting that the plan also would apply to laundromats, car repair shops, and even landfills and steel mills that are considered “minor” pollution sources under the federal Clean Air Act.

The proposal does not demand that states make particular changes to their programs, nor does it alter federal emission standards or weaken environmental protections, Holran said. “Rather, the proposal simply aligns the national program with the Clean Air Act language to ensure that states are in the lead regarding their programs."

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, who has made U.S. leadership in AI a top agency priority, said in a statement that the plan is aimed at “cutting unnecessary and burdensome red tape, unleashing American energy and advancing cooperative federalism” with states. The EPA is expected to make the rule final next year.

President Donald Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both parties criticize them and many communities try to block them. Trump said on social media this week that U.S. communities that don’t have data centers will “end up being backwards and poor.”

Trump says data centers are crucial in the AI race against China

Trump has acknowledged that data centers need “a little public relations help” and has pushed tech companies to generate their own electricity to shield consumers from higher utility bills. The Republican president calls data centers critical to winning the AI race against China.

Environmental groups and other critics say the EPA proposal ignores the reality that many states, particularly in the South and Midwest, do not require public notice or hearings beyond those set by federal agencies. The federal plan would leave many communities in the dark before data centers show up in their backyards, they said.

“It’s beyond cruel for Trump’s EPA to silence front-line communities who bear the brunt of unhealthy air,” said Brandon Jones-Cobb, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, another environmental group.

The EPA “has already turned its back on science, cut enforcement against industrial polluters and eliminated lifesaving air pollution measures," he said. “Now it wants to shut the public out of decisions to build or expand facilities that expose communities to dangerous air pollution, including data centers.”

Powell, whose organization focuses on six southern states from Virginia to Alabama, said many states “only do what is required by federal law” when it comes to public notice of land-use projects and other environmental concerns.

"We rely on a minimum federal requirement to ensure we have environmental protections and a voice," she said in an interview, calling regulation of data centers a crucial issue in a region where the energy-hungry behemoths are proliferating. Virginia and Georgia are both among states with the highest concentration of current and proposed data centers.

Americans worry data centers could cause pollution, job losses

About 4 in 10 U.S. adults say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the environmental impacts of AI, according to a poll last year from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago. Americans are more likely to think that over the next decade, artificial intelligence will do more to hurt than help the environment, the economy and society as a whole, the poll found.

Besides powering AI and cloud computing, data centers are often sources of nitrogen oxide, which helps form ozone, as well as carbon monoxide and other air pollutants. Local communities also have expressed concerns about excessive water use and noise from data centers.

Many Americans worry that AI could increase economic disparities and cause widespread job losses.

Data center advocates stress that local taxes paid by the centers can help fund public schools, reducing the financial burden on homeowners.

Jane Williams, executive director of California Communities Against Toxics, said even if data centers ultimately are approved, "every community should be able to participate robustly in governmental decisions that can pollute our air.''

Rolling back the EPA rule “pulls a dark cloud, filled with soot and toxic chemicals, over communities’ right to know what polluting facilities are planned in their community,” she said.

text:
The 2026 Battery Show is coming to Detroit from October 12th to 15th – and you don’t want to miss it.

The battery and EV industry is moving faster than ever — and staying ahead means having the right knowledge, the right connections, and the right strategies. The Battery Show Detroit 2026 delivers all three.

Join 16,000+ engineers, executives, and innovators at Huntington Place - Detroit for four days of hands-on learning, strategic networking, and direct access to the technologies shaping the future of batteries and EVs. With 1,300+ exhibitors, 250+ expert speakers, and 140+ hours of education, every moment is designed to move your business forward.

5 Reasons to Attend

A hands-on workshop on Monday kicks off this event, and then attendees will dive into three full days of conference programming (Tuesday–Thursday) featuring expert-led sessions spanning advanced battery design, manufacturing, safety, recycling, market strategy, and more.

Workshop

Monday, Oct. 12 | 9 a.m.-4 p.m.

Expo

Tuesday, Oct. 13| 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m.

Wednesday, Oct. 14 | 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m.

Thursday, Oct. 15 | 9:30 a.m.-3 p.m.

Conference

Tuesday, Oct. 13 | 9 a.m.-4:30 p.m.

Wednesday, Oct. 14 | 9 a.m.-4:30 p.m.

Thursday, Oct. 15 | 9 a.m.-3 p.m.

The conference includes five Tracks, each focusing on major components of the battery industry to address the battery and EV industry’s most urgent challenges and opportunities. The Tracks are:

Track A: Battery Development

Innovations in chemistries, intelligence, and safety to power the next generation, covering:

Track B: Battery In-Use

Solutions for supply chain resilience, efficient manufacturing, and recycling, covering:

Track C: EV Development

Insights into investments, regulations, and global competition, covering:

Track D: EV In-Use

Design, infrastructure, and consumer adoption shaping EV & HEV growth.

Track E: Emerging Applications

Expanding electrification into storage, heavy-duty, and aviation markets.

“The Battery Show North America is where this industry’s most important issues are addressed. ‘What’s the best way to compete globally?’ ‘What do the U.S. administration’s tariffs and the Iraq war mean for electric-vehicle and energy-storage-system suppliers?’ ‘Which alternative battery chemistries are closest to full production?’ These and other questions are posed by people whose livelihoods depend on getting answers and are debated by experienced global experts armed with data,” notes Battery Technology Editor-in-Chief Michael Anderson.

“At the same time, the exhibit halls feature booth after booth of new and eye-opening technologies shown by developers from around the world. There is nothing else like it.”

Keynote Sessions

Here are just some of the keynotes and roundtables at this year's Battery Show. Each one presents an opportunity to learn from some of the best leaders in the industry. Visit the website listed below for the full list of keynote sessions.

Tuesday, Oct. 13

Industrial Strategy, Capital Allocation & Scaling the Battery Supply Chain

9:30-10:30 a.m.

This roundtable brings together senior executives from across the battery ecosystem to examine the industrial strategies and investment decisions shaping the next phase of North American battery growth. Panelists will explore manufacturing economics, capital allocation, critical materials and supply chain resilience, evolving demand, technology investment, and the role of public and private capital in accelerating domestic production.

The Next Chapter of Battery Materials: Building a Competitive and Resilient North American Supply Chain

10:30-11 a.m.

Venkatesh Vasudevan, vice president – Graphite Materials at ExxonMobil Product Solutions

This keynote will examine the evolving battery materials landscape and what it will take to build a resilient and globally competitive North American supply chain. The discussion will explore the challenges of scaling domestic production, navigating global supply dependencies, meeting cell manufacturer and OEM requirements, and creating the industrial infrastructure needed to support long-term battery growth

Wednesday, Oct. 14

Energy Storage at an Inflection Point: Scaling for the Next Era of Power Demand

9-10 a.m.

This roundtable brings together leaders from across the energy storage ecosystem to examine what it will take to meet the next era of power demand. Panelists will explore the evolving role of lithium-ion alongside emerging technologies such as sodium-ion and long-duration storage, the challenges of scaling manufacturing and deployment in North America, and more.

Thursday, Oct.15

The Next Battery Era — Technology, Markets & Commercialization

9:15-10:15 a.m.

This roundtable includes senior executives and technology leaders from across the battery ecosystem to examine the innovations positioned to define the next era of the industry and what it will take to move them from development to commercialization. Panelists will discuss technology readiness and scale-up, evolving customer and application requirements, manufacturing economics, investment priorities, and the growing need for application-specific battery solutions across automotive, energy storage, and emerging mobility markets.

Expo

There will be more than 1,300 exhibitors at the show, covering the entire battery and EV supply chain. This is where real decisions are made. In just a few days, attendees can evaluate cutting-edge technologies, compare suppliers side by side, and walk away with the connections and insights that would take months to replicate anywhere else.

From advanced battery cells and pack assembly to materials, testing, and charging infrastructure — everything shaping the future of electrification is here, live and in action. This is your opportunity to see what's next before your competitors do.\\

Innovation in Action

See breakthrough technologies up close with live, 15-minute product demos happening right at exhibitor booths. The New Product Showcase gives you a front-row seat to the latest advancements in batteries, components, testing equipment, and EV systems — all presented by the engineers and experts behind them.

text:
Published on September 03, 2026

At a special meeting on September 2, 2026, the Arlington County Board voted to formally intervene in the State Corporation Commission (SCC) proceeding related to the acquisition of Dominion Energy Inc., by NextEra. The Board will file a notice of participation as a respondent, enabling the County to actively represent Arlington’s interests as this landmark merger moves through the regulatory review process.

“NextEra’s proposed acquisition of control of Dominion Energy carries significant implications for Arlington County residents, businesses, and municipal operations,” said Board Chair Matt de Ferranti. “Residents are already seeing increasing energy bills. I believe we must intervene to protect our resident ratepayers, prioritize affordability, and advance the County clean energy commitments.”

"It is our responsibility to protect and fight for the interests of Arlington and our residents,” said Vice-Chair Maureen Coffey. “The only way for us to do this in this case—which, if approved, would shape energy in Arlington for generations to come—is by being party to the proceedings. It is imperative that we remain active and engaged over the coming months.”

“Any merger cannot jeopardize Arlington’s climate and energy commitments, including becoming a carbon neutral community by 2050,” said Board member Susan Cunningham. “From already 100% renewable electricity County facilities to last year’s Climate Action Resolution and our current Climate Action Plan development, our vision for a greener and cleaner Arlington is non-negotiable. Getting the details of any merger right will be crucial to continuing this progress.”

“The bottom-line for me is affordability, and homeowners and renters alike have already seen their electric rates go up,” said Board member Julius D. “JD” Spain, Sr. “Failure to act in this historic moment is not an option, and runs counter to the core values that I believe are fundamental to being a public servant. I am deeply proud to say that this Board is not beholden to any Utility interest and is centering this decision squarely on the needs and goals of our community.”

"We act on behalf of our residents, but the truth is that all Virginians are in the same boat here,” said Board member Karantonis. “This merger needs to be significantly modified to meet the wide-ranging climate and energy goals we as localities have been working toward and to address the deep affordability challenges that families face every day.”

Background of the Merger

On July 15, 2026, NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy filed a joint petition with the SCC seeking approval for a merger. If approved, this $67 billion buyout would represent the largest energy merger in the history of our nation and would create the largest regulated electric utility in the world. If the merger occurs, this combined company would serve approximately 10 million customers across Virginia, Florida, North Carolina, and South Carolina, including approximately 2.7 million households here in Virginia. The SCC is expected to make a decision January 2027.

The SCC is currently accepting public comments on the proposed Dominion Energy–NextEra merger. November 2 is the last day to file as a public witness before testimony will be given on November 5, 9, and 10. November 9 is the last day to submit written comments. Visit the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) website, go to Submit Public Comments, and search for docket PUR-2026-00112 to share your feedback.

text:
The federal government has launched the Energy and Electricity Workforce Alliance to develop a skilled workforce that can support energy development and grid modernization.

This is the fourth workforce alliance established as part of the broader workforce measures introduced by the government in response to tariff concerns last year. The Energy and Electricity Workforce Alliance will comprise employers, unions, industry groups, post-secondary educational institutions, and Indigenous partners related to conventional energy and clean electricity generation, transmission, and grid modernization.

Electricity Human Resources Canada spearheads the alliance, backed by the Energy Council of Canada and the Canadian Renewable Energy Association. The three organizations will identify and tackle labour market challenges and support skills development by aligning investments and activities at all levels .

The Energy and Electricity Workforce Alliance seeks to champion sector-specific workforce solutions and construct sustainable talent pipelines for present and upcoming needs.

“Amidst global volatility and growing power demand, Canada is taking action to strengthen our position as an energy superpower. The Energy and Electricity Workforce Alliance is a key part of that, bringing together partners to make sure Canadian workers have the right skills and support workforce development across the energy sector,” said Tim Hodgson, Canada’s energy and natural resources minister, in a statement.

Energy Council of Canada chair Howard Shearer added that the nation’s energy capability was “built on its resource endowment and the expertise of a highly skilled workforce across the sector.” The government noted that Canada’s energy and electricity sector is critical to meeting the rising demand in electrification and clean energy sources; thus, it requires significant generation, transmission, and grid modernization investments.

“This investment is a significant step toward building the workforce that Canada’s energy future demands. As our sector is transformed by new technologies, digital innovation and major infrastructure development, success will depend on collaboration, coordination and a shared commitment to workforce planning,” said Michelle Branigan, EHRC’s chief executive officer.

Clean Energy Canada forecasted that 2.2 million new jobs will be created by 2050 at a rate of 7 percent per year. Nonetheless, heavy-duty mechanics and industrial technicians remain in short supply.

“Electricity demand in Canada is set to grow rapidly as industries electrify and the economy digitizes. Wind, solar and energy storage are the fastest and most affordable ways to meet that demand while modernizing the grid. However, none of this happens without skilled workers,” said Vittoria Bellissimo, Canadian Renewable Energy Association’s president and CEO.

Patty Hajdu, minister of jobs and families and minister responsible for the federal economic development agency for Northern Ontario, said the Energy and Electricity Workforce Alliance marked a significant step in securing Canada’s energy future.

Last month, the government established the Advanced Manufacturing Workforce Alliance. The Mining and Minerals Workforce Alliance, launched in June, was the first workforce alliance rolled out.
