text:
LG Energy Solution's new battery manufacturing campus in Lansing, Michigan, is up and running, and its output could affect daily life in more ways than one, from strengthening electric vehicle supply chains to supporting more reliable large-scale energy storage.

The site gives LG Energy Solution a stronger foothold in two rapidly growing markets at once: batteries for the grid and batteries for the road.

Here's what to know

According to Solar Power World, LG Energy Solution launched production at its new campus and plans to scale the site to over 35 gigawatt-hours of annual lithium battery capacity. The plant will manufacture large-format cells for both energy storage projects and electric vehicles.

For stationary storage, the campus is producing lithium-iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells. LG Energy Solution Vertech, the company's U.S. energy storage division, will use those cells in complete systems for utility, grid-scale, commercial, and industrial applications.

Toyota will also source battery cells from the Lansing site, which is set to make nickel-manganese-cobalt, or NMC, chemistry for the automaker. Those higher-energy batteries are intended for battery-electric vehicles assembled at a plant in Georgetown, Kentucky.

Together, those efforts support cleaner transportation options for drivers and expanded battery capacity that can help utilities and businesses store electricity for use when demand rises or the grid is under strain.

More background

LG Energy Solution says it has invested more than $2 billion in the Lansing campus since 2022, per Solar Power World. About 900 people work there, and employment is projected to grow to 1,700 once the site reaches full capacity.

The facility began as a joint venture with General Motors for EV battery production, but GM sold its stake in early 2025, leaving the nearly completed factory under LG's sole ownership.

With Lansing online, LG Energy Solution has two Michigan manufacturing sites, including its Holland plant. The company says its North American LFP cell-making capacity across wholly owned and joint-venture locations is expected to exceed 50 gigawatt-hours by the end of 2026, Solar Power World noted.

Large battery projects can have effects beyond manufacturing jobs. More storage capacity can help cities, utilities, and companies better manage electricity, improving reliability during extreme weather, easing strain during periods of heavy demand, and supporting a grid increasingly powered by renewable energy.

What's being done?

LG Energy Solution is making more and different types of batteries in North America. By manufacturing LFP cells for storage and NMC cells for EVs at the same campus, the company is building a localized supply chain for technologies that can help reduce pollution and strengthen energy systems.

On the storage side, LFP batteries are being directed into systems for utilities and businesses. These installations can store electricity when it is available and release it when it is needed most — a capability that can save money, reduce waste, and provide a layer of protection during outages or disruptions.

On the transportation side, the Toyota-linked production line increases battery availability for EV assembly in the United States. That can support a pipeline for electric models, which can help drivers reduce fuel costs over time.

North America is also becoming a bigger part of the company's storage footprint. LG Energy Solution says the region is on track to account for 80% of its global energy storage system capacity by the end of 2026, per Solar Power World.

"Today marks a defining milestone for LG Energy Solution," CEO David Kim said. "Lansing will produce advanced batteries that support not only the future of mobility but also America's growing energy infrastructure and digital economy."

Where can I learn more?

This ties into a few bigger shifts in batteries, including cell chemistry, factory expansion, and the rapid buildout of grid storage.

• At LG Chem, single-crystal high-nickel cathodes could extend EV battery lifespans by 30%.

• In the U.S., ENTEK is building a lithium-ion separator factory with major federal backing.

• Chemours opened a battery innovation center to speed work on next-generation EV materials.

A plant runs on more than assembly capacity. Progress in storage design, materials, components, and manufacturing oversight helps determine how quickly batteries make it to drivers and onto the grid.

Together, those efforts support cleaner transportation options for drivers and expanded battery capacity that can help utilities and businesses store electricity for use when demand rises or the grid is under strain.

More background

LG Energy Solution says it has invested more than $2 billion in the Lansing campus since 2022, per Solar Power World. About 900 people work there, and employment is projected to grow to 1,700 once the site reaches full capacity.

The facility began as a joint venture with General Motors for EV battery production, but GM sold its stake in early 2025, leaving the nearly completed factory under LG's sole ownership.

With Lansing online, LG Energy Solution has two Michigan manufacturing sites, including its Holland plant. The company says its North American LFP cell-making capacity across wholly owned and joint-venture locations is expected to exceed 50 gigawatt-hours by the end of 2026, Solar Power World noted.

Large battery projects can have effects beyond manufacturing jobs. More storage capacity can help cities, utilities, and companies better manage electricity, improving reliability during extreme weather, easing strain during periods of heavy demand, and supporting a grid increasingly powered by renewable energy.

What's being done?

LG Energy Solution is making more and different types of batteries in North America. By manufacturing LFP cells for storage and NMC cells for EVs at the same campus, the company is building a localized supply chain for technologies that can help reduce pollution and strengthen energy systems.

On the storage side, LFP batteries are being directed into systems for utilities and businesses. These installations can store electricity when it is available and release it when it is needed most — a capability that can save money, reduce waste, and provide a layer of protection during outages or disruptions.

On the transportation side, the Toyota-linked production line increases battery availability for EV assembly in the United States. That can support a pipeline for electric models, which can help drivers reduce fuel costs over time.

North America is also becoming a bigger part of the company's storage footprint. LG Energy Solution says the region is on track to account for 80% of its global energy storage system capacity by the end of 2026, per Solar Power World.

"Today marks a defining milestone for LG Energy Solution," CEO David Kim said. "Lansing will produce advanced batteries that support not only the future of mobility but also America's growing energy infrastructure and digital economy."

Where can I learn more?

This ties into a few bigger shifts in batteries, including cell chemistry, factory expansion, and the rapid buildout of grid storage.

• At LG Chem, single-crystal high-nickel cathodes could extend EV battery lifespans by 30%.

• In the U.S., ENTEK is building a lithium-ion separator factory with major federal backing.

• Chemours opened a battery innovation center to speed work on next-generation EV materials.

A plant runs on more than assembly capacity. Progress in storage design, materials, components, and manufacturing oversight helps determine how quickly batteries make it to drivers and onto the grid.

Danbury-based FuelCell Energy is seeing a surge of interest from data center developers seeking new sources of electricity, with its pipeline of potential projects reaching about 10 gigawatts as the company works to expand production at its Torrington manufacturing plant.

ADVERTISEMENT

The sales pipeline was 4 gigawatts at the end of the second quarter, up from about 1.5 gigawatts earlier this year.

The company also disclosed Tuesday that a major data center operator made an upfront payment to reserve fuel cell equipment for a planned 75-megawatt project in Texas — FuelCell’s first such agreement. The announcement follows FuelCell’s June agreement with Fit Energy USA LP for up to 380 megawatts of fuel cell systems for data center applications.

FuelCell is ramping up production in Torrington, where it expects to be producing fuel cell equipment at a pace equivalent to 100 megawatts annually by October. The company plans to expand the plant’s annual production capacity to 500 megawatts by June 2028, at an estimated cost of $200 million to $275 million.

During the third quarter, however, the facility operated at a production rate equivalent to about 37.1 megawatts annually.

ADVERTISEMENT

The company still faces significant financial challenges.

FuelCell reported a third-quarter net loss of $45.3 million, or 64 cents per share, for the quarter ended July 31, compared with a loss of $91.9 million, or $3.78 per share, a year earlier. The prior-year quarter included a $64.5 million impairment charge related to the company’s solid oxide technology investments.

Third-quarter revenue fell 29% to $33 million, primarily because of fewer fuel cell deliveries to South Korean customers and lower output from FuelCell’s generation portfolio.

The company said its 7.4-megawatt Groton project at the U.S. Navy’s submarine base was offline during the quarter due to an equipment upgrade.

ADVERTISEMENT

The company raised $245.5 million in net proceeds from a public stock offering completed July 9. It said the money will be used for manufacturing expansion, working capital and general corporate purposes.

FuelCell also completed delivery of six fuel cells during the quarter for the Gyeonggi Green Energy project in South Korea, bringing its total deliveries under the project to 42 modules since 2024.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

September 1, 2026

Contact: press@michigan.gov

Governor Whitmer Announces Home Heating Tax Credit Filing Deadline

Qualified renters and homeowners have until September 30 to claim credit, save money on energy bills

LANSING, Mich. — Today, Governor Whitmer promoted the Home Heating Tax Credit, reminding Michigan renters and homeowners that they have until Wednesday, September 30, to submit a claim. This credit helps eligible low-income households save money on energy costs during Michigan’s colder months. Governor Whitmer, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS), and the Community Economic Development Association of Michigan (CEDAM) encourage residents to file before the deadline so they can save money on energy costs and keep more money in their pockets.

“No one should have to choose between keeping the heat on and affording their basic needs,” said Governor Whitmer. “As we enter the colder months, I encourage all eligible Michiganders to submit their claim for the Home Heating Tax Credit before the September deadline. This credit helps families save on their heating bills, putting more money in their pocket for the essentials like food, medicine, and rent. Let’s keeping working together to lower costs for every Michigander.”

Last year, the average qualifying household received $171 in assistance, most often applied directly to utility bills. Food assistance recipients who are seniors, disabled, or veterans and receive a Home Heating Credit of more than $20 may also qualify for increased benefits. The Home Heating Credit cannot be claimed retroactively, so those who miss the September 30 deadline will lose the opportunity to receive this support.

“This is a time-limited opportunity,” said acting MDHHS Director Amy Epkey. “If residents do not file by the end of September, they cannot claim the credit later. The Home Heating Credit helps families manage essential costs and can open the door to additional support. If you qualify, filing now is the best way to make sure you receive what you are eligible for.”

“As we move into another heating season, don’t miss your chance to apply for the Home Heating Credit,” said Chief Deputy State Treasurer Lance Wilkinson. “It’s a helpful way to reduce energy costs and keep more money available for other important needs. If you’re eligible, be sure to apply before the deadline.”

“Many families qualify for support but never receive it simply because they do not file,” said acting executive director of CEDAM Ben Dowd. “By working together with state and local partners, we are making sure residents have the information and assistance they need to keep the money they’ve earned.”

To qualify, Michigan residents must be either a renter with a contracted lease or a homeowner and meet income requirements. The most reliable way to claim the Home Heating Credit, along with other valuable tax credits, is through Michigan’s free tax preparation services, available statewide.

text:
By David Shepardson

WASHINGTON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - A judge in Washington on ⁠Wednesday ⁠blocked the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ⁠from sending landmark California vehicle emissions rules for a potential repeal to the Republican-controlled ​Congress.

The four waivers sent by the EPA to Congress for review granted California authority to enact its own emission standards ‌for cars and trucks as well ‌as lawn-and-garden equipment. The Trump administration has mounted a multi-pronged effort to deny California the ability to require cleaner ⁠and more ⁠electric vehicles. The EPA and Congress have also enacted rules making it easier ​for automakers to sell more gas-powered cars and trucks, while making it more expensive to buy EVs.

If the Trump administration is successful, it would bar California indefinitely from regulating tailpipe emissions and a future Democratic president would be unable to easily reinstate ​its regulatory powers.

In June, the EPA said the vehicle emissions waivers granted to California by the federal Clean ⁠Air ⁠Act under prior Democratic administrations ⁠should have been ​sent to lawmakers under the Congressional Review Act (CRA), which would allow the U.S. Senate to repeal them by ​a simple majority rather than ⁠the 60 votes needed for most legislation.

The CRA allows only regulations to be repealed. California sued to block the action in federal court, saying it was illegal to send the waivers to the Senate under the CRA since they were waivers and not regulations.

The state noted one waiver had been approved in 2009.

U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell said ⁠in a preliminary injunction ruling that the EPA had urged the court to "engage in Orwellian doublethink" ⁠in seeking approval and arguing the agency is ignoring serious inconsistencies.

"The EPA cannot say one thing to Congress while ignoring any consequence from reclassifying these waivers as rules," Howell said. "Such gamesmanship may seem like a clever policy move, but undermines honest compliance with the law."

She directed EPA "to take all necessary steps within the agency’s control to restore the status quo" before June.

The EPA did not immediately comment.

Andy Su, a lawyer at the Environmental Defense Fund, praised the ruling, saying it will help "protect vital safeguards that 40 million Californians have long relied on to cut pollution, protect health and save money."

Lawmakers had ⁠been preparing to vote on the waivers as soon as later this month.

Last year, Congress rescinded authority for California to outlaw gas-powered vehicles after 2035 after Toyota, General Motors and other automakers lobbied for relief from the state's emissions regulations.

The action came after the EPA sent the waivers to Congress ​for repeal. A separate legal challenge from California on that action is pending.

text:
A new EPA decision giving 29 small oil refineries a break from renewable-fuel requirements is drawing concern from Iowa agriculture and biofuel leaders.

The exemptions cover about 1.76 billion ethanol-equivalent gallons of renewable fuel credits. The EPA granted full exemptions to 18 refineries and partial exemptions to 11 others. Three petitions were denied, and two were ruled ineligible.

The Renewable Fuel Standard requires oil companies to use renewable fuels such as ethanol and biodiesel, or obtain credits showing they met the federal requirements.

For Iowa, that requirement helps support a major agricultural industry. Iowa Renewable Fuel Association said the state produced 4.6 billion gallons of ethanol in 2025, accounting for about 28% of U.S. production. The state has 42 ethanol refineries.

The organization's executive director, Monte Shaw, said the exemptions could reduce demand for ethanol, biodiesel, corn and soybeans if steps to combat the impact aren't taken.

“If you start pulling these industries back, the ripple effects are deep and painful,” he said.

Industry groups debate fuel costs

The EPA’s decision comes as gasoline prices remain high.

The national average for regular gasoline stayed above $4 per gallon every single day of August, marking a record high for the month according to AAA data.

The American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, which represents oil refiners and petrochemical companies, has argued that the renewable-fuel requirements create significant costs.

In formal comments on the proposed 2026-27 requirements, AFPM estimated annual compliance costs could approach $70 billion across the industry. The group said those costs could affect refiners, consumers and the broader economy.

Shaw, meanwhile, said greater use of ethanol can help lower fuel prices, which he says is evident by the price of fuel blends at the pump.

EPA plans to restore waived requirements

The EPA says it plans to add the waived requirements back into the 2026 and 2027 renewable-fuel obligations.

The agency expected about 990 million RINs to be exempted in 2025 but ultimately approved about 1.76 billion.

If finalized, the reallocation would require other obligated oil refining companies to make up the difference, helping preserve demand for renewable fuels.

The plan is not final. EPA says it will propose the reallocation by the end of October.

Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, called the announcement a significant improvement over what had been rumored. He said future administrations should follow the precedent of fully reallocating the waived requirements.

Iowa Agriculture Secretary Mike Naig called the exemptions “unfortunate and unjustified.” He said the proposed reallocation could help minimize the impact but urged the EPA to follow through quickly.

Iowa has seen the dispute before

The current debate echoes the first Trump administration’s fight over refinery exemptions.

In 2019, the EPA had issued 85 retroactive exemptions covering the 2016 through 2018 compliance years. The Renewable Fuels Association said those exemptions reduced required renewable-fuel volumes by about 4 billion gallons.

At least 20 ethanol plants nationwide have closed since September 2018, partly because EPA policy reduced ethanol use.

Shaw said the Iowa biofuel industry will be watching to see whether the EPA completes the reallocation.

“Until a rulemaking is done, it’s not done,” Shaw said.

text:
Corpus Christi City Council members have again voted against awarding a design-build contract for the Inner Harbor desalination plant, continuing a year-long division among council members on the project.

The proposed desalination plant seeks to add to the city’s water supply. Because of rainfall experienced in the area during the summer, the board was able to push back the estimated timeline of declaring a Level 1 Water Emergency by a year. The city was also able to move to Stage 1 water restrictions in late August, a first since March 2024.

During the Tuesday meeting, 54 people signed up to speak during the public comment period, according to Kiii News.

Public comments against the proposal included concerns over the project’s closeness to the town of Hillcrest, criticism that the project is a “scam” and not technically or fiscally sound, as well as environmental concerns.

Ardurra, the company responsible for designing the project, presented several possible changes to address environmental concerns.

Some of the proposed changes include real time monitoring of the bay’s salinity levels and a pipeline that would be built during the project’s second phase to discharge brine into the gulf, allowing the plant to potentially produce more water.

Despite these changes, the council rejected the proposal in a 5-3 vote, with council members Carolyn Vaughn, Eric Cantu, Gil Hernandez, Kaylynn Paxson, and Sylvia Campos voting against. Councilmembers Everett Roy, Mark Scott, and Roland Barrera were in favor.

The council previously postponed the vote for the proposed plant during its June meeting, following a lengthy discussion on the environmental impacts.

Gov. Greg Abbott has criticized the city council for delaying the desalination plant project, despite receiving $800 million from the state to fund water projects.

“I think it’s safe to assume the state is watching, and I think it’s safe to assume the federal government is watching,” Councilmember Scott said. “And so I think any delay is going to get a negative reaction from them.”

text:
DONALDSONVILLE — A crowd staunchly divided over whether the state should grant a key permit for the Hyundai steel mill planned in Ascension Parish filled every seat available Tuesday night at the Lemann Center Gymnasium.

T-shirts emblazoned with personal opinions on the project, worn with suits by some and casual attire by others, punctuated the crowd, where a common question passed between people in adjoining seats: “Are y’all for or against?”

This was the first and only public hearing the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality has planned for the Hyundai-Posco Louisiana Steel facility’s air pollution permit. It provided residents, elected officials, industry representatives, and local business owners a chance to share their thoughts on whether the state should approve the project based on its pollution impact.

The 1,700-acre steel manufacturing site was announced in March 2025 as a proposed $5.8 billion investment near the Modeste community. The facility will occupy 10% of an undeveloped tract along the Mississippi west bank known as the RiverPlex MegaPark, an area zoned for industrial development and mixed uses. Promising to bring 1,300 direct jobs to the River Parishes, the mill is expected to produce 2.7 million metric tons of steel for Hyundai and Kia automobile plants in the U.S. and other automakers.

Along with job promises, the facility will produce more than 1.6 million tons of greenhouse gases and release 196 tons of particulate matter and 1,760 pounds of lead into the air each year, according to its air pollution permit application with the state.

“It’s good to have an industry moving in, I understand that part. I worked in the industry for 42 years, I know what it’s all about,” said Paul Troxclair, a Donaldsonville resident whose home lies within 2 miles of the steel mill’s proposed site. “But you’ve got to think of the people that you’ve affected. [The steel mill is] putting a lot more pollution in the air, and it’s not good for people.”

Business owners and people Hyundai has already hired to work on the project spoke in support, though with measured tones, saying that if the emission amounts in its permit application are allowed under the law, the project should move forward.

Rebecca Evans Mouk, who said she lives within 2 miles of the proposed steel plant, said she supports the project in hopes that it will provide jobs.

“We’re already an industrial community,” Mouk said, adding that she owns two industrial equipment businesses in the area that had already seen an economic boost from the project. “Louisiana has an amazing opportunity to continue building on these existing industries and create a future for our children in our communities.”

Other residents without any financial connection to the project were divided in their comments, with some sharing concerns about pollution and construction traffic disruptions.

Kristopher Cayette from Donaldsonville said he grew up right down the street from the RiverPlex site.

“I heard a lot of people who are for the project talk about finance, but I believe this is an environmental quality hearing,” he said. There “aren’t enough safeguards in place to at least diminish the air pollutants” for him to be in favor of granting the air quality permit.

“We already know the financial aspect of it, but it’s about the people who couldn’t sell their land who live right next to it and who won’t be able to go anywhere,” Cayette said.

Troxclair said he moved to Donaldsonville to retire after construction of a Shintech vinyl chloride facility next to his former home in Iberville Parish led him to move away. Now, he said he is experiencing a similar situation with Hyundai Steel.

“I moved here, hopefully to a peaceful environment, nice neighbors, old trees to go sit under,” he said. “Right now, with all the traffic they’ve got with the dump trucks, all the dust, I can’t even go sit outside and enjoy it underneath the oak trees.”

Modeste resident Sherry White said she doesn’t feel the Department of Environmental Quality has adequately addressed the pollution concerns of neighbors next to the Hyundai development.

“When residents say they are concerned about adding more industrial facilities to communities that have already carried an enormous environmental burden, that concern deserves to be taken seriously,” White said. “We should not dismiss people by telling them this project will be different.”

According to White, other facilities offered similar promises of economic prosperity but have not delivered.

“We’ve heard it before,” she said. “We still haven’t seen it. We just won’t go down this rabbit hole again.”

White specifically mentioned CF Industries, which operates an expansive ammonia manufacturing campus in Donaldsonville. The company’s website indicates it employs 500 permanent staff and 485 contract workers there.

CF Industries is also building what it says will be the world’s largest “low-carbon” ammonia plant, a $4 billion project that will add more than 100 more jobs.

Public officials spoke first at the hearing, including state Rep. Jeff Wiley, R-Maurepas, the former sheriff of Ascension Parish.

“They are the straw that stirs the drink …” Wiley said about the tax dollars industry generates. “I can’t imagine any thoughtful person would not be in support of something with such an enormous upside.”

State Rep. Tony Bacala, R-Prairieville, and Sen. Eddie Lambert, R-Gonzales, also voiced their support for the project. Lambert authored a state law that weakened community air monitoring around industrial facilities in the state.

“This is a truly once in a lifetime opportunity, and it will transform Donaldsonville,” Lambert said. “It’s the best thing that has happened to the west bank in years.”

Other local officials also spoke in support of the project, including Ascension Parish President Clint Cointment, St. James Parish President Pete Dufresne and Donaldsonville Mayor Leroy Sullivan.

The Hyundai facility will hold a groundbreaking ceremony for its steel mill Friday. The deadline to submit public comment on its LDEQ permit application was originally set for Wednesday, Sept. 2, but public outcry led state officials to extend the period to Sept. 15.

The project’s ceremonial start will still take place this week.

text:
By David Shepardson

WASHINGTON, Sept 2 (Reuters) – A judge in Washington on Wednesday blocked the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency from sending landmark California vehicle emissions rules for a potential repeal to the Republican-controlled Congress.

The four waivers sent by the EPA ​to Congress for review granted California authority to enact its own emission standards ‌for cars and trucks as well as lawn-and-garden equipment. The Trump administration has mounted a multi-pronged effort to deny California the ability to require cleaner and more electric vehicles. The EPA and Congress have also enacted rules making it easier for automakers to sell more gas-powered cars and trucks, while making it more expensive ‌to ​buy EVs.

If the Trump administration is successful, it would bar ⁠California indefinitely from regulating tailpipe emissions ⁠and a future Democratic president would be unable to easily reinstate its regulatory powers.

In June, the EPA said the vehicle emissions waivers granted to California by the federal Clean Air Act under prior Democratic administrations should have been sent to lawmakers under the ​Congressional Review Act (CRA), which would allow the U.S. Senate to repeal them by a simple majority rather than the 60 votes needed for most legislation.

The CRA allows only regulations ⁠to be repealed. California sued to block the action ⁠in federal court, saying it was illegal to send the waivers ​to the Senate under the CRA since they were waivers and not regulations.

The state noted one ​waiver had been approved in 2009.

U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell said in a ‌preliminary injunction ruling that the EPA had urged the court to “engage in Orwellian doublethink” in seeking approval and arguing the agency is ignoring serious inconsistencies.

“The EPA cannot say one thing to Congress while ignoring any consequence from reclassifying these waivers as rules,” Howell said. “Such gamesmanship may seem ⁠like a clever policy move, but undermines honest compliance with the law.”

She directed EPA “to take all necessary steps within the agency’s control to restore the status quo” before June.

The EPA did ⁠not immediately comment.

Andy Su, a ‌lawyer at the Environmental Defense Fund, praised the ruling, saying it ⁠will help “protect vital safeguards that 40 million Californians have long relied ​on to ‌cut pollution, protect health and save money.”

Lawmakers had been preparing to ​vote on ⁠the waivers as soon as later this month.

Last year, Congress rescinded authority for California to outlaw gas-powered vehicles after 2035 after Toyota, General Motors and other automakers lobbied for relief from the state’s emissions regulations.

The action came after the EPA sent the waivers to Congress for repeal. A separate legal challenge from California on that action is pending.

(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Muralikumar ​Anantharaman and Thomas Derpinghaus)

text:
A proposed 300-megawatt battery energy storage project near Vacaville drew more than five hours of public comment Tuesday, with local officials, residents and energy industry representatives offering sharply different views on whether the facility belongs on agricultural land near the city.

The California Energy Commission heard testimony on the proposed Corby Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project, proposed for about 40 acres of unincorporated land near Kilkenny and Byrnes roads, approximately 250 feet southeast of Vacaville’s jurisdictional boundary and about five miles northeast of downtown.

CEC staff has recommended certification of the project, finding that its potential environmental impacts and operational risks — including noise, fire hazards and containment — can be managed or mitigated within regulatory standards during normal operations. The project is also expected to provide economic benefits and support electric-grid reliability, the staff noted.

But many of the hundreds of residents who attended Tuesday took turns urging the commission to reject the project, citing concerns about lithium-ion battery fires, potential groundwater contamination, noise, loss of prime agricultural land and the lack of permanent jobs the facility would provide.

The proposed facility would be capable of storing up to 1,200 megawatt-hours of electricity. It would include batteries, a project substation, inverters, fencing, a sound barrier, roads, drainage facilities and other infrastructure.

Vacaville Mayor John Carli was the first local official to address the commission. He emphasized that the city is not opposed to battery energy storage as a technology, but argued that the Corby site is inappropriate because of its location and the city’s plans for future growth.

“It’s important that you understand as you consider the importance of this moment,” Carli said. “The City of Vacaville is not against battery energy storage systems at the grid scale.”

Carli pointed to the city’s proximity to the Vaca-Dixon substation and said Vacaville has previously considered land for a battery storage facility. But he said the proposed Corby site is located in an area that the city and county have identified for future development.

He noted that Vacaville is considering residential annexation of hundreds of acres in its northeast and east-of-Liesure Town growth areas, potentially placing the proposed project in the path of future residential and commercial development.

“So it isn’t just prime ag land,” Carli said. “It’s residential and commercial areas.”

Solano County Supervisor Mitch Mashburn also spoke against the project’s proposed location, while stressing that the county recognizes the importance of battery storage to the electrical grid.

The county has adopted an ordinance governing where battery energy storage systems can be located and how they should be regulated, Mashburn said. The proposed Corby site does not meet those local requirements.

He also cited Measure T, the county’s voter-approved orderly growth regulation.

“We recognize the Legislature has given the CEC authority to the opt-in process to supersede local land use authority,” Mashburn said. “However, that does not erase the county’s general plan.”

Vacaville Vice Mayor Mike Silva similarly urged the commission to honor local land-use decisions.

Silva, who said his family includes fruit pickers and people who have worked the land, described agricultural land as a precious family and community legacy.

“Solano County went through a long, deliberate process to evaluate the safety and placement of battery energy storage systems,” he said.

Vacaville City Councilmember Roy Stockton distinguished opposing battery storage and opposing its proposed location.

“Let me make one thing very clear: I am not opposed to battery energy storage,” Stockton said. “I am opposed to putting large-scale lithium-ion battery facilities in locations where consequences of a catastrophic failure could unnecessarily put residents and first responders at risk.”

“There is the difference between opposing technology and demanding that we locate that technology responsibly,” he added.

Residents who spoke during the hearing raised similar concerns.

Neil Serr of Solano County questioned the state’s authority to override local decisions supported by voters and local ordinances.

“If a measure approved by approximately 70 percent of the voters, together with duly adopted city and county ordinances, says that certain uses should not occur in particular locations, how does the state of California justify overriding those decisions?” Serr asked.

Others focused on the potential consequences of a battery fire.

Savannah Haas, a Dixon resident who said she works as an ecosystem scientist and holds a doctorate in soils and biogeochemistry, raised concerns about the project’s location over the Solano groundwater subbasin and the Pudah fan aquifer.

She said the shallow aquifer could be vulnerable to chemical contamination and noted that Vacaville and Dixon rely on groundwater from the area, as do local farmers, ranchers and landowners.

Haas also pointed to the project’s proximity to Kaiser Hospital and Lonza, a major pharmaceutical manufacturing facility.

“If there is a fire at the site,” she said, smoke plumes could reach Dixon within an hour.

Darlene Conner told commissioners she was speaking as a mother and grandmother and that her daughter’s property is directly across from the proposed site.

She urged commissioners to consider locating the facility in an industrial area or using a different battery technology.

“The people living beside the Corby should not have to absorb the unnecessary risk simply because this particular parcel was available to the developer,” Conner said.

Dee Cole, whose family home is across from the proposed project, said residents would have to live with the consequences of the commission’s decision long after Tuesday’s hearing ended.

“This is a rural agricultural community,” Cole said. “It is where families live, where people have invested their savings, raised their children and built their lives.”

Sarah Dunn, speaking on behalf of Keep Vacaville Safe, asked the commission to reject the environmental impact report, raising concerns about what she described as errors in the report’s calculations involving metal deposition.

Michael Geller, who owns the historic Kilkenny House with his wife, also opposed the project, citing its agricultural zoning, the area’s reliance on wells and the potential for groundwater contamination in the event of a thermal runaway.

The hearing was not uniformly opposed to Corby.

Kara Martinson, representing the California Energy Storage Alliance and American Clean Power, spoke in support of the project and the broader need for battery storage.

“Battery storage is an essential part of the grid,” Martinson said, noting that more than 300 battery energy storage sites are operating in California.

She said projects such as Corby can help provide reliable electricity during periods of extreme heat, when demand is high, while allowing more renewable energy to be used and reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

Industry representatives also pointed to the CEC staff assessment, which found the project could strengthen grid reliability, support the state’s clean-energy goals and provide economic benefits to Solano County.

The project’s supporters said it would store electricity when supplies are plentiful and make that energy available when demand rises. They also cited construction jobs, investment and additional tax revenue.

The CEC staff assessment included reviews of environmental impacts, public health and worker safety, fire protection, emergency preparedness and compliance with state and local requirements.

If approved, the project would be subject to safety requirements including NFPA 855, a national standard governing the installation of stationary energy storage systems, as well as emergency response planning.

The commission did not make a final decision Tuesday.

Written comments on the project will be accepted until 4 p.m. Sept. 14. An updated staff assessment and the executive director’s recommendations are expected to be filed by Oct. 19.

The CEC is expected to consider the project’s opt-in application at a business meeting scheduled for Nov. 18.

title: The sub-$30,000 Kia EV3 arrives in the US at the perfect moment - ArenaEV
description:
The 2027 Kia EV3 enters the American market with a base sticker of $29,890 - or $31,385 once you tack on the inescapable $1,495 delivery charge.
Kia managed to avoid the fatal trap of offering a low headline price that saddles you with a useless, city-only battery pack.
Naturally, to hit a $30,000 target without losing their shirts, Kia's engineers had to make some calculated compromises under the skin.
Let's not forget that Kia fitted every American EV3 with a native NACS charge port - no fiddling with clumsy third-party adapters in the pouring rain.
Kia's gas-powered models and hybrids might be smashing sales records for now, but the EV3 is the brand's true long game.
text:
Spend five minutes reading industry headlines, and you could swear the electric transition had hit a brick wall. We love a good crisis - tales of unsold inventory on dealer lots, companies dusting off combustion blueprints, and buyers going back to the familiar embrace of gas station.

But walk into an American showroom right now, and sales don't show any signs of stopping. Automakers are shifting cars at an extraordinary clip. Nobody embodies this slightly cheeky momentum quite like Kia, an outfit that transitioned from building bargain-bin penalty boxes twenty-odd years ago into a design-led titan capable of humbling Detroit and Stuttgart alike.

The Korean brand chalked up its best August in corporate history, delivering 83,793 vehicles in the United States alone - a tidy 1% lift year over year and an all-time monthly high. Through the first eight months of the year, Kia has found homes for 590,377 cars, running 3% ahead of last year's record-smashing pace and practically guaranteeing its fourth consecutive annual sales record.

But look closer at those figures, and there's a glaring split. It's not EVs that are driving all this success in the US. Traditional combustion staples and electrified hybrids are doing all the heavy lifting. The Seltos surged 53%, the Carnival people-carrier jumped 13%, and hybrids across the board spiked 99% in August, spearheaded by the Sportage Hybrid leaping 40% and the Sorento Hybrid climbing 22%. Across the first eight months, Kia's hybrid volume is up 111%.

Then you look at pure battery-electric vehicles, and the champagne stays in the fridge. Pure EVs took a beating last month: the swoopy EV6 plummeted 60% year over year to 712 units, leaving its year-to-date tally down 39% at 5,429 cars. Even the huge three-row EV9 slipped 33% in August to 1,789 registrations, but its year-to-date total still sits comfortably in the black at 10,474 units, up 12%.

The culprit behind this stall is neither range anxiety nor charging phobia - it is cold, hard maths. When you ask middle-class families to drop $60,000 or more on a brand-new crossover during uncertain economic weather, they will naturally walk across the showroom floor and drive home in a hybrid Sportage for half the monthly finance hit.

The 2027 Kia EV3 enters the American market with a base sticker of $29,890 - or $31,385 once you tack on the inescapable $1,495 delivery charge. In an era where the average transaction price of a new car hovers uncomfortably close to $50,000, delivering a design-forward crossover that ducks below the thirty-grand waterline is nothing short of an automotive shock.

Visually, the EV3 pulls off a neat trick: it does not look like a cut-price concession. Too many entry-level runabouts resemble melted lozenges designed inside a wind tunnel with zero regard for human emotion. The EV3, by contrast, looks like someone shrunk the hulking EV9 in a hot wash. It has the same chiseled, cyberpunk jawline, squared-off wheel arches, and intricate vertical lighting signatures that give its big brother such imposing presence. It sits stout and purposeful on the road, broadcasting genuine SUV attitude rather than sheepish econobox humility.

Pull out the tape measure, and you realize how cleverly Kia packaged this machine against its direct peers. The EV3 stretches 169.3 inches from bumper to bumper, spans 72.8 inches wide, stands 61.4 inches tall, and rides on a generous 105.5 inches wheelbase, with curb weights ranging from 3,968 lb to 4,156 lb depending on the battery size.

Consider it against the old Nissan Leaf, which measures a longer 176.8 inches with a 106.3 inches wheelbase and tips the scales between 3,483 lb and 3,814 lb, yet suffers from an outdated chassis, front-wheel drive wheeziness, and awkward proportions. Even Volvo's pocket-rocket EX30, which measures 166.7 inches and weighs roughly 4,034 lb, comes at a premium starting near $36,000 despite back seats so tight they border on punishment. The EV3 nails the size conundrum: tidy on the outside for tight city parking, but genuinely comfy for four adults on the inside.

Kia managed to avoid the fatal trap of offering a low headline price that saddles you with a useless, city-only battery pack. The entry-level EV3 Light FWD at $29,890 packs a respectable 58.3 kWh unit good for an EPA-estimated 221 miles of driving range. That is plenty for daily suburbia, but the real sweet spot is just one rung higher. Step up to the Wind FWD at $34,990 or the Land FWD at $38,490, and you unlock an 81.4 kWh pack that pushes your single-charge leash all the way to an EPA-estimated 321 miles.

Finding that kind of long-legged cross-country endurance at this price point is virtually unheard of. For those living in the snow belt who demand four-wheel security and twin-motor shove, Kia offers all-wheel-drive configurations across the Wind AWD ($38,690), Land AWD ($41,690), GT-Line AWD ($43,490), and top-shelf GT AWD ($45,890), all delivering a hearty 280 miles of range with the big pack while turning the performance dial up a few notches.

Naturally, to hit a $30,000 target without losing their shirts, Kia's engineers had to make some calculated compromises under the skin. Unlike the EV6 and EV9, which ride on a cutting-edge 800V electrical architecture capable of juicing from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes, the EV3 uses a cost-effective 400V setup.

Plugged into a 350 kW DC fast charger, recharging the 58.3 kWh pack from 10% to 80% takes 29 minutes, while the larger 81.4 kWh pack demands roughly 31 minutes. In the real world, an extra ten minutes at the charger is a compromise ninety-nine percent of buyers will happily accept in exchange for keeping thousands of dollars in their bank accounts. Let's not forget that Kia fitted every American EV3 with a native NACS charge port - no fiddling with clumsy third-party adapters in the pouring rain. You simply back into any Tesla Supercharger stall, plug in, and get on with your day.

The clever execution continues in the cockpit. Instead of the button-free desolation that passes for modern minimalism in certain Silicon Valley machines, the EV3 adopts a warm, Scandinavian-inspired lounge vibe. You get textured, sustainable fabrics across the dashboard, tactile switches for climate functions, and a sliding center console that doubles as a laptop desk or picnic tray when parked. It feels cheerful, airy, and clever - a true masterclass in smart automotive interior architecture that punches way above its shy window sticker.

This "charm" explains why the EV3 is already taking over the sales charts in the UK and Continental Europe, where drivers have long favored compact footprints and agile dynamics over bloated suburban tankers. In America, the arrival of this baby crossover is a necessary cultural reset. The electric vehicle conversation in the States has been dominated by thousand-horsepower super-trucks and fragile $100,000 halo machines that normal people can only view from behind velvet ropes.

Kia's gas-powered models and hybrids might be smashing sales records for now, but the EV3 is the brand's true long game. Eye-catching styling, three hundred miles of genuine highway legs, native Supercharger access, and a low entry price - the future of personal transport does not need a second mortgage. It simply needs building an honest, brilliant little car.

text:
The Western Australia (WA) government is funding three WA businesses to support five projects that progress development and manufacture of a range of battery technologies and components for residential, commercial, industrial, and defence applications.

The Round 1 allocation from the WA government’s $50 million (USD 35.8 million) Local Battery Manufacturing Program will enable the three successful applicants to develop and test prototypes, purchase advanced equipment and expand production capacity.

Applications include residential energy storage batteries, large community batteries, inverters, and locally manufactured battery components.

WA Minister for Energy and Decarbonisation and Manufacturing Amber-Jade Sanderson said the projects will support local battery manufacturing.

“We’re helping build resilient supply chains, creating highly skilled jobs, and supporting Australia’s transition to a cleaner energy future,” Sanderson said.

The funding recipients include Magellan Powert, which designs and manufactures industrial-grade AC and DC uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, energy storage units, batteries and electric vehicle (EV) infrastructure.

Adarsh Investments is a WA-owned and operated manufacturer, fabricator and importer of component parts, and ProtoLab Manufacturing produces electronics solutions.

Funding streams under the WA Local Battery Manufacturing Program includes a production-ready stream, which provides up to $100,000 in matched funding to businesses for projects in three categories of pre-production activities.

The production scale-up stream provides up to $5 million in matched funding to existing battery manufacturers for projects that scale-up their operations, including through purchase of capital equipment, workforce training, costs associated with upgrading existing or new premises, and engaging business or manufacturing expertise.

text:
Another month, another disappointment for Ford as combined sales plummeted 10.3% in August to 170,681 units. That’s a decline of nearly 20,000 vehicles and this can largely be chalked up to the elimination of the Escape.

Electric vehicle sales plunged 79.4% and this was partly due to the axing of the F-150 Lightning. Dealers only sold 148 of them last month, which was down 95.4% from a year ago.

More: Ford Showed Dealers Its Cheapest New Car Yet, A Boxy $25,000 SUV

The aging Mustang Mach-E didn’t do much better as sales tumbled 72.5% to a disappointing 1,989. However, it’s important to note last year’s sales were elevated as there was a mad dash to buy vehicles before the clean vehicle tax credit expired on September 30.

Putting EVs aside, overall Ford sales fell 10.3% to 163,175. The top seller was unsurprisingly the F-Series, which found 67,504 takers. That was a slight 1.2% decline from a year ago and this only equates to 814 units.

In a distant second place was the Explorer, which was down 4% to 19,801. It was followed by the affordable Maverick as 13,680 Americans scooped one up last month.

While the sales chart wasn’t terribly interesting in August, the Mustang was up 12.7% to 3,647 units. Furthermore, the Bronco Sport climbed 8.3% while the Bronco fell 8.8%.

It’s also worth noting the recently redesigned Expedition is having a tough go as August sales were down 11% and it’s off 11.6% year-to-date. Part of this can likely be blamed on high gas prices, which makes it a shame we never got the hybrid variant that was originally promised in the 2023 UAW contract.

Ford August 2026 Sales

Mixed Result At Lincoln

Things were also bad at Lincoln as sales dropped 10.4% to 7,506 units. This can be blamed on the discontinuation of the Corsair as sales fell from 2,526 to just 266.

However, Lincoln recently introduced the 2027 Corsair, which comes with a facelift and a Chinese passport. While it looks great and features a new hybrid powertrain, pricing has shot up $7,310 to begin at $46,495 before a $2,295 destination fee.

Speaking of China, the Nautilus had a good month as sales were up 28.9% to 3,627 units. The American-made Aviator also took to the air as sales climbed 22.4%, but dealers only sold 1,732 vehicles.

Unlike the Expedition, the Navigator ended up in the black as dealers moved 1,881 of them for a 15.8% increase.

The Trump administration wants to eliminate the “Endangerment Finding,” a key safeguard for regulating climate pollutants.

Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal Campaign has fought to end pollution from the U.S. electricity industry for almost two decades. With 390 coal plants retired or planned for retirement, the campaign is one of the most successful environmental campaigns in history.

One of Beyond Coal’s bedrock wins was the acknowledgment that the Environmental Protection Agency has authority to make an "Endangerment Finding," to determine whether specific greenhouse gas emissions are atmospheric pollutants that threaten the biosphere. This authority is the legal underpinning for all climate regulations, and Trump’s allies know that killing it will devastate our ability to regulate greenhouse gas pollutants under a future administration. This is an all-hands-on-deck moment for the environmental movement.

We want you to join us in a fierce nationwide pushback against the rollback. Sierra Club and members like you were instrumental in gaining climate pollution protections in 2009, and now's the time for action to preserve our hard-fought victory

text:
How ISAIC and TUKATECH are Building a Blueprint for Workforce Development, Demand Manufacturing, and Domestic Production.

The apparel industry is navigating one of the most significant periods of change in its history. Rising labor costs, increasing material costs, workforce shortages, shorter product lifecycles, and growing sustainability expectations are forcing manufacturers to rethink long-established business models.

For years, these challenges have been discussed at conferences, through pilot programs, and in social media forums. Far fewer organizations have successfully integrated the necessary components into a practical operating model.

With the expansion of its Detroit headquarters, ISAIC has moved beyond proving an idea. It has established a working ecosystem that combines workforce development, digital product creation, entrepreneurship, advanced manufacturing, and commercial production within a single environment.

Jennifer Guarino, President, CEO, and Co-Founder of ISAIC, believes the organization's evolution marks an important milestone.

"We are no longer a proof of concept. We are a working center that brings integrated solutions to industry while making advanced manufacturing technologies accessible to our community."

Addressing Industry-Wide Challenges

Every apparel manufacturer faces the same fundamental pressures: controlling costs, improving speed, increasing flexibility, and responding to changing consumer demand.

According to Ram Sareen, Chairman - Founder of TUKATECH, these challenges cannot be solved simply by shifting production to lower-cost regions. Long-term competitiveness requires manufacturers to improve productivity, reduce material waste, and make greater use of digital technologies throughout the product lifecycle.

"The cost of labor and the cost of material will continue to increase. The question is, how do you control it? Technology allows manufacturers to reduce waste, improve productivity, and make manufacturing competitive where products are actually consumed."

Rather than viewing automation as a replacement for people, Sareen sees technology as an enabler, helping manufacturers produce more efficiently while strengthening regional manufacturing capabilities.

Building on a Proven Foundation

ISAIC's expansion is significant because it builds upon measurable accomplishments rather than future aspirations.

Over the past several years, the organization has established itself as a nationally recognized resource for apparel manufacturing, workforce development, and product innovation. Its integrated operating model combines technical education, commercial manufacturing, product development, entrepreneurship, and technology adoption in a single facility.

That approach has already been validated through collaborations with leading organizations, including Carhartt, supporting domestic manufacturing initiatives, workforce development, and product innovation. At the same time, ISAIC has provided entrepreneurs, emerging brands, and manufacturers with access to professional development and manufacturing capabilities that would otherwise require substantial capital investment.

The expansion into its new headquarters strengthens a model that is already operating successfully while significantly increasing its capacity to serve the industry.

Expanding a Complete Digital Manufacturing Ecosystem

ISAIC's expansion is about far more than adding new equipment. It is creating one of North America's most comprehensive environments for apparel product development, workforce training, and demand-driven manufacturing.

The expanded facility brings together every major stage of the product lifecycle within a single integrated workflow. Designers can develop products digitally, validate fit in a virtual environment, engineer patterns, optimize material utilization, produce prototypes, manufacture production-ready components, and move seamlessly into commercial production—all within the same facility.

The new environment combines advanced digital product development with modern manufacturing technologies, including CAD and pattern engineering workstations, marker making, 3D fit evaluation and virtual sampling, automated fabric spreading, high-ply cutting, single-ply laser cutting, production-length cutting tables, plotting systems, and integrated sewing production capabilities. Dedicated education laboratories equipped with the same professional software used by industry ensure that students and workforce participants learn using current production technologies rather than simplified classroom tools.

For manufacturers, entrepreneurs, and brands, the result is access to a complete digital-to-production ecosystem that supports everything from initial product concepts and rapid prototyping to production planning, workforce development, and commercial manufacturing.

As Guarino explains, "We can now demonstrate these technologies in real time while delivering integrated manufacturing and training solutions from one location."

For Sareen, the significance extends beyond the equipment itself.

"The real value isn't any individual machine or software application. It's the integration of the entire workflow—from product development through manufacturing—allowing companies to access the capabilities they need while preparing for future growth."

Rather than investing in isolated technologies, ISAIC is expanding an operating environment where innovation, education, and production reinforce one another every day.

Connecting Design to Manufacturing

One of the industry's longstanding challenges has been the disconnect between product development and production.

Design, pattern engineering, manufacturing planning, cutting, and production have traditionally operated as separate disciplines, often involving multiple organizations, disconnected workflows, and repeated handoffs.

ISAIC's integrated environment helps eliminate those barriers by bringing together the technologies, expertise, and production capabilities required throughout the development process.

As Sareen explains:

"Our industry has historically been fragmented. ISAIC brings those capabilities together, allowing companies to access the services they need without having to build an entire infrastructure themselves."

Instead of managing disconnected processes, designers and manufacturers can move seamlessly from concept to production through an integrated digital workflow.

Learning in a Production Environment

Perhaps ISAIC's most distinctive characteristic is that education takes place alongside commercial manufacturing.

Rather than separating classroom learning from industrial practice, students, entrepreneurs, designers, and manufacturers work within an environment where products are actively being developed and produced using the same technologies and workflows found throughout the industry.

This creates a learning experience that extends well beyond operating software or equipment. Participants gain an understanding of the complete manufacturing process—from product development through production—while experiencing the realities of quality, workflow, collaboration, and commercial execution.

Guarino believes that people and technology must advance together.

"You can advance technology, but if people don't have the skills to use it, the industry won't move forward. Likewise, you can train people, but without access to modern technology, they won't be prepared for the future."

Sareen sees ISAIC as a modern version of apprenticeship.

"People learn best when they experience the complete process—from design through manufacturing. That creates better professionals and stronger businesses."

ISAIC is not simply teaching the future of manufacturing. It is manufacturing while preparing the future workforce.

Lowering the Barriers to Innovation

Many entrepreneurs and emerging manufacturers possess innovative ideas but lack access to the technology, expertise, or infrastructure required to bring products to market.

ISAIC addresses that challenge by providing access to professional development and manufacturing resources without requiring businesses to make significant upfront investments.

Sareen compares the concept to a familiar service model.

"It's like Kinko's. If you only need a few copies, you don't need to buy a copier. Entrepreneurs can access exactly the technology they need, when they need it, and grow their businesses at the right pace."

This philosophy has guided TUKATECH's global TUKAcenter network for more than two decades, supporting thousands of entrepreneurs and manufacturers as they progressed from initial concepts to successful commercial businesses.

Sustainability Through Better Manufacturing

For manufacturers, sustainability must ultimately align with operational performance.

Reducing physical sampling through digital product development, improving fabric utilization, minimizing material waste, and producing closer to actual demand all contribute to both environmental responsibility and improved profitability.

As Sareen summarizes:

"The first question isn't how we become sustainable. The first question is, how do we sustain the business?"

Technology enables those improvements not by changing individual processes, but by connecting them into an integrated workflow that improves both business performance and environmental outcomes.

A Blueprint for the Industry

Perhaps the greatest significance of ISAIC's expansion is not the installation of new technology.

It is the validation of an operating model.

A model where workforce development, entrepreneurship, digital product creation, education, and advanced manufacturing reinforce one another rather than operating independently.

Guarino believes that model helps organizations move forward with confidence.

"Transformation can feel risky. By bringing people, technology, and manufacturing together, we're helping organizations understand what's possible and giving them the confidence to transform."

For Sareen, the long-term vision is equally straightforward.

"Make what you need, when you need, for who you need."

Detroit may be where this model continues to evolve, but its implications extend well beyond one city. By integrating people, technology, education, and manufacturing into a single ecosystem, ISAIC has established a blueprint that communities, educators, manufacturers, and economic development organizations can adapt as they strengthen the future of domestic apparel manufacturing.

The future of apparel manufacturing is no longer a concept waiting to be proven.

text:
The Trump administration is making moves critics said could slow down the transition to greener transportation and increase emissions. They warned the changes would mean more health issues and higher costs for Oregonians.

As the administration moves forward with lowering federal fuel economy standards, Congress is set to vote to block states from limiting tailpipe pollution.

Rachel Sakata, transportation strategies section manager for the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, said transportation is the state's largest source of greenhouse gases, responsible for 35% of emissions.

"With the higher emissions that we're going to continue to see, you're going to have more people who may be suffering from adverse health effects such as asthma, respiratory and cardiac diseases, which can lead to more hospital visits and reduced work time," Sakata outlined.

Oregon has joined other states in suing the administration over plans to drop light-duty vehicle fuel economy targets from about 50 to 35 miles per gallon. The White House argued lowering the standards will make cars cheaper for average Americans, estimating purchase costs to drop by nearly $1,000.

While Sakata acknowledged there is a higher up front cost for buying electric cars, the savings from buying less gas and from lower maintenance costs add up. Sakata added with batteries getting cheaper and what would have been increased production by auto manufacturers, EV costs were expected to go down.

"In Oregon, we've seen at least 12% of new vehicle sales were EVs, and so by limiting the types of EVs that are out there, it just makes it harder for people to find the EVs that they really want and are enjoying and are investing in," Sakata explained.

Last year, Republicans in Washington ended federal tax credits for EVs years before they were to expire. Sakata said the Oregon Clean Vehicle Rebate Program can still help reduce the upfront cost of buying or leasing an electric vehicle.

Source: Public News Service

text:
To compare two very different approaches to EV value, a New Jersey family took both on the same 500-mile round trip between New Jersey and Vermont.

The matchup paired Rivian's new R2 against a Chevy Equinox EV 2RS priced roughly $15,000 lower.

Here's what to know

A video from EVenture Family (@Eventurefamily) followed a Rivian R2 Catalina Cove Launch Edition and a Chevy Equinox EV 2RS over almost the same highway loop. Both started fully charged, and each vehicle ran on 21-inch wheels.

Rather than making it a flat-out race, the couple used the drive to look at the issues families tend to care about on longer EV trips: highway energy use, charging stops, navigation and planning, and overall comfort.

Despite the large price gap, the creator said he expected both SUVs to end up "probably right around 3 miles per kilowatt-hour."

EPA ratings make the range comparison look straightforward, but the drive suggested the answer is messier in practice. The all-wheel-drive Equinox EV is rated at 285 miles, while the R2 carries a 330-mile EPA estimate, though the creator said of the Rivian, "nobody's getting that."

Charging specs also didn't tell the whole story on this route. The Equinox can top out at about 150 kilowatts, and the R2 is capable of higher rates, but the available stations did not include the hardware Rivian needs to reach its best numbers, so both SUVs mostly ended up using Tesla Superchargers.

More background

When the Equinox arrived at a Tesla Supercharger in Bennington, Vermont, it still had about 25% battery left, which was better than predicted.

A charger error appeared after about five minutes at one stall, so the driver moved to another unit, and the session then continued normally until charging began tapering near 70%.

One commenter wrote, "Efficiency without compromise is my gold standard to assess real advancement in this space."

What can be done?

How long an EV trip really takes depends on more than the window sticker, including speed, weather, wheel choice, charger access, and whether the route lets the vehicle use its fastest charging capability.

The test also underscored how competitive cheaper EVs have become. The Rivian offers a newer design and a more premium cabin, but the Equinox still looked like a credible road-trip choice because of its strong efficiency and lower purchase price.

One commenter put it this way: "Really conflicted. Don't need another crossover/small suv thing in my stable, but the R2 clearly is the better vehicle ... is it $30k better? ... ehhhh ... EQ is absolutely 100% a great value and a good car, but it's looking like it will be getting replaced shortly because I make bad decisions."

Where can I learn more?

The Vermont run showed how quickly EV value turns into a real-world question of price, charging access, and everyday efficiency — not just EPA range. The coverage here digs into those same tradeoffs, from Rivian's push to win over more buyers to the cost and range questions that can sway a family toward a premium model or a cheaper one.

• As prices keep shifting, misunderstood myths about EVs still shape family buying decisions.

• Over a decade of ownership, shocking cost differences of maintaining EVs kept showing up.

• For many households, surprising savings from owning an EV can outweigh sticker shock.

Each one adds a little more context to the question hanging over this road-trip test: how much extra capability is really worth paying for. That calculation gets tougher as lower-cost EVs keep getting better.

text:
The US Department of Energy (DoE) announced $500 million in grants for battery materials, manufacturing and recycling towards the end of August 2026. The grants went to a range of battery minerals and materials including next-generation anodes, direct lithium extraction (DLE), cobalt, electrolyte, and recycling. These are the third round of grants from the DoE’s “Battery Manufacturing and Recycling” and “Battery Materials Processing” programmes, which each have $3 billion in funding available. Previous rounds were announced in 2022 and 2024 under the Biden Administration. These grants follow a recent announcement of $2 billion in investment for critical supply chain projects.

A White House Executive Order (EO), published on 26 August, has declared a national emergency, citing national security risks relating to hardware and software in the US power system made overseas. This new measure, EO 14420 is the second attempt to put such a measure into place after the previous Trump administration’s EO 13920 in 2020. The new order is broader in scope, including software as well as hardware, and sets a 120-day deadline for the Department of Energy to set implementation guidelines. Benchmark senior BESS research analyst Pete Tillotson said the order could be “highly disruptive to the US grid should it be implemented to its fullest extent”.

CATL's Jianxiawo lepidolite mine, China's largest lithium mine by capacity, is back in care and maintenance after a brief and informal restart in July. Any return to production is now gated by an environmental review since the mine’s Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) was revoked. Completing the review could stretch into the fourth quarter or into 2027. Benchmark has cut its 2026 mined output forecast for Jianxiawo to 32,000 tonnes LCE, from 62,500, almost halving the mine's expected contribution, while its 2027 forecast is so far unchanged at around 99,000 tonnes.

CATL became the largest shareholder in Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-duty truck battery swapping network operator. CATL bought the entirety of the 24.87% stake held by China Power, a subsidiary of the State Power Investment Corporation for RMB2.6 billion (USD380 million). This raised CATL’s total stake to around 30%. The move helps CATL to secure Qiyuan’s battery swapping infrastructure. Qiyuan currently leads the market with over 1,800 stations nationwide, giving it a market share of over 70% across various heavy-truck settings, including mining zones. Combined with CATL’s own QIJI Energy battery swapping network, this move makes the company China’s largest heavy-duty battery swapping operator.

Benchmark has observed no cobalt hydroxide trades over the past 10 days, leading to the daily price assessments to hold steady at $22.00–$23.00/lb. However, Benchmark has noted a widening spread between bids and offers, which are reported between $17.00–$22.00/lb in Benchmark’s weekly cobalt price assessment. Benchmark's daily CIF Asia cobalt hydroxide assessment only accounts for confirmed transactions rather than indications, sentiment, or levels at which somebody says they would be willing to deal, which means it tracks evidenced trades and nothing else. That design choice is usually invisible to the user, because in a functioning market the distance between a trade and a well-informed indication is small, but in a week like this one it becomes the whole picture. Put those two series side-by-side and the market becomes legible, because the sell-side remains anchored to the level where material last actually changed hands while the buy-side has marked itself down five dollars, or roughly 23% below it. Nothing has traded across that gap, so the bid has not been validated by a single transaction and the offer has not been tested by a single buyer willing to lift it.

In early August, US auto giant General Motors (GM) announced it was relinquishing its 49.9% stake in SynergyCells, a JV with Samsung SDI, and as such its stake in the under-construction cell plant in Indiana, US. It is the third battery cell production plant for which GM has ceded its stake back to the South Korean partner, and follows similar moves by Stellantis and Ford over the past two years that have given South Korean firms a tighter grip on US cell manufacturing.

Africa is a key mining destination for a range of critical minerals across the energy transition supply chain. However, the majority of these minerals are exported for processing outside of the region. Most notably, Africa is the largest source of mined cobalt, where the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the subject of a previous Regional Spotlight, is the world’s leading supplier. The continent also leads global supply of mined manganese ore; it was responsible for three quarters of this in 2025.

Hakainde Hichilema was declared president-elect of Zambia on 18 August. Hichilema was re-elected after securing nearly 3 million votes, more than 1.1 million votes ahead of his opponent, Brian Mundubile of the NRPUP, and comfortably above the 50% threshold required to avoid a run-off. "The result is expected to deliver policy and geopolitical continuity, including the continuation of the beneficiation agenda set out in Zambia's 2024 critical minerals strategy," said Benchmark's lead policy and geopolitical analyst Bryan Bille. Copper is a crucial export for Zambia, accounting for around three-quarters of the total value of the country’s exports. Mined production in 2026 is estimated at 901kt, a healthy growth of 11% over last year, as assessed by Benchmark’s Copper Service. The Zambian government is aiming to increase output to 3Mtpa by 2031.

The greater deployment of drones is having a profound impact on the modern battlefield and has put the geopolitics of the battery supply chain into a new spotlight. In 2025, drones accounted for 39.2% of defence demand for batteries, according to Benchmark. This is up from just 20% in 2020. Soldier power and bases are the two next largest drivers of defence demand for batteries. "Drones have clearly risen to be the most influential aspect of modern military battery demand,” said Will Roberts, Benchmark’s automotive research lead. “Major militaries are still just getting started in their strategic investments relating to them which is about to set off a flurry of activity to domesticate supply chains, something which is getting significant attention from major battery manufacturers and new entrants alike."

Much of the attention on South & Central America’s transition to electric vehicles (EVs) focuses on Mexico and Brazil owing to their large total vehicle markets and automakers establishing EV production capacity in both. However, it is Uruguay that has quietly risen to lead EV adoption in the region. It achieved a penetration rate of 40% over the first seven months of the year, surpassing numerous European countries, including France, Germany and the UK. "Uruguay is a testament to how tax policy can be a really effective tool to create quick change regarding EV adoption in a relatively short period of time under the right market and economic conditions,” said Benchmark EV analyst George Whitcombe.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, delivered the following opening statement at today’s markup of 10 bills.

Chairman Guthrie’s opening statement as prepared for delivery:

“Good morning, and thank you all for attending today’s markup. We are taking up several bills that highlight the Committee’s effort to support energy innovation, cut burdensome red tape, and lower costs for hardworking American families.

“We know that success for the nuclear industry—from the fuels, manufacturers, and reactors to the operators and workers—will be essential for long term American technological leadership globally and for reliable and abundant energy here at home.

“We must strive to return to a pace of nuclear expansion that surpasses other nations. And we must do so in a way that strengthens public confidence in American technology.

“This morning we are considering six nuclear related bills that build on the bipartisan reforms we started two years ago with the ADVANCE Act, which improved nuclear permitting, brought the benefits of nuclear energy to Americans faster, and maintained our commitment to safety.

“The bills before us today clarify pay authority, improve transparency, and eliminate unnecessary Atomic Energy Act requirements to ensure licensing runs more smoothly.

“The continued bipartisan work on nuclear policy reflects well on this Committee’s ability to advance critical energy policies, and we’ll see that bipartisan spirit reflected in several of the amendments to the bills before us today. And all of these bills deserve strong bipartisan support.

“We are also examining legislation that would provide needed updates to the Clean Air Act. Outdated provisions in the law have created counterintuitive and burdensome policies that increase costs and negatively impact quality of life across this country. These are commonsense solutions.

“The bills before us will cover a range of issues, including ensuring that the federal government retains the authority to regulate interstate commerce on our nation’s railways, preventing one state from being able to dictate policy for the rest of the nation; and reauthorizing a successful grant program to help bus operators replace old equipment with new technology.

“We will also consider a bill to support the recovery of critical minerals from domestic sources by modernizing and streamlining EPA regulations of lithium-ion batteries, providing greater clarity and certainty for our domestic battery recycling industry.

“I want to thank all of the Members who have worked so hard to help bring these important bills before the Committee today.

“Thank you, and I yield to the Ranking Member for his opening statement.”
