text:
A Conversation with ‘Miracle Road’ Co-Author Mack Paul

Mack Paul, co-author, with his late father Allen, of “Miracle Road: The Story of Research Triangle Park,” co-founded Morningstar Law Group, where he is a partner. He teaches land use law at North Carolina State University and North Carolina Central University. In July, he sat down for a conversation with Site Selection Senior Editor Alexis Elmore about the book and the RTP region’s history. —Ed.

Site Selection: Did anything surprise you when learning about the modern foresight early players such as Romeo Guest, Pearson Stewart, George Simpson, George Watts Hill and former Governor Luther Hodges had for the Triangle region?

In the most recent North American Airport Satisfaction Study, MCI ranked number three in overall customer satisfaction.

Mack Paul: I had thought a lot about that aspect — their foresight, their vision. Thinking about all of them together, most of them had some really interesting insight about what the world was going to be like where an RTP would exist.

They really believed in investing in the state. We have a great university system. One of the first to have a state art museum and symphony. All these things, they just had a civic aspect to them and belief in the state. RTP sort of came out of that line of thinking of an investment. Even people in the [Piedmont] Triad giving a lot of money to create something not in their backyard, but in another part of the state, to benefit the state. It just happened that these figures who got involved in the project brought different things to the table and had some really interesting insights.

Romeo Guest doesn’t really get the recognition he deserves. He kind of gets picked on because he was trying to make money. His construction company was struggling because there was very little happening. The textile companies were struggling and the type of work they typically did was not thriving, so he came up with this idea to build a center in North Carolina that would attract research and development labs. He happened to go to MIT in the late ’20s, and MIT just happened to be one university in the United States that was at the forefront of research labs and commercialization at that time. You didn’t really see that anywhere else. He saw the Polaroid camera being developed, a lot of the research along the Charles River, and he continued to correspond with a lot of his friends from MIT in the ’30s. He finished right at the Great Depression, so he’s really struggling through the ’30s. But he kept seeing this idea that companies might want to be near a university, and you really never had that before. Then in World War II, massive research dollars from the federal government to go to the universities with the decision being made not to provide money to private companies, but to go through the universities to do the research that was needed. He understood that and he’s looking on the map and saw we’ve got Duke, NC State and UNC kind of nearby. Wouldn’t it be great to build a center where we could attract and leverage those universities for this R&D? So, had he not gone to MIT, had he not had those relationships, had he not continued to look and struggle for a way to bring companies to North Carolina, that idea of RTP never would have happened.

Luther Hodges is kind of a more traditional figure, having run a major division for Marshall Field’s, overseeing all these textile companies and kind of bringing himself up by the bootstraps. He was the guy who had the idea of the modern community college system. One of his main issues was what he called Industrial Training Centers and getting funding for that in the legislature. He helped create it and then it went on in the next administration, Governor Terry Sanford, to turn it into the community college system. It’s become one of North Carolina’s strongest economic development tools.

Pearson Stewart was another fascinating guy who grew up around Boston and went to Amherst. He went to MIT for grad school in urban planning, came down to Chapel Hill to work as a planner and got hired by the next person I’m going to talk about to be the first planner for RTP. Nobody had ever planned a research and development park or science park at that time. What is it? How do you lay it out? He just had this really keen insight. He talked about trees. He loved the environment, and he thought deeply about the topography and the geography and the ridges and the valleys and how to lay it out in a way that would be attractive to workers. They had a plan that the firm up in New York had drawn up for RTP and he just took a look at it and threw it in the trash can. He said, “This doesn’t fit with North Carolina,” and he came up with it on his own. Then he became a huge conservationist and helped create the Triangle Land Conservancy later on in his career.

The last I’ll talk about is George Simpson because he was my favorite among all of them, in terms of his insights into what the future might be. He was really young, at this time he studied under a guy named Howard Odom, who was a sociologist at UNC, apparently very well known nationally, writing about the South and culture and development. Simpson felt really strongly that the South could do better economically, but it needed to figure out a new industrial approach instead of just poaching companies coming from the Northeast. They had a committee that was supposed to hire the first director of the Triangle Committee, which became the foundation later. He was the first hire. Hodges couldn’t control himself and went to Bill Friday, who was a really young new president of the UNC system, and he immediately said, “You need to hire George Simpson.” George could deal with faculty and he also understood the economic imperative of North Carolina and the South. At that time, they were having a hard time getting universities to buy into RTP. There was just wasn’t this sense that academics and industry mixed together. George could be like that glue between the two, or at least the middleman to help bridge that gap.

Simpson understood this new world of technology coming out of World War II research and development. It was really a different type of worker who could operate very independently, go and study and research, come up with ideas, think deeply about problems and be innovative. That was a really different type of worker. He came up with how to describe an environment that is attractive to this worker and he put together a really great brochure called “The Dream and the Dilemma.” It laid out the whole picture of what tech centers might look like as a high quality of life for these workers, where you could have a really interesting, demanding job and also have the respite of coming back to a home and having your little oasis. It was kind of the post-World War II suburban environment with recreation, but you get access to really great jobs. RTP would be that job center in the center of the region, and people would live in other environments around it.

Besides sheer persistence toward RTP’s vision, another common theme in “Miracle Road” is the impact of unforeseen events, including Gertrude Cox’s arrival, Chemstrand’s decision to locate in RTP and entrepreneurial impacts of the Glaxo effect. What should state leaders seeking their own dedicated research or innovation parks take from the consequences of such events?

Paul: There’s always going to be unforeseen events. Sometimes those unforeseen events can be helpful. Sometimes they can be like the pandemic, something that comes out of nowhere and is a real problem that has to be dealt with. The lesson I took away from it is the leaders who created the vision of RTP. It was very collaborative, strategic economic development, a plan that had multiple facets to it.

RTP was just one of those elements. At the beginning, they didn’t even really think they were going to have an RTP. They just were going to bring companies here. They eventually realized they needed to have a physical place to show a company, “Hey, this is ready to go, this site is prepared,” etc. But a great example of why that persistence is so important is the early years.

George Simpson put together an army of faculty — hundreds of faculty members — to go out around the country to meet with all of these companies and try to talk to them about locating their research and development facilities or labs in North Carolina. After a year of doing that, they came back with zero interest. Or there was interest, but not one success of a company being serious about coming to North Carolina. Then, just by happenstance, one of the members of the faculty, really the ringleader of it, was a guy named William Little. He was a chemistry professor at UNC. He happened to be at the RDU airport after one of his trips and he ran into some of the executives from a company called Chemstrand, which is down in Decatur, Alabama. They were there to interview some of the chemistry students at UNC. They did a lot of kind of textile research, new types of materials with textiles. He just struck up a conversation with one of them, and it came out that they were looking at another site to build a facility. He’s like, “Hey, have you looked at RTP?” And they’re like, “No, never thought about it.”

He seized that opportunity. He had all this material with him. He talked them into taking the time to do a site visit to RTP. They already were way down the path of going to Princeton, New Jersey, and I think they were trying to hedge their bets. This is after Brown v. Board of Education. There was a lot of turmoil in the South and they needed a place their workers can go and don’t have to deal with some of the strife around desegregation. But they decided to look at RTP. Then ultimately, that was the first major coup of a company in the 1960s right after they created the Research Triangle Park. I think it’s a great example of happenstance. But this guy was persisting, meeting after meeting, all of that effort, not giving up and having a plan so when those unforeseen things happen, you were there, ready to take advantage of it. So that’s why I really feel it’s the persistence that’s the most important thing.

RTP got a generational head start on addressing challenges — cross-institutional collaboration, legislative and community buy-in, and targeted ecosystem building— many states now grapple with. Since the guidance of “industry hunter” Governor Hodges, how vital has North Carolina’s state leadership been in maintaining RTP growth?

Paul: It’s really critical. I first want to say something because I think it’s kind of a lesson of hope for any community, whether it’s in the United States or outside the United States, that’s thinking about this kind of model. While timing is important and it helps to be on the ground floor in certain industries, you can do it even though you may not be the first to do it. You talked about the generational head start. We forget —

and I didn’t really focus on it until I worked on this book — that MIT and Silicon Valley are gold standard for tech centers. Both of those areas are very closely tied to one another. They had essentially very similar leadership during World War II. There’s an engineering professor at MIT, Vannevar Bush, who ended up heading up the Office of Science and Scientific Research and Development (OSRD). They oversaw the Manhattan Project in World War II, and he was the one who really convinced the federal government that the universities ought to be the channel for this funding for research if we want to come up with new technologies.

At the time, it was mostly defense. A lot of it ended up having commercial application, and he was doing that to really build up MIT. He believed in the institution and he saw research and development as a way to build upon MIT’s preeminence. One of his students was a guy named Fred Terman who grew up a faculty brat at Stanford and went to MIT for engineering. He was, I think, Bush’s first PhD engineering student and worked with him at OSRD. He went back to Stanford after World War II and he essentially followed the same model Bush did at MIT. A the time, no one really knew Stanford. It was like a backwater. He started getting these federal contracts and he created the Stanford Research Institute. Both Stanford and MIT in the 1940s began getting these federal contracts and they built into the ’50s and the ’60s. So, 20 years before RTP got started, both of those regions had a huge head start.

You may remember Eisenhower’s farewell address talking about the military-industrial complex and being concerned about that concentration and dependence on the defense industry. MIT and Stanford were really at the center of that. The funding that they got was enormous, billions of dollars. RTP, it was just a field of nothing, and it was coming in after those two areas had such a head start and still, look what it was able to do through that persistence and strategic vision.

I think it’s a lesson. Don’t think just because you’re falling behind these other places that have existed or exist and are thriving that you can’t create something. Leadership is essential to it. State leadership, I believe, has been critical to RTP and not just throwing dollars at it. The state didn’t pay to create RTP. That was done through private money. What the state did, though, was create the community college system. It helped seed certain institutions like the NC Biotech Center and the Microelectronics Center. It’s created one of the best systems of higher education in the country. I didn’t fully appreciate what an incredible benefit it is to workers who move to North Carolina for their kids to be able to go to NC State or UNC, and the value of those educations is just amazing.

Also, there is the fact that our state has viewed RTP through a nonpartisan lens. We have a Democratic governor in North Carolina and we have a Republican House and Senate. When they’re talking about economic development projects coming to North Carolina, our commerce secretary says there’s zero daylight between Republicans and Democrats. That’s the only time you ever see them standing together smiling is when there’s an announcement of a company coming to North Carolina. The only way you could succeed is that approach.

SS: The Research Triangle Institute was paramount to proving early viability of RTP. Do you believe innovation and research parks require that same anchor today?

Paul: No, I don’t. I think we kind of touched on a little bit, but RTI was absolutely critical to RTP’s initial success. There was a professor at Duke, Paul Gross, another nationally recognized chemistry professor, who came to the table at the very beginning and he said, “Unless you create a research institute like RTI, Duke is not going to support RTP.”

It was really the vehicle to engage the faculties at UNC, NC State, and Duke in the project of RTP. To be able to have adjunct professors who came to the region to be at RTI doing that applied research but could be also teaching at the universities. Universities control RTI through its governance structure. It was interesting, RTP almost went down in flames. The options were about to expire on the land and they had this meeting at the beach with Archie Davis and the governor. They came back to the mansion. They brought Paul Gross and George Simpson, all the founders together saying, “Hey, we’ve got to get on the same page.” They had a big argument about RTI in that meeting and whether the foundation would control RTI. Paul Gross said, no, we’ve got to have it independent. The universities are going to control it. Once they got to an agreement on that, they raised money for RTI to buy the land, and RTI was the first institution to exist in RTP.

It was the only thing they had to sell RTP. We got RTI here, universities are involved, so it was really important. RTI became one of the largest independent research organizations in the country. It’s been a huge success. Many technologies have come out of it. We had a lot of changes in laws to make it easier for faculty to do research in the university and not have to have this buffer institution outside the university. And in fact, professors started seeing the actual benefits of commercialization and the universities creating offices around commercialization.

I think the role of RTI in that type of institution is just not nearly as important today as it was in 1959 or 1960. But the important point is RTP wouldn’t exist without RTI. It’s just that the world’s different now.

Of all of the organizations or initiatives formed in the development of RTP which do you consider to be its greatest gamechangers?

Paul: I talk a lot about RTI and the community college system. Those are definitely at the top. But another really interesting one, and I think unique and critical, is the NC Biotech Center. I think it’s really reflective of the leadership of the state, the governors and how important that is.

Governor Hunt coming in in 1976, young guy, he was looking for ways to innovate and energize the North Carolina economy. He put together a committee of scientists and one of the ideas was creating this biotech center. Genentech had just gone public and there was a Nobel Prize awarded to some of the first gene sequencing that was accomplished in the United States. So it was a very new idea and no one knew what was going to happen with biotech. They had the foresight to create an institution to try to promote that industry in North Carolina and they just happened to hire an amazing choice to lead it, a guy named Charles Hamner, who came from Southern Virginia and ran the UVA Medical Center. He had served as president of UVA. He did one of the first in vitro fertilizations in the world, so he was a renowned scientist. I think he had met with Governor Chuck Robb about this idea of the biotech center and Virginia just didn’t get it. They didn’t support it, and North Carolina came calling.

To him, it was a chance to build a whole new industry from the ground up. So he took the job, left Virginia, and came to RTP in this new institution. He had the insight and knew all of these scientists from his work. He started with hiring the superstars, successful or promising scientists in the world in biotech and gene research. One of his first hires was a guy named Oliver Smithies who came to UNC. He got the Nobel Prize, and he went to Governor Hunt and Governor Hunt asked him what he needed, and he told him, “I need $70 million and I’m going to go out and bring the best scientists here.”

He brought these labs from other universities. Later studies have shown, the places that brought the best scientists by measure of patents, academic papers, work product during the ’80s and ’90s, they became the leading centers for biotech. Once they became those leading centers — just like L.A. with film or Detroit with automobiles — you tend to keep that lead as long as you’re doing the right things. And so, the biotech center in North Carolina having the foresight to create that institution, bringing the right leadership together and bringing these scientists here, ended up being one of the biggest game changers. Life sciences is a major strength for RTP. Certainly IT is important, but the industry was much more mature when we tried to enter IT.

Novo Nordisk President and CEO Mads Øvlisen said that every state visited by the company in the 1970s offered incentives, but North Carolina uniquely provided “knowledge incentives” more powerful than locating near manufacturing resources. Now, over 50 years later, do the region’s big three universities, community colleges and the state’s focus on public education still stand as its most critical site selection factor?

Paul: Yes, I do, absolutely. North Carolina’s always been of a mind it’s not going to try to compete on incentives and just financial incentives like other states have done. It’s going to build this infrastructure around knowledge and education and talent. And fortunately, we got a really early start on the community college system, which we’ve continued to improve over decades.

It’s really hard to come in now and replicate what we’ve been able to put together over many, many years. One example of how we’ve done that, and Novo Nordisk I think is an interesting tie into it, is there was a meeting between Mads and Governor Hunt back in the 70s. [Hunt] went over to Denmark — we did a lot of these industry hunting trips to Europe and Asia — and so they met. He was really impressed by Hunt, then they were looking at a facility for an enzyme production. A lot of what goes into enzyme is agricultural products, corn. They were looking at a place in Nebraska. Ultimately, they decided to come to Franklinton outside of RTP and the Triangle, because of the talent here. The knowledge incentives.

Tobacco was a huge part of our economy and it was going down. Even in the 50s it was declining, and then by the ’90s there was a lot of litigation against the cigarette manufacturers over advertising and all of that. There was a settlement with the tobacco companies, and Mike Easley, who was the attorney general at the time and became governor later, did a settlement. I think it was like $4.6 billion and he took that money, and we created the Golden Leaf Foundation, which was to help build new industries, particularly in the tobacco regions of the state. NC State got a big chunk of that and created the Bio Manufacturing Training and Education Center (BTEC) with it. BTEC does a lot of really interesting things both undergrad and master’s programs. But it also welcomes regulators, people in industry and suppliers to learn about biomanufacturing. I’m not aware of any other state having anything like it.

It’s been hugely important to a lot of the biotech and biomanufacturing companies here, and Novo Nordisk has been really involved in its development. They’ve ended up contributing tens of millions dollars to the BTEC program and 100% of the students coming out of there get jobs within six months. There’s a lot of demand for the students coming out of that program. But it is an example of how creative and innovative we’ve been to build on what we already have. So it’s always looking at what the need is out in the industry and where those opportunities are, and creating these new programs and institutions.

How does the new mixed-use development approach introduced by RTP 3.0 complement initial goals of redefining the traditional suburban model, especially when considering connectivity aspects like Chuck Flink’s greenway plan?

Paul: It really is a needed template for changing that suburban model. It creates the ability for a range of different uses, which didn’t exist before. RTP was simply an office park, essentially. Each company had its own large site and office uses. So now, it creates the ability to have a type of environment a lot of people like, which is mixed-use. You have apartments above retail, you have a hotel and office all within a walkable area.

Zoning isn’t a restriction. It’s not a requirement. RTP has always been based on selling property to owners, who then decide what they want to do, how they want to develop it. Of course, it had to be office. Now it creates an ability to do this type of framework, which is great. I think it’s important to know it doesn’t ensure it happens; it just allows it to happen. And certainly, there’s a demand for it to happen now. The world has changed a lot. At RTP’s beginning, there was very little development in the region. We had some people living in Raleigh, Durham, Chapel Hill. Now the region has grown tremendously, and RTP is ringed by development.

You’ve got apartments and industrial uses and office uses, and it’s right near RDU Airport, so it’s at the center of tremendous development pressure. So we can expect when you take the constraints off, it’s going to respond because of where it’s located. The connectivity is a really important part of that. We started the greenway system at RTP in the 1980s. The plan now contemplates this major greenway spine north to south through the park that will link up to a lot of that existing greenway, both inside and outside the park, which is going to help with the connectivity. But it’s really critical. I talk a lot in the book about the need for alternative transportation modes, because we’re super auto-dependent.

We’re finally settled on this bus rapid transit system. It’s starting to come together regionally, and I think ultimately, as I said, these new templates are critical. But you need the supporting infrastructure to get people out of their cars.

From your perspective as a land use lawyer, are RTP 3.0’s various development typologies the ideal future direction to attract future growth?

Paul: I do. I think they’re reflective of best practices in planning circles. They’re templates that allow certain development forms to occur. There’s a lot more to the story than that but that’s an important piece of it. They’ve had good guidance from professional planners in developing these typologies. The mixed-use density node is more of a form-based type of zoning. If you choose that option you have to build the building close to the street with wide sidewalks and transparency on the ground level, so all of those things are features important to creating that environment. They also kept the traditional, such as not opting into any typology and you continue to operate under the existing RTP structure. Or you could choose the enhanced corporate campus, which has more public-facing uses like having restaurants or structured parking.

I think there is going to be a large demand for those corporate campuses. There’s a lot of questions around tech companies investing in new campuses. It’s going to be interesting to see everyone still hold their breath about Apple, which has gotten an extension on their time. But we see particularly life sciences and labs thriving in RTP. Workers have to go to their labs and they operate on these large campuses, so there is still going to be demand for that.

I think the innovation hubs we’re going to see emerge in a few areas are the ones served by transit. We have a new transit hub with bus rapid transit and the commuter line that’s coming to RTP in the future. I also think it’s important for RTP to focus on Park Center, which is well underway. We have a Boxyard RTP and then The Hub that’s coming in now and it’s a proof of concept that you can get people to live in RTP and have all of these amenities.

Is this new template a model you find could be successful in other regions of the state?

Paul: I think it is something you’re going to see in other regions. I want to talk about two aspects of this. When we say the model, I think we’ve been talking a lot about the real estate standpoint — built environment that’s creating this mixed-used hub that has a walkable environment, a street network, transit access, apartments, hotels and offices. All of those things are important but that does not necessarily mean you’re going to get R&D going there. On one hand, I would say you’re going to see that real estate model, it’s commercially viable and we see it all the time. The more interesting question is are you going to see true innovation hubs happening? Just because you build doesn’t mean you’ll have what RTP has going on in terms of invention and research. You need a lot of softer support and I think it’s quite easy to overlook that.

We talked about RTI and how important it was to have the institutions brought into RTP early. RTP has largely been these suburban office campuses that are really kind of a black box where all that work is going on inside. What does it look like when you build this mixed-use environment to make it an innovation hub? Now that they finally have approval for RTP 3.0, I think they’re going to shift into more of these softer support systems of re-engaging universities through institutions that haven’t been super active. We have the Triangle University Center for Advanced Studies, and things like that can bring the universities into new places that we’re trying to create, making sure there are accelerators here, that there are service providers and maker space.

We do have Frontier in Park Center, using old IBM buildings that were basically handed over to entrepreneurs to come in and start operating. Now every single one of those buildings is full. I think there is going to be demand, but that question is “Do you have the soft infrastructure in place to get that activity going in these hubs?” If not, it’s a nice place to live.

There’s a panel coming up on design at NC State and I was in a meeting with the Emerging Issues Forum in North Carolina and they mentioned these innovation hubs they’re pursuing in Greensboro, Asheville, Wilmington and Wilson. Each one is attempting to focus on a particular industry. It was showing me there are a lot of communities that are pursuing not just physical space, but a space to create.

What better way to spend time with your late father Allen than to interview and learn from over 160 government, university and business leaders and more to lay out the history of the Research Triangle Park and the Triangle region? What did building “Miracle Road” together mean to you and your dad?

Paul: It was a once-in-a-lifetime chance for us to do this kind of project. We’d talked about working together. He’s obviously been writing for a lot of his career and I’ve been grinding away as an attorney, so there’s no way I could have ever approached a project like this without working with him, or someone like him. What was great was we just have such different approaches and we respected each other’s even though we debated a lot around the outline and structure of the book.

I would never try to take away what he brought to the table as a storyteller. Doing most of the 160 interviews, for him, was almost an oral history project. Giving a forum for these people’s lives that they had built RTP and wanting to honor that. In an example of how important these stories were, one of the interviewees that had worked at Burroughs Wellcome in the 1970s talks about being mentored by Gertrude Elion — who was a Nobel Prize winner and overcame so many obstacles for a woman in science in the 1960s and 1970s — working with her and then ending up founding her own successful company. She’s now at a big venture capital fund, but hearing what that experience was like, sharing it with my dad and making it a part of the book was special. I tried to provide structure and continuity between all of these stories, so it has a narrative arc to it. Hopefully, it came through how RTP evolved over time.

My dad had been working on this for five years, then I came in around two years ago to repackage it and fill in the gaps. He passed away on Memorial Day, but I had been telling him over the past six months as we were finalizing it, “Hey, I really think this has come together and I feel proud about it because it does reflect those two very different perspectives.” It’s important to tell this story because it’s not just the stories that make it of interest to people, but also understanding those larger lessons.

Can you share a few impactful moments you two shared in this process?

Paul: This is kind of an anecdote to finish on and it’s kind of sad in the sense that it didn’t happen together, but it’s great because it really, for me, helps carry on my dad’s presence. After he passed away, people started to become aware of it. I started hearing from people who were interviewed and I’d always hear he loved learning about each of the people he interviewed, connecting with them and talking to them about all sorts of things unrelated to RTP. He wanted to understand them, and it really resonated with one person after another.

I heard from Mary-Dell Chilton, one of the scientists that had come here, who died weeks after my father. Her caregiver wrote me this nice note about my dad and how much Mary-Dell just loved my father. He interviewed her a couple of times and told her life story. I didn’t mention how incredibly important documenting these people has been. Since we started the project, Fred Brooks, Mary-Dell Chilton, Charles Hamner, Jim Hunt and Bob Lee passed away. So, being able to capture their lives and their stories, that would have been lost forever.

When he first talked to me about working on this project, he told me it was going to be a collaborative process. We would be building a community around this book, it’s not going to be something you hammer out through research, and that was truly reflective of him.

I totally bought into it, but it wasn’t necessarily something I would have done because I’m different in the way I might’ve approached it. He got the NC Biotech Center to put together this committee of iconic RTP figures to open doors to all these scientists and all the interviewees and got them interested and excited about this project. Even with him gone now, so many people want to be involved in getting the word out. It’s much bigger than somebody writing a book. It’s a vehicle for all of the people who’ve expended their lives trying to make this happen. They can see it told and how they fit into that story, even if it’s just a small part of it. You’ll see yourself and know you made a difference.

title: Clean Fuels Disappointed with EPA?s New Small Refinery Exemptions
description:
In the 2026-2027 RFS rule announced in March, EPA estimated that it would grant SREs totaling 990 million RINs for 2025.
The agency established supplemental volumes for 2026 and 2027 to ensure that the exemptions would not undercut current biodiesel and renewable diesel production and halt investments in additional production capacity.
President Trump and EPA have promised to restore all 770 million RINs exempted above the prior estimate through a forthcoming supplemental rule.
“Clean Fuels fundamentally disagrees that small refiners need reprieve from the tepid 2025 RFS volumes set by the prior administration.
We appreciate the White House’s commitment to hold biofuel producers harmless and will work with EPA to quickly finalize the promised supplemental rule.
text:
EPA also announced its intention to finalize a supplemental rule before the end of October to ensure that the RINs exempted today are restored to 2026 and 2027 RFS volumes. In the 2026-2027 RFS rule announced in March, EPA estimated that it would grant SREs totaling 990 million RINs for 2025.

The agency established supplemental volumes for 2026 and 2027 to ensure that the exemptions would not undercut current biodiesel and renewable diesel production and halt investments in additional production capacity. President Trump and EPA have promised to restore all 770 million RINs exempted above the prior estimate through a forthcoming supplemental rule.

Kurt Kovarik, Clean Fuels’ Vice President of Federal Affairs, stated in reaction, “America’s biodiesel, renewable diesel and SAF producers have been working overtime to meet the historic RFS volumes announced just last March. The industry is producing at record pace today, providing a strong domestic market for America’s farmers, investing billions in rural communities, contributing to America’s energy security, and providing American consumers a price break at the pump – in short, delivering measurable results on the administration’s goals for the RFS.

"We’re hopeful that today’s action won’t reverse the progress we’ve made and that our industry can maintain faith in the RFS program.

“Clean Fuels fundamentally disagrees that small refiners need reprieve from the tepid 2025 RFS volumes set by the prior administration. We appreciate the White House’s commitment to hold biofuel producers harmless and will work with EPA to quickly finalize the promised supplemental rule.

“Clean Fuels and its members are extremely grateful for the quick action of Senators Chuck Grassley, Joni Ernst, Representative Ashley Hinson, and numerous other congressional champions who worked to ensure that EPA’s relief measures for small refineries do not come at the expense of America’s biofuel producers and farmers.”

name: Louisiana Environment
title: SpaceX's $100B Louisiana deal comes with $27.5B in tax incentives
description:
Louisiana officials have offered SpaceX an estimated $27.5 billion tax incentive package to secure the company’s planned $100 billion Starbase Louisiana facility in coastal Vermilion Parish, Louisiana Illuminator reports.
A completed $100 billion facility could generate roughly $1.3 billion in annual property taxes, but under the agreement, SpaceX would make an initial $25 million annual payment shared by local governments.
According to Together Louisiana analyst Broderick Bagert, this means the upfront payment would amount to only about 2% of what the facility could otherwise generate in property taxes.
Supporters also believe the project will generate additional economic activity and tax revenue through workers, suppliers and other businesses.
However, environmental and transparency advocates have raised concerns about nondisclosure agreements and new laws providing aerospace companies with additional legal and public-record protections.
text:
Louisiana officials have offered SpaceX an estimated $27.5 billion tax incentive package to secure the company’s planned $100 billion Starbase Louisiana facility in coastal Vermilion Parish, Louisiana Illuminator reports.

The largest portion, about $23.8 billion, comes from a 25-year property-tax exemption. A completed $100 billion facility could generate roughly $1.3 billion in annual property taxes, but under the agreement, SpaceX would make an initial $25 million annual payment shared by local governments.

According to Together Louisiana analyst Broderick Bagert, this means the upfront payment would amount to only about 2% of what the facility could otherwise generate in property taxes. Critics, including Invest in Louisiana director Jan Moller and Bagert, argue that the incentive is excessive, particularly because SpaceX has committed to creating at least 3,000 permanent jobs.

Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois defended the deal, arguing that it should not be considered a giveaway because the state is securing a $100 billion private investment, thousands of high-paying jobs and potentially significant coastal restoration and hurricane-protection projects. Bourgeois emphasized that SpaceX must deliver the promised results to receive the incentives.

Supporters also believe the project will generate additional economic activity and tax revenue through workers, suppliers and other businesses. However, environmental and transparency advocates have raised concerns about nondisclosure agreements and new laws providing aerospace companies with additional legal and public-record protections.

title: Climate medicine deserves the seriousness we gave HIV - KevinMD.com
authors: Mark T. Gladwin, MD, Mark T. Gladwin, Umayr R. Shaikh, Dana Y. Lujan, Tien Vo, Katrina Gipson, Michele Luckenbaugh, Manisha Kaliaperumal, Evan C. Wells, Yodhin Aggarwal
description:
While commonplace in the West, wildfire smoke has once again drifted in from Canada to reach the East Coast.
I call climate medicine an urgent generational health challenge, and I believe it deserves the same institutional seriousness we once gave the emergence of HIV/AIDS when I was a medical student in the 1980s.

Global health as climate health Through the decades, University of Maryland faculty have helped screen and treat more than a million people for HIV across Africa, a reminder that disease containment abroad protects health here.
Academic medical centers sit at the intersection of science, clinical care, and community impact of a changing climate.
text:
This summer has offered a compelling case study on why there’s a pressing need for the emerging field of climate medicine and what the medical system must prepare for in the years ahead as extreme heat waves, powerful storms, and out-of-control wildfires become the norm. While commonplace in the West, wildfire smoke has once again drifted in from Canada to reach the East Coast. Catastrophic flooding has devastated communities in Texas. And in Europe, a June heat wave is now estimated to have caused more than 5,700 excess deaths in France alone, the large majority in people over age 75. These are not three unrelated news stories. They are the same underlying phenomenon (a warming, crowded, highly connected planet reshaping human disease) showing up in three different clinical forms within a matter of weeks.

I call climate medicine an urgent generational health challenge, and I believe it deserves the same institutional seriousness we once gave the emergence of HIV/AIDS when I was a medical student in the 1980s. The evidence is no longer speculative; it shows up in emergency departments, in hospitalization data, and increasingly in our own patients. Physicians and health care leaders need to be thinking about planning for natural disasters and newly emerging infectious diseases caused by climate shifts. We need to act to save patient lives.

Turning wildfire smoke into actionable data

In 2023, smoke from Canadian wildfires traveled more than 2,100 kilometers to reach Baltimore, a preview of what we’re seeing again this summer as smoke drifts east. In a study published in JAMA Network Open, our University of Maryland Institute for Health Computing (UM-IHC) linked satellite smoke-plume tracking with electronic health records from 2.5 million patients across Maryland and found a roughly 20 percent increase in cardiopulmonary hospitalizations tied to that exposure. That kind of real-time linkage between environmental sensors and clinical data is exactly the capability we’re building out further: the ability to see a health effect developing in a population that resides hundreds or even thousands of miles from the source, and to prepare for it in order to prevent illness and death.

Treating heat as a cardiovascular and public health emergency

The numbers coming out of Europe this June are sobering, and they track a pattern we already understand clinically: Extreme heat drives measurable increases in emergency department visits and mortality, concentrated overwhelmingly in older adults, along with young children, pregnant women, and people with existing cardiovascular or respiratory disease. Part of our work is making sure that pattern is recognized early: by clinicians, by hospital systems planning for surge capacity, and by public health officials deciding when and how to issue heat warnings.

Understanding what flooding does beyond the water itself

The damage from flooding events like the one in Texas isn’t limited to drowning and physical injury. Floodwater overwhelms sewage and water treatment systems, contaminates food and water supplies, and creates conditions for pathogens such as Cryptosporidium, Vibrio vulnificus, and Leptospira, the last of which recently forced us to shut down a hospital water supply on our own Baltimore campus. It also displaces people, disrupts health care delivery, and drives significant downstream mental health impact. Our researchers are working to map these secondary and tertiary health effects so that emergency response accounts for them, not just the immediate flood damage.

Staying ahead of zoonotic and vector-borne threats

My career has spanned roughly eighteen significant zoonotic disease events: HIV, SARS, H1N1, Ebola, mpox, and now recurring strains of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) moving from poultry into dairy cattle. Our faculty’s work in vaccinology and emerging pandemics, including one of the largest COVID-19 clinical trial enrollments in the country through our vaccine translational unit, is the same infrastructure we need ready for the next one. We’re also expanding surveillance and research on tick- and mosquito-borne disease as warming lengthens transmission seasons and shifts their geographic range northward.

Investing in mRNA vaccine platforms

The technology that earned Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine allows researchers to sequence a novel pathogen, synthesize a vaccine candidate, and begin production within roughly a month of an outbreak. Sustaining that capability, and the federal research infrastructure behind it, is one of the highest-leverage investments we can make against future pandemic threat, avian influenza included.

Studying microplastics before the evidence is decades old

Two recent studies (one in the New England Journal of Medicine linking microplastic deposits in arterial plaque to cardiovascular events, another in Nature Medicine documenting rising plastic concentrations in human brain tissue) echo, in their early stages, the pattern of the twentieth century’s leaded-gasoline crisis: widespread exposure, a vulnerable population, and causation still being established. Through our Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology, we’re beginning to study microplastic accumulation in the food chain. We don’t yet know whether plastics will prove as consequential as lead did. We should find out before, not after, the fact.

Global health as climate health

Through the decades, University of Maryland faculty have helped screen and treat more than a million people for HIV across Africa, a reminder that disease containment abroad protects health here. That same global orientation now applies to climate-linked disease: What happens with avian influenza in Southeast Asia or dengue’s northward spread affects Maryland directly.

Academic medical centers sit at the intersection of science, clinical care, and community impact of a changing climate. We also train the majority of the country’s health professionals, so building climate medicine into that training (teaching the next generation of physicians to recognize a heat-driven cardiac event, a wildfire-smoke asthma exacerbation, or a case of leptospirosis for what it is) is as much a part of this work as the research itself. That’s the work already underway at our institution, and it’s only becoming more urgent as summers like this one make clear.

title: Minister Hajdu establishes the Energy & Electricity Workforce Alliance - Canada.ca
authors: Employment and Social Development Canada, Social Development Canada
description:
The Government of Canada is taking decisive action to bolster vital industries and enhance workforce development in the energy and electricity sector for a sustainable and independent future.
In alignment with this commitment, Minister of Jobs and Families and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency, the Honourable Patty Hajdu, announced today the launch of the Energy and Electricity Workforce Alliance – the fourth Workforce Alliance in a series of Government of Canada efforts towards establishing strong partnerships across key sectors.
The new Energy and Electricity Alliance will bring together respected leaders and experts known for their work in the sector, including employers, workers, educators and Indigenous partners, to help build the skilled workforce needed to support energy development, grid modernization, and a more productive energy and electricity sector.
Canada’s energy and electricity sector, which includes oil, gas, and electricity, plays a pivotal role in supporting the growing demand for electrification and clean energy sources.
The Energy and Electricity Alliance will be led by the Electricity Human Resources Canada, with support from the Energy Council of Canada, and the Canadian Renewable Energy Association.
text:
September 2, 2026 Ottawa, Ontario Employment and Social Development Canada

As Canada modernizes its energy systems and expands electricity generation capacity, its labour market continues to face uncertainties driven by tariffs, skills shortages, supply chain disruptions, and rapid technological advancements. The Government of Canada is taking decisive action to bolster vital industries and enhance workforce development in the energy and electricity sector for a sustainable and independent future.

In alignment with this commitment, Minister of Jobs and Families and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency, the Honourable Patty Hajdu, announced today the launch of the Energy and Electricity Workforce Alliance – the fourth Workforce Alliance in a series of Government of Canada efforts towards establishing strong partnerships across key sectors. This includes working collaboratively with provincial and territorial governments.

The new Energy and Electricity Alliance will bring together respected leaders and experts known for their work in the sector, including employers, workers, educators and Indigenous partners, to help build the skilled workforce needed to support energy development, grid modernization, and a more productive energy and electricity sector.

Canada’s energy and electricity sector, which includes oil, gas, and electricity, plays a pivotal role in supporting the growing demand for electrification and clean energy sources. As a result, substantial investments in generation, transmission, and grid modernization are increasingly necessary. Addressing skills mismatches in certain energy occupations, as well as notable shortages in other critical occupations such as heavy-duty mechanics and industrial technicians, will be essential to take advantage of significant growth opportunities in liquefied natural gas and various clean energy technologies, including hydro, wind, solar, and nuclear power.

The Energy and Electricity Alliance will be led by the Electricity Human Resources Canada, with support from the Energy Council of Canada, and the Canadian Renewable Energy Association. Together, these organizations will work to strategically identify and address pressing labour market challenges and align investments and activities at all levels to support skills development. By fostering collaboration among stakeholders, including employers, labour representatives, training institutions, Indigenous partners, industry associations, and equity-deserving groups, the Alliance will promote sector-specific workforce solutions and build sustainable talent pipelines that meet both current and future needs.

Drawing on their experience and expertise in current labour market data affecting the energy and electricity workforce, this Alliance will inform evidence-based approaches and initiatives that recognize the importance of workforce strategies for reskilling, regional labor mobility, and the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and renewable energy systems.

This critical work will advance Canada’s broader economic objectives and ensure the sector has access to a skilled, mobile, diverse and future-ready workforce capable of supporting long-term sector resilience and growth.

title: Tennessee issues commercial fusion license to Type One Energy for Bull Run site
description:
The NRC decided to regulate fusion energy systems as byproduct material facilities back in April 2023, in a move that would allow Agreement States to set their own fusion regulations.
Project Infinity: The license from TDEC allows Knoxville-based Type One Energy to break ground on the first phase of its Project Infinity at the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run Energy Complex, near Oak Ridge.
Type One intends initially to build its Infinity One stellarator prototype at the site, followed by its 400-MW Infinity Two pilot fusion power plant.
The company expects a full startup of the power plant by 2034.
Tennessee’s licensing process is now the international benchmark for how to ensure fusion power plant ‘safety by design’ in a manner that can unlock the compelling economics of this transformational power generation technology.
text:
The NRC decided to regulate fusion energy systems as byproduct material facilities back in April 2023, in a move that would allow Agreement States to set their own fusion regulations. In early June, Tennessee implemented its own regulatory framework for nuclear fusion machines.

Project Infinity: The license from TDEC allows Knoxville-based Type One Energy to break ground on the first phase of its Project Infinity at the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run Energy Complex, near Oak Ridge. Type One intends initially to build its Infinity One stellarator prototype at the site, followed by its 400-MW Infinity Two pilot fusion power plant. The company expects a full startup of the power plant by 2034.

The Bull Run site, to which Type One relocated its headquarters from Madison, Wis., in 2024, is also slated to function as a fusion development campus, hosting collaborative projects involving Type One, TVA, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and the University of Tennessee.

OAS annual meeting: The issuance of the TDEC license to Type One was announced at an August 31 event coinciding with the annual meeting, in Nashville, of the Organization of Agreement States (OAS), the scientific and professional organization of state radiation control directors. Participating in the announcement were Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, TDEC Commissioner David Salyers, and leaders from TVA and Type One.

Gov. Lee observed, “By creating a clear path for emerging technologies like fusion, we’re advancing the reliable, abundant American energy we’ll need for generations to come.”

Commissioner Salyers noted that the license was “a significant milestone that solidifies Tennessee’s reputation as the global hub for nuclear innovation,” adding, “We are proud to develop this groundbreaking regulatory framework for fusion energy that will serve as a model for other states.”

name: Detroit and Evs
title: Is China's EV market takeover inevitable as Chinese automakers prepare to gain a foothold ...
description:
Is it a metaphor for what's ahead, as China appears to be on course to dominate the global auto market?
Asked if Chinese EVs are better than models made in the U.S., he didn't hesitate.
At that level, Chinese imports will represent almost 25% of last year's total EV market in Canada.
But Chinese EVs have a key advantage: Significantly lower prices make them very appealing to many buyers.
Zhao said consumers in the U.S. and around the world deserve the driving experience offered by Chinese EVs.
text:
Beijing — On the outskirts of the Chinese port city of Ningbo, surrounded by lush green hills topped with giant wind turbines to harness the power of the gales off the East China Sea, is a factory where bosses believe they're making the cars of the future.

It's where the Geely Auto Group, one of China's largest EV makers, produces its luxury brand Zeekr. The name is a merging of two concepts — Zee stands for Generation Z, and Kr is the chemical symbol for Krypton. Yes, the same element at the heart of the rock that drains Superman's powers.

Is it a metaphor for what's ahead, as China appears to be on course to dominate the global auto market?

Inside the massive plant, which started operating in 2023, giant mechanical arms guided by artificial intelligence work in unison to assemble the vehicles. The plant is 99% automated; machines building machines. The occasional human worker monitors the process.

Zeekr Vice President of manufacturing Zhao Chunlin used to work for General Motors. He told CBS News he admires and respects U.S. automakers, as he discussed the 100-year-plus legacies of GM and Ford.

But Zhao, and China, are focused on the future, not the past, and he was confident that he's now working for a company in a country that many believe will dictate the future terms of the auto industry — and potentially obliterate the opposition.

Zhao said he believed Chinese customers' demand for excellence had propelled his nation to the forefront of the EV industry.

"We are the best because we have the biggest market in the world, so customers' requirements are very high because there is so much choice. They want it better, better, better. They want everything!!"

Asked if Chinese EVs are better than models made in the U.S., he didn't hesitate.

"Yeah, sure," he said. "Even Tesla made in China is better quality than Tesla made in America."

Zeekrs will very soon be sold in North America, thanks to a trade deal that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney signed in January during a meeting in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

A total of 49,000 Chinese EVs will be sold in the first year under the deal, with Canadian tariffs on the imports dropping from 100%, to just 6%.

At that level, Chinese imports will represent almost 25% of last year's total EV market in Canada. They will be competing for market share against U.S. brands including Tesla, GM and Ford. But Chinese EVs have a key advantage: Significantly lower prices make them very appealing to many buyers.

If Australia is any guide to what can happen when Chinese companies gain traction in the EV market, then U.S. automakers, beware: Chinese-made vehicles have gone from zero market share 10 years ago, to over 30% today.

A similar trend is playing out in Europe where, despite higher tariffs on some brands, Chinese EVs are grabbing an ever larger share of the market, jumping from 9% to about 14% already this year compared to last.

Could it happen in Canada, too?

It's too soon to say. It's a very different market, and U.S. automakers obviously have a geographical advantage, but the Chinese foothold in the Canadian market could offer a window into the future, and the view should be of concern to America and its auto industry based, just over the Detroit River.

The U.S. government has so far refused to allow Chinese vehicles into the market, blocking them with prohibitive tariffs and bans, citing concerns about national security and protecting the domestic auto industry.

At the Zeekr factory, Zhao said nobody, in the U.S. or anywhere else, should view China's automakers as a threat. He said that while China, and Geely, have plans to one day sell and potentially manufacture cars in the U.S., it would be in the form of collaborations and joint ventures.

"It's not necessary to be fearful. The market is very huge," he said, adding with a smile: "Trump, don't worry!"

Zhao said consumers in the U.S. and around the world deserve the driving experience offered by Chinese EVs. To prove his point, they let CBS News test drive Zeekr's most luxurious, top-of-the-line model, the 9X plug-in hybrid.

They call it China's Rolls Royce. The design, however, is a clear mimicking of the iconic British Range Rover SUV. Geely acquired Swedish autogiant Volvo in 2010, so the vehicle incorporates European design with Chinese technology.

As soon as you open the door, it exudes luxury. From the leather interior to the plush seats, the sound system — made by British luxury brand Naim Audio, which can also be found in Bentleys — and the technology, including a largely autonomous driving capability.

The engine is barely audible, and the drive is incredibly smooth. The hybrid can go from 0-100 kilometers per hour (about 62 mph) in just four seconds, and it has a combined range of 745 miles on one tank of fuel and charge.

Another highlight: The 9X can park itself while you stand outside and watch — a potential game changer for drivers who hate to parallel or reverse park.

But most importantly, it retails for about $70,000, about half the cost of a Cadillac Escalade.

Only 10 years ago, Chinese cars weren't really taken seriously in most Western markets. Now, they're considered by many to be just as good, if not better than many U.S. and European brands, especially for the price paid.

Zeekr is now selling its vehicles in more than 50 countries, and it will begin exporting the 9X to Europe and the Middle East this month.

description:
Commercial Capital vs. Total Investments The implication is practical: building the conditions that let commercial capital in, market by market, is what will allow these markets to reach the scale the transition needs.

Renewable commercial finance follows conditions that make revenue and returns predictable, so unlocking it means building those conditions where they are missing, not adding to where capital already gathers.
Understanding what draws commercial capital into a market is where this series goes next.

text:
Renewable energy capital mix, cumulative (2017-2021)

This is not a smooth progression from mature markets to emerging ones. The sample splits into two distinct groups: countries that attract commercial finance at scale, and countries that still rely heavily on development finance, with very few in transition between the two.

The concentration is not only in how each country finances its own projects; it is in how little of the total is shared. 88% of all commercial capital in the 23 selected countries sampled went to just five markets: India, Chile, Japan, the Republic of Korea and Brazil, with the top three alone taking more than 60%.

Technology type follows a clear ranking. Wind draws the highest commercial share, followed by solar and then hydropower. However, high commercial shares do not mean broad participation. Across all three technologies, commercial investment still concentrates in the same few markets.

Capital mix of renewable energy commitments, by technology (2017-2021)

A low commercial share is not a failing grade. Our analysis shows that the countries at the bottom of the list finance their renewables almost entirely through development capital. The OECD notes that fragile and nascent markets often require high levels of concessionality before private capital can enter, and this is where development capital can provide more impetus. From our analysis, nascent markets are not those that are necessarily falling behind; they are markets where commercial capital has yet to scale alongside public finance. By the same OECD benchmark, progress would see commercial finance increase and reliance on concessional support decline over time. That is where the greatest opportunity for growth lies.

Commercial capital and market scale

The 23 countries span an enormous range: Botswana attracted USD 42 million in renewable energy investment over five years, while India attracted nearly USD 35 billion, a difference of more than 800-fold, and the more plausible reading is that commercial capital is what lets investment reach that scale.

The message from the graph is clear: within this sample, the scale of investment the energy transition requires has only been reached by markets with a substantial commercial share. No country has reached the top of the investment range while still relying mainly on development finance to get there.

Commercial Capital vs. Total Investments

The implication is practical: building the conditions that let commercial capital in, market by market, is what will allow these markets to reach the scale the transition needs.

Where commercial capital remains limited, development finance carries much of the investment burden. For example, for every dollar of commercial capital committed, Sub-Saharan Africa drew around 59 cents of development finance over the period, Latin America just 6 cents, and East Asia none at all. In those markets, public money is not only filling a gap, it is helping build the conditions that private investment needs to follow.

Public money per commercial dollar in the 23 selected countries, by region, cumulative (2017-2021)

Making room for commercial capital

The task now is to crowd private investment into the markets commercial capital has so far skipped. The data shows where that counts most: the 11 countries financing less than a fifth of their renewables commercially, where public money is currently doing nearly all the work. For policymakers, that is where energy transition planning has most to gain. For development finance institutions and investors, there is an opportunity to deploy catalytic capital to unlock private money that would not otherwise flow.

Renewable commercial finance follows conditions that make revenue and returns predictable, so unlocking it means building those conditions where they are missing, not adding to where capital already gathers.

Understanding what draws commercial capital into a market is where this series goes next. This first piece maps where the money flows and how it relates to market scale. The posts that follow explore the factors that shape commercial investment decisions, including financial development, policy incentives, political commitment, regulatory frameworks, infrastructure and the broader business environment. Together, they help explain why private capital flows to some markets and not others, and what governments and partners can do to change that.

Follow the series as we build the full picture of how to unlock commercial capital for renewable energy.

text:
US-based Aqua Metals has signed a six-year letter of intent with commodity trader WMC Group. The deal covers all lithium carbonate planned from the upcoming Project Headwaters plant in the American Midwest.

This site represents the first full-scale commercial use of the company’s AquaRefining system. The technology extracts battery-grade materials from spent batteries using electrochemistry instead of high-heat smelting.

Most battery recycling plants rely on pyrometallurgical smelting. These systems burn shredded battery scrap at very high temperatures. While smelting recovers nickel and cobalt, it burns away lithium or leaves it trapped in slag. The alternative approach is hydrometallurgy, which dissolves the metals in acid.

However, traditional hydrometallurgical plants consume large volumes of one-time chemical reagents. These chemicals produce substantial hazardous waste, including sodium sulfate salt cakes that require landfill disposal.

A closed-loop circuit

AquaRefining operates through a closed-loop, room-temperature circuit. It treats “black mass,” the powder created when spent lithium-ion batteries are crushed and shredded. The process uses electricity rather than consumable acid-base neutralizers to recover the dissolved metals.

Within the cells, electricity plates out pure elemental metals and selectively precipitates battery compounds like lithium carbonate. Because the chemical bath regenerates continuously during the electrical cycle, the facility avoids producing the massive liquid and solid waste streams common in older plants.

More from Energy

See All

Project Headwaters aims to start operating in 2028 with an initial output of 250 metric tons of lithium carbonate. Production plans call for a steady ramp to 2,250 metric tons each year by 2032.

Over the six-year span, the site is designed to deliver roughly 7,000 metric tons of the compound. That volume holds an estimated market value of 135 million dollars, though final revenue will reflect prevailing metal spot prices and purity checks. The non-binding agreement with WMC Group also covers refined nickel and cobalt. Both companies plan to sign a final, binding contract by September 30, 2026.

Plans for feedstock sourcing, too

Aside from raw product sales, the firms are setting up joint plans for feedstock sourcing and tolling arrangements. Under tolling agreements, third parties deliver raw black mass to the site to be refined for a processing fee.

The partnership arrives just as federal rules force battery scrap to stay inside the United States. Under the Defense Production Act, the White House classified recycled battery minerals as industrial materials critical to national security.

In addition, the Bureau of Industry and Security enacted a rule requiring scrap processors to sell black mass entirely to domestic firms.

American battery recyclers can no longer export unprocessed black mass overseas, creating immediate demand for domestic refining plants that can turn raw scrap into finished precursor chemicals.

Completed the first commercial sale

This processing capacity carries strategic utility beyond waste management. By generating a local supply of low-cost refined minerals, facilities like Headwaters directly feed domestic battery manufacturing, energy storage grids, defense systems, and electric vehicle production.

Aqua Metals recently completed its first commercial sale of recycled lithium carbonate to an American buyer at market rates. The transaction confirmed that chemically recycled lithium meets the chemical tolerances needed for battery manufacturing.

text:
Whilst the development of low-emission hydrogen is primarily associated with production from renewable sources, projects based on so-called ‘blue hydrogen’ – produced from natural gas by capturing and storing the CO₂ generated during the process – are also continuing to take shape. This is demonstrated by two initiatives recently announced in the United States and Japan.

In Louisiana, the US-based company CF Industries, the world’s largest producer of ammonia, has announced, together with JERA, a Japanese energy group, and Mitsui, a Japanese conglomerate active in trading and investment, the start of construction on Blue Point One, a $3.7 billion project for a plant that will use hydrogen derived from natural gas to produce low-carbon ammonia. The plant is designed to capture and permanently store 98% of CO2 generated during production.

Once fully operational, the plant will have an average capacity of 1.4 million tonnes of ammonia per year, which, according to the developers, will make it the largest of its kind in the world. The new site will be built in Modeste and is expected to come on stream in 2029.

The joint venture leading the project is owned 40% by CF Industries, 35% by JERA and 25% by Mitsui, whilst the transport and permanent storage of CO2 The project will be managed by a joint venture between 1PointFive, a subsidiary of the US oil group Occidental, and the Canadian company Enbridge.

In Japan, however, the energy company INPEX has begun injecting CO2 in a depleted gas field in Kashiwazaki, in Niigata Prefecture, where it is trialling the production of blue hydrogen and blue ammonia combined with carbon dioxide capture and storage.

The hydrogen is produced from natural gas extracted from the Minami-Nagaoka field, which is operated by INPEX itself. Part of it powers the power generation plants at the Kashiwazaki Hydrogen Park, whilst another part is used to produce ammonia for local customers. The CO2 The carbon dioxide generated during hydrogen production is, however, separated and captured and, from now on, injected into a geological formation in the nearby depleted Higashi-Kashiwazaki field for permanent storage.

As the Japanese company points out in a statement, the separation of CO2 This is achieved using HiPACT, a technology developed by the engineering firm JGC Global in collaboration with the German company BASF. The system enables carbon dioxide to be captured whilst it is still under high pressure, thereby reducing, according to Inpex, the energy required and the costs of subsequent injection operations.

text:
Los Angeles, Calif. – Clean Power Alliance (CPA) is now accepting applications for its 2026-27 Community Benefits Grant. The program, launched in 2021, is a partnership between CPA and Calpine Community Energy that provides funding to nonprofit organizations working to advance clean energy, community resilience, workforce development, environmental education and stewardship, and equitable access to clean energy in the communities CPA serves. This year, a total of $358,000 will be distributed among successful applicants across Los Angeles and Ventura counties.

“At Clean Power Alliance, we believe meaningful progress happens when we invest in the organizations that understand and serve our communities every day,” said CPA Senior Director of Government Affairs, Gina Goodhill. “Through this grant program, we are proud to support nonprofit partners whose work advances sustainability, strengthens community resilience and expands access to opportunities that help create a cleaner, healthier and more equitable future for the people we serve.”

The Community Benefits Grant is open to organizations and projects focused on five pathways to advance clean energy: 1) Research 2) Education 3) Environmental and Social Justice Communities 4) Workforce Development 5) Resilience.

The grant application period is open from Sept. 1 through Sept. 15, 2026. Grants ranging from $20,000 to $35,000 will be awarded. Eligible nonprofits must be working within at least one of the 38 communities CPA serves throughout Los Angeles and Ventura counties.

“We’re honored to continue our partnership with Clean Power Alliance and support the nonprofit organizations that play such a vital role in their communities,” said Josh Brock, vice president of CCA commercial operations at Calpine Community Energy. “These organizations bring local knowledge, trusted relationships and innovative solutions to the challenges communities face. By expanding access to funding, we can help strengthen their capacity, advance meaningful initiatives and build on the positive impact Clean Power Alliance is creating across the region.”

With grant support, numerous organizations over the years have been able to bring diverse and inspiring projects to life. Last year, grant funding was provided to several nonprofits working on a variety of initiatives. Recipients included:

API Forward Movement ($20,000) Funds were provided to support a six-week, hands-on environmental justice leadership program for high school students from communities in the West San Gabriel Valley.

California Green Business Network ($26,400) Funds were provided to support the expansion of the Green Business program in Ventura County, which helps small businesses in disadvantaged areas overcome barriers to clean energy adoption.

California Housing Partnership ($30,000) Funds were provided to help modernize Public Housing Authority (PHA) Utility Allowances in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. Through comprehensive research, the partnership analyzed how PHAs account for modern technologies like heat pumps and induction cooktops, creating a public tracking database to identify gaps and best practices.

Climate Mental Health Network ($21,516) Funds were provided to expand the Climate Emotions Toolkit and professional development for teachers in Los Angeles County, equipping educators to address students’ emotional responses to climate change.

Community Environmental Council ($26,000) Funds were provided to expand clean energy and heat resilience efforts through the Ventura County Heat Action Plan by delivering bilingual education, technical assistance and outreach to vulnerable Latino, Indigenous and low-income communities.

Designing Resilience ($28,500) Funds were provided to support expanding the Altadena Community Designing Resilience Initiative into a year-long program focused on education, engagement and resident-led planning.

Food Education and Discovery ($30,000) Funds were provided to support Food Ed’s Entrepreneur Program—a hands-on climate and sustainability education initiative serving Title I middle and high schools in the cities of Arcadia, Temple City and Monrovia.

Grades of Green ($20,000) Funds were provided to support the SOAR (Service, Ownership, Achievement, Respect) Eco-Innovation Virtual Academy and a community outreach day in Los Angeles County—advancing education, workforce development and environmental justice.

MERITO Foundation ($25,000) Funds were provided to support MERITO Foundation’s Energy & Climate Education, Skill Building & Green Workforce Development project for economically disadvantaged 7th–12th grade students from Title I schools to become climate innovators and future green workforce leaders.

Pando Populus ($22,500) Funds were provided to support a project-based learning initiative that takes sustainability ideas from Southland college and university classrooms and turns them into real-world projects.

Reel Guppy Outdoors ($15,000) Funds were provided to expand the Dockside Multimedia Learning and Research Center, a floating laboratory that provides Ventura County youth and families from underserved communities with hands-on environmental science, clean energy education and workforce development opportunities.

Ventura County Community Foundation ($24,933) Funds were provided to strengthen the Environmental Workforce Collaborative (EWC), a regional partnership of five nonprofit organizations that builds environmental resilience, advances green workforce pathways and delivers hands-on education across Ventura County.

Nonprofit organizations interested in learning more and applying for the 2026-27 Community Benefits Grant can visit www.cleanpoweralliance.org/CBG.

In addition to grants, CPA provides scholarships at 11 community colleges and supports pre-apprenticeship and labor training programs that connect people in marginalized communities with clean energy careers. Learn more at www.cleanpoweralliance.org/workforce/.
