General Motors (NYSE:GM) Consumer Cyclical General Motors Company (NYSE:GM) 85.63 USD -0.690 ↓ 0.799% stayed firmly in view as the automaker advanced a recalibrated electric strategy that blends battery-electric trucks and sport-utility vehicles with a renewed emphasis on hybrids, underpinned by sizeable commitments to domestic factories and battery capacity. The evolving approach positioned the long-established manufacturer at the center of a wider industry conversation about how to pace the transition to electrification while sustaining the truck and utility franchises that anchor the business today.

Sector backdrop for the transition

The moves came against a backdrop in which automakers are rethinking how quickly to shift toward battery-electric transport, tempering earlier ambitions with a more measured cadence that leans on hybrids as a bridge. Coverage of that recalibration has tracked how heritage manufacturers adjust product plans and factory footprints, and readers following the theme can explore related developments on this automobile stocks hub, where the shift across established and emerging players continues to take shape.

For a company with deep roots in trucks and utility vehicles, the transition demands careful sequencing. The franchises that generate the bulk of the business must be defended even as capital flows toward electric platforms and battery supply. Striking that balance, funding the shift without undermining the products that sustain it, has become the defining task, and the recalibrated strategy reflects an attempt to navigate it with greater flexibility.

A recalibrated electric strategy

At the heart of the story lies a pivot toward a more balanced mix, pairing continued commitment to battery-electric vehicles with an expanded role for hybrids, trucks and utility vehicles. Rather than racing toward an all-electric lineup on an aggressive timeline, the company has signaled a willingness to meet demand as it actually materializes, offering electrified choices across a spectrum of powertrains. Electric vehicles have been described as remaining a guiding aim even as the path toward them grows more pragmatic.

A balanced approach acknowledges that adoption of battery-electric vehicles has not advanced in a straight line, with demand ebbing and flowing across segments and regions. By broadening the menu to include hybrids, the maker aims to serve buyers seeking improved efficiency without a full plug-in commitment, while continuing to build electric capability. The strategy trades the clarity of a single technology path for the resilience of a diversified lineup, a stance many peers have adopted.

Major factory commitments

Reinforcing the strategy, the company unveiled a substantial commitment to its domestic production facilities, including funds earmarked to convert an existing plant for the manufacture of electric versions of its flagship pickups. Directing significant capital toward electrifying the truck lineup signals intent to carry heritage strength in pickups into the battery-electric era, a segment where brand recognition and customer loyalty run deep. The scale of the commitment underscored the seriousness of the effort.

Converting established plants for electric production is a demanding endeavor, requiring retooling, workforce training and coordination across a complex supply base. Yet anchoring electric truck manufacturing within existing domestic sites leverages infrastructure and expertise built over decades. The commitment framed the electrified pickup as a cornerstone of the strategy, aligning the transition with the products that most define the company identity in the market.

Battery capacity and materials

Complementing the vehicle plans, the company advanced commitments to battery manufacturing, including support for an additional cell plant, alongside moves to secure the raw materials that batteries require. A finalized government-backed loan tied to a domestic lithium project, pursued through a joint venture, reflected an effort to build a more secure and localized supply of a critical mineral. Controlling more of the battery chain has become central to the economics of electrification.

Batteries account for a large share of an electric vehicle cost and performance, so securing capacity and materials is a strategic priority rather than a peripheral concern. By investing in cell production and upstream mineral supply, the maker seeks to insulate itself from shortages and price swings while improving control over quality and cost. That vertical reach into the battery chain strengthens the foundation on which the electrified lineup rests.

Supply chain resilience

The company also moved to shore up its supply base, signing a sizeable arrangement described as guarding against parts constraints. Recent years have taught the industry hard lessons about the fragility of global supply chains, as shortages of components rippled through production and disrupted output. Securing supply through longer arrangements represents an effort to build resilience and reduce the vulnerability that intermittent shortages can impose on a complex manufacturing operation.

A more resilient supply chain supports steadier production, which in turn underpins the ability to deliver both established and electrified vehicles reliably. For a maker managing a transition, dependable access to components is essential, since disruptions can stall the ramp of new electric products just as much as they hamper existing lines. The arrangement fit within a broader emphasis on stabilizing the operational base amid an uncertain environment.

Trucks and utility franchises

Underpinning the whole strategy are the truck and utility franchises that have long defined the company. These vehicles command strong customer loyalty and generate the resources that help fund the transition, making their health central to the broader plan. Carrying that strength into electrified and hybrid forms, rather than treating electrification as a departure from heritage, has emerged as a guiding principle behind the recalibrated approach.

Electrifying pickups and utility vehicles seeks to blend the appeal of established nameplates with the efficiency and technology of new powertrains. If executed well, that path could preserve the loyalty attached to the brands while extending it into a lower-emission era. The emphasis on trucks throughout the factory and battery commitments underscored how central these franchises remain to the company sense of its own direction.

Autonomy and software adjacency

Beyond hardware, the company has maintained involvement in efforts around automated driving and connected-vehicle software, threading it into the wider automation theme reshaping the sector. As value migrates toward software and services, engagement with driver-assistance and autonomy keeps the maker relevant to a dimension of competition that increasingly complements the traditional work of designing and building vehicles. That adjacency broadens the story beyond metal and batteries.

Software-defined features and automated capabilities are becoming differentiators as much as horsepower or range, and staying engaged with those frontiers helps a heritage maker avoid ceding ground to technology-focused entrants. The company activity in this space complements its hardware strengths, positioning it to compete on the services and experience layer that is coming to define the modern vehicle.

Competitive landscape

The company contends with traditional rivals, electric-focused newcomers and global manufacturers pushing into battery-electric segments. In trucks and utility vehicles, its heritage offers a strong base, yet the electrified versions of those segments are drawing determined entrants. Prevailing depends on converting scale, brand loyalty and manufacturing depth into electric products that resonate on price, capability and dependability across an increasingly crowded field.

A recalibrated strategy that leans on hybrids as a bridge distinguishes the company approach from makers pursuing faster all-electric timelines. Whether that measured cadence proves advantageous will depend on how demand evolves and how effectively the electrified truck and utility offerings land with buyers. The competitive stakes keep pressure on execution across every element of the plan, from factories to batteries to software.

Market environment and index context

The developments unfolded amid a broad market animated by technology and automation themes alongside caution over trade and demand. As a long-standing member of major benchmarks, the automaker sits within the S&P 500, and shifts in its fortunes feed into how the wider gauge of large domestic companies is read. That membership ties the name to the broader movement of market sentiment across sectors.

Within a tape shaped by cross-currents, a heritage automaker recalibrating its electric plans tends to trade on the balance between confidence in its measured strategy and questions about the pace of the transition. That interplay was visible across the period, as commitments to factories and batteries vied with broader uncertainty over demand and trade for influence over how the shares were perceived.

Business positioning

Taken together, the strands present the company as a heritage manufacturer steering a pragmatic course through electrification, blending battery-electric trucks and utilities with hybrids while committing heavily to domestic factories, battery capacity and supply resilience. The recalibrated strategy embodies an effort to match the pace of the transition to real demand, protecting core franchises while building toward a more electrified lineup over time.

For a market weighing established automakers against nimble entrants, the story turns on execution, on whether scale, brand loyalty and manufacturing depth can be translated into electrified products delivered profitably. The steady attention on the shares reflected a market prepared to credit the measured approach while remaining alert to the considerable work involved in carrying it through.

Operational focus and execution

Underlying the strategy is the demanding daily discipline of operating an expansive manufacturing enterprise, where assembly plants, supplier networks and dealer relationships must work in unison to keep vehicles reaching customers. That operational rigor frequently shapes how the forward-looking commitments are judged, since a credible electrified roadmap rests on a demonstrated ability to build and deliver reliably at scale. Managing the cost of the transition, while preserving the quality and dependability that customers associate with the brand, forms the practical bedrock beneath the announcements about new plants and batteries.

The company also draws strength from a vast installed base of vehicles already on the road, supported by extensive service and parts operations that sustain a lasting connection to customers. That footprint provides steady activity and a familiar audience to which new electric and hybrid products can be introduced. Carrying those relationships into an electrified era, where servicing needs and ownership habits evolve, represents both a test and an advantage, giving the maker a broad platform from which to stage its transition over time.

Industry developments shaping the theme

The wider automobile industry has been passing through a stretch of rapid transformation, as electrification, software and shifting supply dynamics reshape how vehicles are conceived, manufactured and sold. Heritage makers have been adjusting product plans, retooling factories and forming new supply arrangements to keep pace. Within that current, the company recalibrated strategy has been read as one template for managing the transition, its measured blend of battery-electric and hybrid offerings watched as a signal of how the established side of the industry is adapting to conditions that remain unsettled.

Adoption of battery-electric vehicles has progressed unevenly, shaped by pricing, charging access and the readiness of supporting infrastructure. Those practical realities have led many makers to hedge across powertrains rather than commit fully to a single path, and the company measured cadence reflects exactly that caution. By leaning on hybrids as a bridge while continuing to build electric capability, the maker positions itself to meet demand as it actually emerges, mirroring a pragmatism that has spread across the sector in recent times.

The economics of batteries and critical minerals have moved to the center of that industry conversation, since the cost and availability of cells shape how affordably electric vehicles can be built. The company commitments to battery capacity and localized mineral supply speak directly to that reality, aligning it with a broader push across the sector to secure the foundations of electrified manufacturing rather than leaving them exposed to distant and volatile supply chains.

title: Data center projects in Pennsylvania face stronger local scrutiny after Shapiro's executive order
description:
Governors across the country are relying on their executive powers to address the increasing public backlash against data center proposals.
Josh Shapiro signed executive order 2026-05 on Aug. 18, 2026, placing restrictions on the state’s review of permits related to data centers.
What the executive order does Shapiro’s executive order does not completely stop data center permitting activities.
It prohibits any agencies under the governor’s oversight from entering into nondisclosure agreements in connection with a data center project.
Collectively, the policies in the executive order are likely to both slow down the permitting process for data centers and give local officials more leverage over data center projects.
text:
Governors across the country are relying on their executive powers to address the increasing public backlash against data center proposals.

In July 2026, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul placed an effective moratorium on data center permitting until the state’s Department of Public Service creates a generic environmental impact statement regarding the impacts of data centers. Similarly, in August 2026, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on data centers until state agencies can audit data related to impacts on the electric grid.

In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed executive order 2026-05 on Aug. 18, 2026, placing restrictions on the state’s review of permits related to data centers.

I am the executive director of Penn State’s Center for Energy Law and Policy, and I have been tracking policy responses to data center proposals in Pennsylvania and across the country. I find it notable that one of the justifications the governor appears to cite in his order is a little-used but potentially powerful legal tool: the Environmental Rights Amendment to the Pennsylvania Constitution.

What the executive order does

Shapiro’s executive order does not completely stop data center permitting activities. But it does add requirements that may slow their development and give local officials more influence over the process:

The order makes all data center projects ineligible for the PA Permit Fast Track Program, which streamlines permitting for certain high-impact projects.

It prohibits any agencies under the governor’s oversight from entering into nondisclosure agreements in connection with a data center project.

It requires the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection to create a public map that shows permitting information about all known data center projects in the state.

Perhaps most significantly, it prohibits officials from issuing state permits for data center projects until after the developer has demonstrated it has complied with local plans and received all required municipal approvals. This ordering of permitting has the potential to enhance local power over data center projects.

The order also creates a two-tiered system for permitting review. One tier is for developers that agree to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, standards. The other is for developers that do not comply.

Among other things, the GRID standards call for developers to secure all energy needed to power their facility, including a portion powered by clean energy; pay 100% of the costs of their project; and comply with environmental operating and reporting requirements.

Developers that agree to comply with the GRID standards will have their state permit applications reviewed on a rolling basis when they are submitted and issued on a rolling basis after all local requirements are met.

For projects that do not comply with the GRID standards, the state’s Department of Environmental Protection will not even begin reviewing state permit applications until the developers have obtained all necessary local permits.

Collectively, the policies in the executive order are likely to both slow down the permitting process for data centers and give local officials more leverage over data center projects. Municipal officials have significant authority over local land use decisions. Now that state permit review is contingent on local approvals, data center developers will have more incentive to work with local decision-makers to minimize delays.

The Environmental Rights Amendment

Beyond the scope of the order itself, I find it significant that the executive order cites “Pennsylvanians’ constitutional rights” as part of its justification.

Although the order does not specify which constitutional rights it is referring to, it appears to be a reference to the Pennsylvania Constitution’s Environmental Rights Amendment.

The Environmental Rights Amendment is in Article 1 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, along with political rights such as the freedom of speech and freedom of religion. It guarantees the people’s “right to clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment.”

Although it was added to the state Constitution in 1971, the impact of the Environmental Rights Amendment has been muted until recently. Earlier court decisions limited the legal power of the amendment. But recent opinions from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court have given it new life, raising legal questions about how the amendment will be interpreted in the future. Those cases clarified that it is not necessarily enough for the state to simply comply with environmental statutes. A law or state action that “unreasonably impairs” the right to clean air, pure water or other environmental values can be deemed unconstitutional.

If the commonwealth cites the Environmental Rights Amendment in litigation defending the executive order on data centers, courts will have another opportunity to interpret the amendment’s language – and therefore its power. Judges will be called upon to weigh how Pennsylvania’s constitutional obligations to protect its citzens’ rights to a clean environment are properly balanced against industry’s procedural and property rights to develop land. Depending on how courts decide those cases, the commonwealth – and even citizens – may have a more robust weapon in their fight for “clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment” going forward.

title: China Tells Carmakers To Play Nice Abroad After Years Of Encouraging Them To Fight Dirty ...
description:
The specter of China hangs over the rest of the car industry, which means it floats above The Morning Dump as well.
Chinese automakers aren’t alone.
China To Carmakers: Export Cars, Not Problems The Chinese government, via the Ministry of Commerce, has sent some guidelines out to automakers hoping to take advantage of global markets.
It’s why so many Chinese carmakers are barely profitable, if profitable at all.
To just heap more ironies on the pile, it’s also why Chinese carmakers need export markets.
text:
The specter of China hangs over the rest of the car industry, which means it floats above The Morning Dump as well. The country’s government has created a massive customer base and a large number of automakers to feed it. It’s also created a monster, and now Chinese authorities are having to wrestle with what that means.

Right off the bat, having created an industry built on undercutting rivals, Chinese authorities have released guidelines telling its own automakers to stop doing that crap when it goes to other markets. The so-called “China Speed” that’s allowed for quick evolution of models is also putting carmakers ahead of regulators, and the regulators are hoping to curb that behavior as well.

Chinese automakers aren’t alone. Volkswagen is having to contend with the its own ghouls. Specifically, the modular platforming that allowed it to spin off more than a hundred nameplates is now haunting the automaker. In the United States, August sales numbers are starting to roll in, and the ghost of tax incentives past must be confronted.

China To Carmakers: Export Cars, Not Problems

The Chinese government, via the Ministry of Commerce, has sent some guidelines out to automakers hoping to take advantage of global markets. The basic premise is that the outrageous price war waged on its own turf, the sales trickery, and all the other crap that automakers pulled shouldn’t be tried in foreign markets.

Nikkei Asia has the full rundown of guidelines, which include some real gems:

The guidelines state that automakers should “establish pricing strategies based on cost and guided by international market supply and demand,” and “refrain from disrupting market competition in order to gain unfair competitive advantages.”

The document also warns that companies’ promotional activities must comply with local regulations. They must avoid “false advertising, deceiving or misleading consumers, and safeguard the image of Chinese automotive brands.”

One chapter is dedicated to localization. Carmakers should “avoid exporting products that do not meet the needs of the target market and usage environment.” In local operations, enterprises should “recruit employees according to the principles of equal opportunity and fair treatment.”

The ironies embedded in all of this are a little hard for me to reckon with this early in the morning. First of all, I have to acknowledge that I’m not sure my own country has this kind of commitment to market fairness anymore, so any critique I have of Chinese automakers has to be set against that reality.

Having nodded to my own position inside a glass house, the biggest contradiction here is that Chinese automakers act like this because China’s government put a huge amount of focus and money behind spinning up as many carmakers as possible to start producing good cars, consequences be dammed. It’s why so many Chinese carmakers are barely profitable, if profitable at all. To just heap more ironies on the pile, it’s also why Chinese carmakers need export markets.

One way to look at it is that China created all the necessary conditions for carmakers to thrive (money, quick permitting, regulations, buyer incentives) without enough of the conditions necessary for a healthy market (competition). It’s like what happens with deer if there’s no hunting season.

Having been essentially kicked out of the United States and with Europe warily approving Chinese cars, it makes sense that the government doesn’t want carmakers to bring their bad habits abroad and risk losing access to those markets entirely.

[Ed Note: I find the advertising guideline to be rather fascinating. Here’s an entire nation — scores of companies — working together because it clearly believes that all it takes is one misstep from one company to ruin the reputation of all cars from that nation. -DT]

China Speed Is Too Speedy For Regulators

Even with all my critiques of Chinese business practices, the way that the company has been able to conquer the electric car market is still impressive. The rest of the industry is in awe of how fast China moves. The Chinese government? Maybe a little less so these days.

Per Bloomberg:

Chinese regulators are pushing hard on safety, launching a yearlong campaign that includes surprise inspections at carmakers to address concerns that quality could deteriorate in the pursuit of speed. Their view is in line with recent comments from executives at Zhejiang Geely Holding Group, Great Wall Motor Co. and Chery Automobile Co., who have warned that the faster development times essentially turn customers into guinea pigs who test durability or safety in real time.

“Cars aren’t fast-moving consumer goods. They touch the safety of millions of families and must endure the test of diverse road conditions, climates, and driving habits worldwide,” Li Xueyong, vice-president at Chery, said in an Aug. 26 social media post. “There are simply some development timelines we cannot afford to shortcut.”

Someone please tell that to Tesla.

Volkswagen’s Own Modular System Is At The Root Of Its Problems

As I mentioned in July, Volkswagen is looking to cut a bunch of its nameplates as it looks to a future that’s a lot more competitive. I didn’t hit the irony of this hard enough, which is that the modular platform expansion is what fueled VW’s growth over the last two decades. Thankfully, S&P Global Mobility is here with a hammer:

In practical terms, the plan will require the company’s engineers and accountants to scrutinize every model’s profitability. That process could prove useful given the size of VW’s portfolio, which currently includes nearly 150 models.

Ironically, this unwieldy lineup stems from the very strategy that fueled VW’s sales and profit growth: platform sharing across brands and segments. The iconic VW Golf, for example, has shared its platform with the Audi A3, the SEAT Leon and the Škoda Octavia since the late 1990s.

This kind of overlap can also occur within a single brand. The VW passenger car brand currently offers three models—the Tiguan, the T-Roc and the Taigo—that compete against each other in the European SUV-C segment. In today’s more challenging market, maintaining multiple models that compete within the same segment is increasingly difficult to justify.

You leave my Škodas alone!

It’s Going To Be A Hard Month For Automakers Who Sold A Lot Of EVs Last Year

With tax credits for EVs expiring last year, there was a rush of sales as both automakers and customers tried to claim the credits while they could. That’s starting to show up in August sales reports. Right now it looks like Hyundai’s monthly sales streak is going to end (it’ll still probably set an annual record), whereas Honda, which didn’t have a lot of EVs to sell, is doing better.

Automotive News has the early data, and hybrids continue to be the bright spot:

Honda continues to get a major boost from hybrids, with the Accord hybrid up 16 percent and CR-V hybrid up 8 percent last month.

The Honda brand’s light-truck sales fell 3.8 percent last month on weaker Pilot volume and the discontinued Prologue EV.

Three Acura models ― Integra, ADX and MDX ― posted double-digit gains of 17 percent or more last month.

Hyundai, too, saw hybrid sales rise.

What I’m Listening To While Writing TMD

Speaking of haunting, no one does ethereal quite like Phoebe Bridgers, who has a new album out that I’m digesting. There’s a little Bon Iver in it, for sure. Some Sufjan. I’m not sure I’ve got a favorite song yet, but the video for “I Can’t Wait” has some nice moves and a sweet Toyota truck.

The Big Question

What’s your all-time favorite MQB vehicle?

description:
Element Zero’s $53.6 million project could help create new opportunities to add value to Australia’s world-class iron ore resources, build specialist skills and strengthen Australian industrial supply chains.
Iron and steel production is one of the world's largest industrial sources of emissions, as conventional ironmaking typically uses coal and other carbon-based materials to convert iron ore into iron.
The first stage will involve a pilot plant capable of producing around one tonne of iron per day.
The pilot will test different types of Australian iron ore, including hematite and magnetite, and help demonstrate the technology to Australian and international steelmakers.
“Backing WA companies to develop new technologies means more opportunities to turn our world-class resources into higher-value products right here at home.”
text:
The Hon Chris Bowen MP, Minister for Climate Change and Energy

The Hon Madeleine King MP, Minister for Resources

Senator The Hon Tim Ayres, Minister for Industry and Innovation

The Hon Anne Aly MP, Minister for Small Business and International Development

The Hon Josh Wilson MP, Assistant Minister for Climate Change and Energy

The Albanese Government is backing Australian innovation and manufacturing with up to $26 million for technology that could turn Australian iron ore into lower-emissions iron using renewable electricity.

Through the Future Made in Australia Innovation Fund, administered by the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), the Government is supporting Perth-based Element Zero to test whether Australian iron ore can be converted into high purity iron at pilot scale, using an electricity-based process powered by renewables.

Element Zero’s $53.6 million project could help create new opportunities to add value to Australia’s world-class iron ore resources, build specialist skills and strengthen Australian industrial supply chains.

Iron and steel production is one of the world's largest industrial sources of emissions, as conventional ironmaking typically uses coal and other carbon-based materials to convert iron ore into iron.

Element Zero's project will test whether an alternative process – electrochemical ironmaking, which is powered by electricity and uses molten salts – could produce lower-emissions iron efficiently without relying on coal.

The pilot will test a process designed to operate at temperatures of around 400 to 450°C, which are lower than the temperatures typically used in traditional ironmaking processes.

The project will be delivered in two stages. The first stage will involve a pilot plant capable of producing around one tonne of iron per day.

Subject to a formal review, the second stage will scale production up to 10 tonnes per day.

The pilot will test different types of Australian iron ore, including hematite and magnetite, and help demonstrate the technology to Australian and international steelmakers.

This investment is part of ARENA’s efforts to build a portfolio of projects, also including hydrogen-based approaches, aimed at unlocking viable pathways for producing green iron at scale.

Green metals is a key priority under the Albanese Government’s Future Made in Australia agenda, helping Australia take advantage of our world-class iron ore resources and renewable energy to make more products here and capture new opportunities as the global economy decarbonises.

Quotes attributable to Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen:

“Australia has the iron ore the world needs and some of the best renewable energy resources in the world – the opportunity is to bring those advantages together and make more things here.

“This investment backs Australian technology that could add more value to Australian iron ore, support Australian manufacturing and help cut emissions from one of the hardest parts of the global economy to decarbonise.”

Quotes attributable to Minister for Resources, Madeleine King:

“Australia's iron ore industry has long been a cornerstone of our economy, and projects like this are helping position it for the future by developing new ways to turn our world-class resources into higher-value products here in Australia.”

Quotes attributable to Minister for Industry and Innovation, Tim Ayres:

“Australian researchers and companies are developing world-leading technologies, and this $53.6 million project is an important step in turning Australian innovation into Australian manufacturing capability.”

Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Josh Wilson:

“Ironmaking is one of the most emissions-intensive parts of steel production, which is why investing in cleaner ways to make iron is such an important opportunity for Australian industry, particularly here in Western Australia.”

Quotes attributable to Member for Cowan, Anne Aly:

“Western Australia has powered our economy for generations, and projects like this are about making sure we’re also at the forefront of the industries and jobs of the future.

“Backing WA companies to develop new technologies means more opportunities to turn our world-class resources into higher-value products right here at home.”

title: Partnering with Form Energy - Sequoia Capital
description:
During my garden leave before joining Sequoia, I kept thinking about Form Energy.
During my family vacations, I’d tell my siblings about Form Energy.
I first met Mateo Jaramillo , the CEO of Form Energy, in spring 2020.
Lithium-ion was a great chemistry for cars, and it could store grid-scale energy for 4-6 hours, but it was never going to store energy for multiple days.
Nine years in, Form had done the thing it set out to do: build battery systems that can compete with gas.
text:
There are certain companies you can’t stop thinking about.

During my garden leave before joining Sequoia, I kept thinking about Form Energy. During my family vacations, I’d tell my siblings about Form Energy. For me, it was always one of these companies that represented what venture capital was all about: a phenomenal team of entrepreneurs pursuing a world-changing idea that, if successful, could scale into a category-defining company.

I first met Mateo Jaramillo , the CEO of Form Energy, in spring 2020. It was a memorable meeting because it was the first in-person founder meeting I had in the COVID pandemic and we were all wearing masks. At that time, Mateo described a simple idea: solar and wind were going to take over the grid, but we needed batteries to store that energy. Lithium-ion was a great chemistry for cars, and it could store grid-scale energy for 4-6 hours, but it was never going to store energy for multiple days. Thinking from first principles, Mateo, who previously started and ran Tesla’s energy business, had assembled the battery Avengers, including legendary battery scientist Yet-Ming Chiang as Chief Scientist and Billy Woodford as CTO. The team set their sights on building an iron-air battery: iron, because it’s cheap and abundant, and air, because it’s free. The goal was to turn those cheap materials into a battery that could compete with gas peaker plants on cost while delivering a clean and reliable baseload energy resource.

Knowing very little about batteries at the time, I reached out to a group of professors to diligence whether the science worked. I ended up selecting a Harvard professor and hired him as a consultant. At the end of the project, he gave us a thumbs up, and as a sign of his excitement, asked if he could roll his consulting fee into our investment.

When I arrived at Sequoia in mid-2023, Mateo was one of my first calls. At that time he was just starting construction on Form Energy’s first high-volume battery manufacturing facility, located on a shuttered steel mill site in West Virginia. I flew out for a factory visit with my partner Isaiah Boone in July 2024, and we were astounded. So many companies come to us talking about reindustrializing America, and here was a company that was actually doing it, and creating more than 400 new jobs along the way. Given that China is the epicenter of battery manufacturing globally, we were energized by the potential to build a US national battery champion, starting with a fundamentally new technology, which is what America excels at.

The following year, the company went through what is colloquially termed “production hell.” This is exactly what Tesla, SpaceX and others had gone through before them. If you really want to reindustrialize this country, these things don’t happen overnight, and they are far from easy. Companies that go through this gauntlet come out sturdier and stronger. To Mateo and the team’s credit, they doubled down. He had by then relocated his entire family from San Francisco to Western Pennsylvania, a short drive from the plant. Having experienced this type of scaling at Tesla, Mateo knew what to do: live it, sleep it, breathe it — until you've pulled through.

And pull through he did. I knew he’d turned the corner when finally, the company received the order that everyone knew would eventually come: a large hyperscale project. Nine years in, Form had done the thing it set out to do: build battery systems that can compete with gas. In the meantime, luck worked in their favor too: AI provided a huge catalyst in the market, where suddenly rebuilding the grid went from “nice to have” to “need to have.” As an AI investor, this company, which had spent years building deep relationships with utilities and regulators, was now in a prime position to serve emergent AI demand.

Isaiah and I flew back to West Virginia, exactly two years after our prior visit. This time we had an agenda: convince Mateo to partner with Sequoia. Although he’d already closed his Series G round, we persuaded him to let us invest. Initially, we proposed a $50M investment. But when Mateo came to present to the Sequoia partnership, they were so blown away by his clarity of vision and substantive, execution-oriented mindset that we upsized to $100M.

As I wrote in my very first note to Sequoia in 2023 about Form Energy, this is a company like SpaceX or Nvidia where it can take a decade to get off the ground, but once you get off the ground, the market opportunity is very large — Form is addressing a terawatt-scale market. The opportunity to now scale up from a handful of initial projects toward completely transforming the US grid is tremendous. Not only that, but it is no longer optional — it is something that we as a country will absolutely have to do for AI to achieve its long-term potential.

However, applying small modular nuclear technology in real life has proved challenging and not a little expensive.
Yet this has not deterred the Trump administration from pursuing a greater role for nuclear energy in the country’s energy mix.
Earlier this year, the federal government announced it was looking into floating nuclear power as President Trump seeks to boost U.S. nuclear power capacity fourfold by 2050.
Not everyone agrees that floating nuclear reactors are conducive to greater security, but small modular reactors remain quite popular.

text:
The port of Corpus Christi has become one of two ports selected for a project aimed at integrating small modular reactors in a bid to expand the use of nuclear power in more industries—and propel SMR technology forward.

Small modular reactors are all the rage, at least on paper. They can be installed more quickly than conventional nuclear reactors, and their locations can be more flexible. They are also significantly cheaper to build than conventional reactors and can be constructed incrementally to meet the growing energy demand of a site.

However, applying small modular nuclear technology in real life has proved challenging and not a little expensive. In the United States, NuScale, which was set to build the country’s first SMR, canceled the project, citing a lack of interest amid rising electricity costs.

Yet this has not deterred the Trump administration from pursuing a greater role for nuclear energy in the country’s energy mix. Earlier this year, the federal government announced it was looking into floating nuclear power as President Trump seeks to boost U.S. nuclear power capacity fourfold by 2050.

“Submerged reactor systems have been safely deployed in naval applications for decades, demonstrating their potential as a reliable source of energy in demanding marine environments. While no commercial deployment on the Outer Continental Shelf is planned or approved at this time, it could greatly strengthen America's energy security in the future,” the acting director of the Marine Mineral Administration, Matt Giacona, said last month.

Not everyone agrees that floating nuclear reactors are conducive to greater security, but small modular reactors remain quite popular. The port of Corpus Christi, along with Long Beach, were selected for the project due to their importance in U.S. trade. Long Beach handles $300 billion worth of cargo annually, according to the port’s CEO, as cited by Forbes. Corpus Christi is a major oil and fuel export terminal, with fuel exports in 2024 alone worth $80 billion, according to data from the Comptroller’s office, cited by Forbes.

The potential integration of small nuclear reaction at the two ports would aim to make sure that “our critical Gulf Coast maritime supply chains remain resilient against any contingency, from extreme weather to power grid disruptions, while training the next generation of high-skilled American mariners,” according to Maritime Administrator Stephen Carmel. The Maritime Administration is the Department of Transport’s division directly in charge of the small modular reactor project.

Nuclear power fell out of favor as wind and solar rose to fame, but over the past couple of years, the one baseload, emission-free source of electricity has begun making a comeback as the shortcomings of intermittent power generation become too obvious to ignore. While battery storage grows, to reduce these shortcomings, nuclear is increasingly being accepted as an inevitably greater part of the global energy mix if emission reduction targets are to be met without plunging the world into energy poverty.

Even the International Energy Agency has thrown its weight behind nuclear power, seeing as wind and solar could not shoulder the forecast surge in electricity demand on their own, even with batteries. Now, the Persian Gulf crisis has become the latest driver behind nuclear expansion—a genuine homegrown source of electricity, even though the world’s uranium supply mostly comes from a handful of countries.

Whether or not small nuclear reactors live up to the promise remains to be seen, yet the fact that interest in them remains quite alive and eager means that, chances are, at some point, they will make commercial sense. In the meantime, nuclear as a whole is getting another chance, not least thanks to Big Tech and the projected surge in electricity demand in the future, driven by artificial intelligence.

description:

text:
Virginia Environmental News

Local advocates are petitioning to bring passenger rail to Harrisonburg and the surrounding Shenandoah Valley in Virginia’s 2026 State Rail Plan. Learn more at the Blue Ridge Rail website where you can also sign the petition. The goal is to provide clean, affordable, and reliable public transportation to DC, Richmond, and beyond.

The Faith Alliance for Climate Solutions’ 10th annual Climate Crisis Forum will be on Oct. 22, 6:15-8:45 p.m. It will examine the public health consequences of extreme heat and explore local solutions such as tree cover. This is related to their urban heat mapping project in Northern Virginia with George Mason University. You can grab a ticket with a virtual option.

NextEra Energy is slashing its clean energy commitments and downplaying its public communications about renewable energy since President Trump returned to the White House. This is raising concerns in Virginia about its plans to merge with Dominion Energy.

The Trump administration is pushing for a full repeal of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule that protects millions of acres of virgin forestland nationwide. In Virginia, it would open up about 400,000 acres of forest, largely across the Shenandoah Valley region, to development.

Our Climate Crisis

A massive glacial collapse caused a catastrophic flash flood in the Himalayan border region of Nepal ⁠and Tibet. The death count is more than 900 people with over 4,400 still missing. The mountainous region is especially vulnerable to extreme weather events such as melting glaciers that have become more common because of global warming.

The world’s oceans hit their hottest temperatures ever recorded for July and August. It was fueled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific and heat waves in Europe and the Mediterranean.

Deaths increased by 16,000 in one week in June during Europe’s record heatwave. Most of the deaths were in France, Belgium and Germany, which are not accustomed to such heat.

Our climate crisis is affecting corporate bottom lines — making insurance harder to get, disrupting supply chains, and lowering crop yields. This, in turn, makes debt and equities markets riskier and could filter through to stock index funds and retirement portfolios.

Hotter summers are buckling roads and bending railroad tracks in the U.S. Engineering and construction standards have remained static while weather patterns have been changing.

Politics and Policy

Solar and EV sales cratered after Congress eliminated federal tax credits. Home batteries, however, bucked the trend partially because they offer people the ability to radically reduce their reliance on the centralized electrical grid in the midst of rising electric costs.

Canada is betting big on hydro and wind power in what could be North America’s largest-ever clean energy investment. At the same time they’re doubling down on oil sands in Alberta, alongside plans to build additional pipelines to get the oil to market.

President Trump is taking extraordinary steps to attack California’s position as a national leader in environmental protection. He is enlisting at least a half-dozen federal agencies to undermine the state’s efforts to pivot away from fossil fuels.

The Trump administration is promoting the opening of two new grid-scale battery manufacturing facilities in Michigan and Maine.

A tenured science professor at West Point was ordered last year to cut information about the human causes of climate change from his curriculum. He was fired when he refused.

Energy and Technology

What will be the world’s largest green hydrogen facility is near completion in Saudi Arabia. This reflects a broader shift in Saudi Arabia’s energy strategy by establishing itself as a major producer and exporter of renewable energy and clean fuels.

Indonesia is planning to start the mass production of homegrown electric motorcycles and cars. They set a target to have 13 million electric motorcycles and 2 million ​electric cars on their roads by 2030.

Sales of electric trucks and buses nearly doubled globally in 2025. China accounted for nearly 90% of these sales, while sales were also up substantially in the EU and India.

Tesla is advancing plans to build a $10.1 billion solar cell factory in Texas, and Translucent Solar says it will soon begin production at its South Carolina panel assembly site.

The South Korean grid-battery company DeltaX plans to construct a $141 million manufacturing headquarters outside of Atlanta. The company will join the Southeast’s battery belt that began expanding during the Biden administration.

Startup Sage Geosystems is now producing power from its first next-generation geothermal plant in Texas. The enhanced system involves drilling deep into hot rocks and fracturing them to create water pockets, then using the heat to generate power.

Climate-friendly electric heat pumps are becoming the norm among American home builders. Factors driving the change include improvements in the technology, energy savings, and the need for air-conditioning during hotter summers.

The dream of future, small-scale, and inexpensive nuclear reactors lives on despite repeated startup failures. Two former SpaceX engineers now seek to revive a long-dormant nuclear reactor experiment near Lynchburg, Virginia, to power the needs of data centers.

In our warming climate, the increase in electricity demand for air conditioning systems will exceed that for data centers by 2030. Yet this is receiving far less attention than is needed.

Land, Food, Agriculture

Farmers using regenerative farming and grazing are protecting Spanish land from wildfires.

In many orchards across the U.S., fruit has all but disappeared this year as trees bloomed three weeks early and were then hit by a devastating severe frost that killed the blossoms.

Tyson Foods will close or sell three of its beef facilities as the industry struggles due to the decreased number of cattle. Numbers shrank to a 75-year low after a prolonged drought burned up grazing lands in the western U.S. Other large meatpackers are also retrenching.

German hops farmers are struggling with hotter and dryer summers. One farmer’s solution is to grow his hops in the shade of solar panels. Farmers in other parts of the world, including Egypt, are experimenting with similar strategies.

Ecojustice

Mary Sprunger, professor of history at Eastern Mennonite University, reflects on The More-With-Less Cookbook, which sold more than one million copies. She says it was “a response to hunger crises in parts of Africa and Central Asia.” It invites “the relatively wealthy of the world to consume less so that others would have enough.”

Urban heat islands pose a growing health threat in our rapidly warming climate. There are solutions such as creating shade by planting trees, constructing green roofs and walls, and painting roofs light colors. Many tropical cities, however, cannot afford them.

Ecological and Climate Action

EVs are equipped with one-pedal driving, meaning that the electric motor functions to brake the car when you lift your foot off the accelerator. This converts some of the energy normally lost during braking back into electricity and eliminates the wear-and-tear of brake pads.

title: US begins fuel loading at 40-year-old Palisades nuclear plant ahead of restart
description:
As countries look to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, nuclear energy is making a major comeback.
Once a popular energy source, nuclear power plants took a back seat because of high initial costs and long lead times.

The Palisades nuclear power plant, located on Lake Michigan and decommissioned after 40 years of operation in 2022, is now getting a new lease of life after energy company Holtec International is working to restore it to active operation status. The first-ever such transition in the U.S. reached an important milestone when fuel loading began at the site recently.

As countries look to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, nuclear energy is making a major comeback. Once a popular energy source, nuclear power plants took a back seat because of high initial costs and long lead times.

With limitations of renewable energy sources coming to the fore, nuclear power offers a reliable and round-the-clock source of carbon-free energy, prompting countries to embrace it. Interesting Engineering previously reported that China is building a record number of nuclear reactors toward its net-zero goal to be achieved by 2060.

Although the US isn’t matching China’s pace, it is bringing back a nuclear power plant that had commercially shut down: the Palisades.

Palisades nuclear power plant

The Palisades nuclear power plant is located five miles away from South Haven, Michigan, and was owned by CMS Energy before its sale in 2007. Located on a 432-acre site, the power plant features a single pressurized water reactor and uses a Westinghouse turbine generator to produce upto 725 MW of electricity.

The facility’s initial license expired in 2011 but was renewed for an additional 20 years. However, its then owner, Entergy, decided to shut down the nuclear plant after the business decided to exit the civilian nuclear power sector.

The plant entered decommissioning after its sale to Holtec International, which then applied to the Civil Nuclear Credit Program to reopen the plant. With help from a power purchase agreement, $300 million in funding from the Michigan state government, and a $1.5 billion loan from the Department of Energy, Holtec began the process of restarting the power plant.

First-ever restart

As part of the restart process, Holtec carried out extensive inspections of the facility and equipment upgrades or refurbishments depending on the requirements. Among them were replacement of control rod drive mechanism nozzles, reinforcement of tubes in steam generators, removal of accumulated corrosive species from these generators, and decontamination and passivation of the primary system.

After years of work, the facility has reached a milestone where fuel loading can begin and will be performed in Mode 6 under the plant’s Technical Specifications as it works toward a restart of operations.

“Loading fuel into the Palisades reactor is an important milestone and a reflection of the tremendous effort of the men and women who have brought this plant to this point,” said Holtec International’s Chief Nuclear Officer Fadi Diya in a press release.

“I am proud to lead an organization with such talented and dedicated people who have a deep sense of pride in this plant and a deep commitment to their community. We remain focused on disciplined execution of the remaining work and returning Palisades to safe and reliable operation.”

The reactor core now consists of 204 fuel assemblies, including new and partially used fuel, and will support the plant’s 805 MW output.

text:
A federal judge ruled on Monday that New York cannot enforce a 2024 state law that sought to force fossil fuel companies to contribute $75 billion over 25 years into a fund to pay for damage caused by climate change.

Chief US District Judge Brenda Sannes in Syracuse, New York sided with 22 Republican state attorneys general, as well as industry groups including the US Chamber of Commerce, in finding the state measure preempted by federal law.

Sannes, an appointee of Democratic president Barack Obama, said the Clean Air Act, which gave the federal Environmental Protection Agency authority to regulate carbon-dioxide emissions, did not authorize states to adopt emissions compensation schemes such as New York's.

She said enforcing New York's Climate Change Superfund Act risked upsetting the balance between preventing global warming, "a project that necessarily requires national standards and global participation," and promoting economic growth, energy production, foreign policy interests and national security.

"The Climate Act conflicts with the overriding need for a uniform rule of decision on matters influencing national energy and environmental policy, and basic interests of federalism," she wrote.

West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey, a Republican who led the states' opposition, in a statement hailed the decision, calling the state law "a money grab by the elites in New York."

The office of New York Governor Kathy Hochul, a Democrat who signed the state law in December 2024, is reviewing the decision to determine possible next steps, spokesperson Ken Lovett said.

"Taxpayers shouldn’t have to foot the bill for damages caused by polluters," Lovett said.

New York demands fossil fuel companies contribute to climate change superfund

New York was the second US state to create an industry-financed "superfund" to address climate change. Vermont was the first state, and its law also faces legal challenges.

The New York law required fossil fuel companies to contribute $3 billion annually to the superfund starting in 2028, divided based on their greenhouse gas emissions between 2000 and 2018.

The law applied to companies that the state's Department of Environmental Conservation considered responsible for 1 billion tons of greenhouse gas emissions during that period. Money would have gone to build roads, water systems, sewage systems, and other infrastructure to protect communities and coastlines from weather events such as extreme heat and flooding.

In their February 2025 lawsuit, the Republican attorneys general called New York's law a politically motivated "overreach," which punished traditional energy companies that now comply with applicable laws. They said payouts from coal, oil and natural gas producers could wipe out thousands of jobs if the producers were forced to shut down.

The US Department of Justice under Republican President Donald Trump had filed a similar lawsuit last year and supported the state attorneys general in the case before Sannes.

text:
There’s never been a better time to build energy storage in the U.S. than right now.

Grid batteries — which sop up power when it’s abundant and discharge that energy when it’s needed — have been ascendant for a decade, as the price of the underlying lithium-ion cells fell precipitously. Bolstered by plummeting costs and increasing familiarity with the tech, developers started building bigger and in more parts of the country.

Now, the U.S. power sector has added more battery capacity in the second quarter of this year than any quarter ever, according to a report out today from the Solar Energy Industries Association and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Even as the wind and solar industries face uncertain futures, the outlook for continued battery growth is so strong that Benchmark Minerals upped the prediction for cumulative installs through 2030 by 11.5% from its previous report, issued just three months ago.

The 20.2 gigawatt-hours of battery capacity built from April through June represents one-tenth of the nation’s entire grid storage capacity. Seven of the new projects mustered at least 1 GWh or more of storage capacity, reflecting developers’ rising appetite for megabatteries.

To contextualize the numbers, the second-quarter installations can inject 6.7 gigawatts of instantaneous power onto the grid — equivalent to nearly seven big old-school nuclear reactors, but without the decade-plus wait time for construction. That comparison has its limits, though, because nuclear plants can generate around the clock, whereas batteries must refill and discharge.

Batteries can make a huge difference in places where the grid is stretched thin, and can be built quickly and closer to centers of energy consumption than new fossil-fuel-burning plants with their smokestacks and emissions.

Those qualities make the tech attractive in places where capacity is scarce, which happens to include California, Texas, the Southeast, the mid-Atlantic, the Northeast, and just about anywhere else. AI data center developers are turning to batteries to ensure they can keep the algorithms running during peak demand hours. And solar developers leverage batteries to turn their clean electrons into a more valuable on-demand resource; 44% of the new storage capacity was built alongside solar plants.

This widespread zeal for batteries extends to the Trump White House, which revoked wind and solar subsidies last year but kept Biden-era tax incentives for batteries. As the executive branch found novel and often legally dubious means to thwart wind and solar construction, it has left battery developers to go about their business.

Recently, the administration has more proactively encouraged the battery industry, loaning $490 million dollars to a battery project in Puerto Rico as well as funding efforts to reshore the supply chain for critical minerals used to make the tech. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who regularly blasts solar power on his official platforms, recently stopped by the Maine site of a novel iron-air battery that Form Energy plans to build, with help from Department of Energy grant funding.

An observer unencumbered by historical nuance might conclude that Trump is the battery president, and that no president has done more for batteries than he. SEIA even gestures in that direction, noting in its press release that large-scale storage nearly doubled during the first year and a half of the second Trump term, and that 74% of the second-quarter storage additions happened in states that voted for him — like Texas, Utah, and newly minted battery storage powerhouse Arizona.

The reality is these outcomes took years to build up to. Technologists tinkered with batteries in big boxes; California mandated its utilities buy storage and subsidized it for smaller customers; Texas wildcatters took big risks on early battery investments and made windfall profits; and companies like LG and Tesla built huge factories to solidify domestic battery supplies. Now, all that hard work is paying off with installations on a scale we’ve never seen before.

text:
WADENA — House District 5A candidates made their case to voters at a candidate's forum Thursday, Aug. 27, in Wadena, hosted by the Todd-Wadena Electric Cooperative.

Dan Mitchell of rural Pequot Lakes is the DFL candidate for Minnesota House District 5A. He is running against Republican incumbent Krista Knudsen of Lake Shore.

Mitchell, a cybersecurity engineer, is married with two boys — the youngest in the Air Force. Mitchell has 20 years of experience in emergency services work, including EMS and firefighting.

He said that at some point, the political parties quit working together and now they just play politics. “I don’t think the middle class is being represented anymore,” he said. “I would like to defend the middle class. The American middle class is the most powerful force in the world, but it’s being hollowed out.”

Knudsen is a former city council member and mayor of Lake Shore, where she lives with her husband and four children. She said that when she first ran for Minnesota House in 2022, ”I felt something was wrong with our state. We ran a restaurant in Lake Shore and had just survived COVID (shutdowns). We could go back to church again. Children were back in school again. We should never go back (to those mandatory shutdowns) again.” She said she has learned a lot in her first term in the Minnesota House.

Renewable energy was raised in the forum, especially regarding a 2023 DFL-passed law that requires electric utilities to provide 100% carbon-free electricity by 2040.

Under the law, investor-owned electric utilities are required to be 80% carbon-free by 2030. That requirement is 60% for other electric utilities – like Todd-Wadena Electric Cooperative. However, all electric utilities must be 90% carbon-free by 2035, and 100% carbon-free by 2040.

Mitchell said that he has written about green energy from a national security standpoint, and that the current war in shows the need for America to hedge its bets with wind, solar and nuclear energy, which he supports. “We need to recycle the spent (radioactive fuel) rods. Other countries do it,” he said.

When it comes to climate change deniers, Mitchell said they are going off incorrect information. “There are all kinds of facts out there," he said. "Just saying it’s true doesn’t make it true. We should (have) green energy on our grid.”

Mitchell also spoke strongly against data centers, which he said are costly in various ways to locals who live near them, and exist to make the tech billionaires even richer. The public should not fund data centers, he said. “The people making the most money should pay the most money,” he said.

Knudsen said that “renewable energy is a hot topic in the (Minnesota) House,” adding that there may be room in the mix for renewable energy, but it can’t be the only solution. “We can’t depend on solar or wind in Minnesota — it (electricity) must be affordable and reliable.” Consumers should quit subsiding green energy, she added, and the state has to seriously consider generating more nuclear power.

The current requirement for 100% renewable power in Minnesota by 2040 is unworkable, she said. “It will bankrupt our state to do that.”

Fraud is a big issue in Minnesota, and could end up being as much as $9 billion, then-First Assistant U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson said in a news conference in December. Or not. As of Aug. 25, documented cases being prosecuted total less than $500 million, which includes the $250-$300 million in the Feeding Our Future case.

Asked about fraud in Minnesota, Mitchell said “fraud is a big issue. It’s unacceptable that you lost track of millions. All that money was sent out for COVID (relief) — it was the wild, wild West. They should have known it was ripe for fraud.”

But two wrongs don't make a right, and “the people of Minnesota are being punished,” he said, for ideological reasons by the federal government. To take legitimate federal food benefits and social services funding away from honest Minnesotans under the guise of fighting fraud “is unacceptable,” he said.

He also attempted to turn the tables on Republicans at the forum, noting that many of them were in office at the time and also failed to notice or stop the fraud. “Why,” he asked, “aren't we pointing the finger at them?”

Knudsen said that “fraud is rampant in the state,” she said. “We have to clean house in our agencies — there’s no way anyone can tell me they didn't know what was happening."

Safeguards must be put in place to prevent fraud, she said. “Money is being thrown at nonprofits with zero results, zero accountability," she said. “Fraud is a huge concern, and it will take a long time to address it adequately."

Asked how to stabilize the farm economy, Knudsen said that “agriculture is the backbone of rural Minnesota,” and she advocated reducing property taxes, including on agricultural property, making energy “affordable for all of us,” and lowering input costs, like fertilizer, for ag. “We need government to get out of the way — one-size fits all mandates hurt rural Minnesota the most.”

Mitchell said, “how do we save the small farm and the farm-to-table operations? The connection (in the public mind) between farmers and food is almost gone. We’re losing that. How do we fix that? It’s not easy.”

At Farmfest, there were representatives from drone companies, banks, giant tractor manufacturers and others who serve large farm operations. “I will fight for the small farm,” he said.

text:
Congress passed a short-term government funding bill Tuesday, giving the hemp industry more time to fight off a looming federal crackdown on hemp-derived THC products.

The continuing resolution (H.R. 6500; BGOV Bill Analysis), which had already been approved by the Senate and was passed by House lawmakers under suspension of the rules in a bipartisan 370-48 vote, keeps the government funded through Dec. 11. It also postpones changes to a loophole in the 2018 farm bill that would have effectively banned certain products containing THC, including gummies, balms, and beverages.

The delay on the ban, which was scheduled to take effect Nov. 12, provides the hemp industry with an additional month to persuade lawmakers to replace the coming restrictions with a new regulatory framework for hemp-derived cannabinoid products.

The move to bring the short-term funding patch for a vote under suspension drew the ire of some conservative Republicans. Among them was House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris (R-Md.), who threatened to vote down a procedural measure that would have unlocked a host of unrelated bills, citing his opposition to delaying the hemp ban.

“If the rule comes out without the CR in it, with a hemp amendment to undo what the Senate did, I’m voting against,” Harris, who oversees federal spending on agriculture programs, told reporters Monday.

text:
September 1, 2026

WASHINGTON – On August 31, 2026, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced decisions for 34 small refinery exemption (SRE) petitions under the Renewable Fuel Standards (RFS) program for 2025. EPA reviewed and considered information submitted by each petitioning small refinery in consultation with U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and then evaluated each SRE petition consistent with the Clean Air Act and case law. Based on that analysis, EPA is exempting 1.76 billion RFS compliance credits, known as Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs), for 29 small refineries. EPA will propose to reallocate 100 percent of the difference between projected and actual exempted volumes for 2025 SREs into the 2026 and 2027 Renewable Volume Obligations (RVOs) before the end of October 2026.

Here’s what people are saying:

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin: “Through today’s Small Refinery decision, the Trump Administration delivered a massive WIN-WIN for America's farmers and small refineries!”

U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins: “Thank you, President Trump, for continuing to reaffirm that you are the most pro-biofuels President in history. What today’s 100% reallocation announcement means for our farmers and rural America cannot be overstated.”

America’s refineries were under attack for years by the radical Democrats, but President Trump put a stop to it by unleashing refineries and powering American energy dominance.”

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds: “Thank you President Trump for listening to farmers and reallocating 100% of exempted biofuels. Now, EPA must move quickly to ensure the final rule supports producers in Iowa and consumers at the pump.”

Senator Joni Ernst (R-IA): “Thank you, President Trump, for listening to Iowa farmers and protecting the strongest biofuel volumes in history! Homegrown biofuels mean cheaper fuel at the pump, strong markets for our farmers, and greater energy security. Next up: nationwide, year-round E15!”

I appreciate that the President and his team were willing to work with farmers and ranchers on this issue. Consumers deserve affordable gas. Farmers deserve stable markets. Today’s SRE decision reinforces why we have to pass E15.”

Representative Brad Finstad (R-MN-01): “Today, the EPA committed to reallocating 100% of exempted biofuel gallons in 2026 and 2027, protecting record high volumes. Thank you, President Trump, for listening to farm country and continuing to invest in our homegrown biofuel industries.”

text:
As more than 90% of North Carolina contractors report difficulty filling craft and salaried positions, the Lowe’s Foundation on Tuesday announced the launch of a nationwide initiative to train 1 million people for skilled trades careers by 2035.

The cross-sector coalition brings together more than 75 founding members, including Charlotte-based Bank of America and Duke Energy.

The initiative — the Building Futures Skilled Trades Coalition — comes as the United States faces a nationwide skilled labor shortage driven by retiring workers and expanding infrastructure investments.

Federal projections indicate that 2.1 million skilled trades jobs could go unfilled by 2030, resulting in potential economic losses of up to $1 trillion annually, the Lowe’s Foundation said in announcing the initiative.

The coalition builds on the Lowe's Foundation's Gable Grants program, which launched in 2023 and currently supports 73 community college and nonprofit partners across 30 states. The foundation recently expanded its mission to individually train 250,000 tradespeople by 2035 through a $250 million investment.

“The next industrial revolution won’t be built by algorithms alone. It will be built by the millions of skilled trade professionals who power, connect and move this country forward,” Marvin Ellison, Lowe’s chairman and CEO, said in a statement.

In a three-minute YouTube video, Ellison lists some of the great construction projects in U.S. history — the Golden Gate Bridge, the Hoover Dam and the Empire State Building. "While so much about how we have lived and worked has changed," he says, "one thing hasn't: Progress still depends on people who know how to build."

For every five skilled trades workers who retire, only two are entering the workforce, Ellison says in the video, adding: "The consequences could be enormous."

text:
A decision by the Environmental Protection Agency to exempt 29 small refineries from nearly 1.8 billion renewable fuel credits is raising fresh concerns across farm country — but a commitment to put those credits back into the nation’s fuel-blending requirements could prevent a major hit to demand for corn ethanol and soybean-based biofuels.

EPA announced Monday that it had approved 29 small refinery exemption petitions covering 1.76 billion Renewable Identification Numbers, or RINs, for the 2025 compliance year.

RINs are essentially credits used to demonstrate compliance with the federal Renewable Fuel Standard. The program requires petroleum companies to blend renewable fuels — including corn ethanol, biodiesel and renewable diesel — into the nation’s fuel supply.

When a refinery receives an exemption, it does not have to meet some or all of those renewable fuel obligations.

That is why farmers and biofuel producers have been watching the EPA decision so closely.

The concern is simple: fewer obligations can mean less demand for renewable fuel and, ultimately, less demand for the corn and soybeans used to make it.

EPA granted full exemptions to 18 refineries and 50% exemptions to another 11. Three petitions were denied and two were ruled ineligible.

The 1.76 billion RINs exempted are significantly more than EPA originally anticipated.

Under its existing methodology, EPA had projected about 990 million RINs would be exempted for 2025. The actual number was roughly 770 million RINs higher.

That difference is now at the center of the administration’s effort to protect biofuel demand.

EPA says it will propose reallocating 100% of the exempted volume into the 2026 and 2027 Renewable Volume Obligations, or RVOs, before the end of October.

In practical terms, that means EPA intends to make other obligated petroleum companies pick up the renewable fuel volume that otherwise could have disappeared because of the refinery exemptions.

For farmers, that reallocation could be the difference between a temporary policy disruption and an actual reduction in the market for their crops.

Renewable Fuels Association President and CEO Geoff Cooper said the exemptions themselves are difficult to justify, but he credited EPA for taking steps to prevent a net loss in renewable fuel demand.

“While we continue to believe most of the SREs issued today are completely unjustified, we are somewhat encouraged that EPA is taking steps to minimize the damage through reallocation,” Cooper said.

The concern among biofuel advocates is particularly sharp because many refiners have reported strong financial results.

Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor questioned whether the refineries receiving exemptions have demonstrated the economic hardship required to qualify.

“It’s difficult to see how these refiners have met this threshold when they’re simultaneously reporting sky-high and, in some cases, record-setting earnings,” Skor said.

For corn farmers, the issue goes straight to one of the largest domestic markets for their crop.

The United States uses billions of bushels of corn every year to produce ethanol. That ethanol is then blended into gasoline, creating a major source of demand for U.S.-grown corn.

National Corn Growers Association President Jed Bower said farmers need strong markets for their crops, particularly at a time when agricultural producers are facing significant economic pressure.

“We need vibrant markets for our products, particularly when it comes to corn ethanol, and the nation’s drivers need affordable fuel,” Bower said.

Bower also argued that the large number of refinery exemptions has not proven to be an effective way to reduce gasoline prices.

The American Farm Bureau Federation echoed those concerns while expressing support for EPA’s reallocation plan.

Farm Bureau President Zippy Duvall said renewable fuels have become a major success story for rural America by supporting farm income, creating jobs, reducing dependence on foreign oil and helping provide lower-cost fuel to consumers.

“While we have concerns about granting any small refinery exemptions that undercut a strong domestic biofuels market for farmers, we are pleased to see EPA’s commitment to toward 100% reallocation of exempted volumes before the end of October,” Duvall said.

The soybean industry has even more at stake because soybeans are an important feedstock for biodiesel and renewable diesel.

The American Soybean Association estimates that without full reallocation, biomass-based diesel demand could fall by 500 million gallons, potentially costing soybean farmers nearly $1 billion in revenue.

That is why soybean growers are pressing EPA to move quickly.

“Any delay in reallocation risks undermining the domestic market demand that soybean farmers urgently need as we enter harvest season,” said Dave Walton, ASA vice president and an Iowa soybean farmer.

The soybean group also wants EPA to address potential increases in small refinery exemptions for 2026 and 2027 so farmers are not forced to revisit the same issue every year.

Meanwhile, producers of biodiesel, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel say they are already operating at a rapid pace to meet federal renewable fuel requirements.

Kurt Kovarik of Clean Fuels Alliance America said producers are operating at record levels but remain concerned about the uncertainty surrounding the Renewable Fuel Standard.

The EPA has also pushed back the 2025 RVO compliance deadline by 30 days, moving it to Oct. 1, 2026, giving the market additional time to absorb the impact of the exemptions.

For farmers, however, the next major deadline is likely to be the end of October.

That is when EPA has pledged to complete supplemental rulemaking to restore the roughly 770 million RINs that exceeded its original 2025 exemption projection.

The outcome matters because RINs may sound like an industry-specific technical issue, but the consequences reach directly into farm country.

More renewable fuel demand means more demand for the corn and soybeans used to produce that fuel. Less demand puts additional pressure on crop markets.

That makes EPA’s next move just as important to farmers as Monday’s exemption announcement.

The Renewable Fuels Association, National Corn Growers Association, American Farm Bureau Federation and American Soybean Association all expressed some version of the same message: the exemptions are a disappointment, but full and timely reallocation could prevent the damage from spreading into the farm economy.

Now, farm and biofuel organizations will be watching EPA to make sure that commitment becomes reality.

The stakes are particularly high as farmers head into harvest.

For corn and soybean growers, this is no longer simply a debate over refinery regulations or federal fuel policy.

It is a question of whether the government will maintain one of agriculture’s largest homegrown markets — and whether the demand created by America’s renewable fuel policy will continue to translate into demand for crops grown on American farms.

title: BYD Expands Globally with Innovations in Battery Technology
description:
The company announced the 2nd Generation Blade battery (one of the fastest-charging EV batteries in 2026) and FLASH charging technology.
BYD announced 20,000 FLASH charging stations across China, and it has initiated a large-scale global rollout by the end of 2026.
