text:
Solar power has just become the single largest electricity capacity source in China, toppling coal in a landmark achievement of the Chinese renewable energy rollout.

Solar power capacity in China stood at 1,286 gigawatts (GW) at the end of July, Chinese media cited the country’s National Energy Administration as saying on Tuesday.

Thus, solar capacity accounted for 31.5% of total installed power generation in China as of July 31.

In July, Chinese authorities said that China would have more installed solar power capacity than coal-fired generation capacity as early as this quarter.

As of the end of June, solar power capacity stood at 1,274 GW, just below the total coal-fired installed capacity of 1,275 GW.

The solar capacity has now risen to 1,286 GW, exceeding coal as the single biggest electricity capacity.

Official Chinese data showed earlier in July that the share of coal in China's electricity output fell in the first half of 2026 to below 50% for the first time on record, in a landmark achievement of the Chinese policy to boost non-fossil power sources.

The share of coal averaged 49.7% of China's total electricity output in the first half of this year, official data showed.

As the share of coal slipped, electricity generation from renewable energy rose by about 9% from a year earlier, according to the data from China's National Energy Administration (NEA).

Renewable energy accounted for 41.2% of China's total electricity generation in the first half of 2026, with wind and solar combined generating almost 25% of the total power output.

Despite the milestone of reducing coal power output to below 50% of total generation for the first time ever, China continues to rely on coal for power for industry and to maintain the reliability of the power grids.

Moreover, the renewable energy boom has slowed in recent months amid policy changes, while grid constraints and rising coal-fired generation have led to soaring curtailment rates of solar and wind power generation.

text:
In a move that has been under close scrutiny from farm and fuel groups, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced decisions on Monday for 34 small refinery exemption (SRE) petitions, granting exemptions to 29 refineries.

According to the National Corn Growers Association (NCGA), the exemptions equate to almost 1.8 billion credits known as Renewable Identification Numbers, or RINs, to small petroleum refineries.

The decision exempts dozens of refineries from blending renewable fuels as required by the Renewable Fuels Standard (RFS), but EPA said it will reallocate 100% of the difference between projected and actual exempted volumes for 2025 SREs into the blending requirements for 2026 and 2027.

That reallocation was met with sighs of relief from major commodity and biofuels organizations, who all noted their disdain for SREs in general, but were largely complimentary of the decision to reallocate the exempted fuel volumes.

The American Soybean Association had estimated that biomass-based diesel demand would drop by 500 million gallons, and soybean farmers would suffer almost a $1 billion loss in revenue without a 100% reallocation in the current period.

READ NEXT: WHY SMALL REFINERY EXEMPTIONS COULD DELIVER A BIG BLOW TO FARMERS

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin called the SREs a “massive win-win for America’s farmers and small refineries” and Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins said the 100% reallocation’s impact for farmers and rural America “cannot be overstated.”

Ag groups weigh in

American Farm Bureau Federation President Zippy Duvall touted renewable fuels as a “tremendous success story” for the U.S. and rural economy, noting how the fuels reduce dependence on foreign oil, lower prices at the pump, support farm income, and provide good-paying jobs.

“While we have concerns about granting any small refinery exemptions that undercut a strong domestic biofuels market for farmers, we are pleased to see EPA’s commitment to 100% reallocation of exempted volumes before the end of October,” Duvall said.

“Reallocation is necessary to maintain robust demand for American grown crops. We called on the president to carefully consider the impact of changes to the Renewable Fuel Standard that would destabilize this important market, and we’re pleased that our concerns were heard.”

ASA also urged EPA to include 100% reallocation of updated expected SRE levels for 2026 and 2027.

“EPA proactively accounted for expected exemptions in setting those volumes, but SRE levels are now expected to be higher if new assessment methodology does not change,” the group wrote.

“Addressing updated 2025–2027 SRE levels together would protect the integrity of the RFS and avoid the need for annual supplemental rulemakings.”

NCGA President Jed Bower said his organization was disheartened by the high number of SREs, but thankful for the reallocations.

“We need vibrant markets for our products, particularly when it comes to corn ethanol, and the nation's drivers need affordable fuel,” Bower noted.

“Biofuels are a homegrown solution for increasing our country’s energy supply and reducing fuel costs. Recent history has shown that issuing SREs at this volume does nothing to reduce the price of gas.”

Biofuels group says SRE program is ‘broken’

Renewable Fuels Association President and CEO Geoff Cooper said unwarranted SREs continue to plague the RFS with uncertainty and instability, noting that reform of the “broken SRE program” is needed.

“While we continue to believe most of the SREs issued today are completely unjustified, we are somewhat encouraged that EPA is taking steps to minimize the damage through reallocation,” Cooper added.

“The proposed plan laid out by EPA today creates a pathway for ensuring no net loss in renewable fuel demand, and it is crucially important that the agency moves quickly to faithfully implement this approach.”

June polling for the Renewable Fuel Association found that more than 75% of respondents with an opinion want oil companies to be required to meet their renewable fuel blending requirements. Less than a quarter want oil companies to be allowed to avoid them.

Biofuels trade association Growth Energy thanked lawmakers who stepped up to voice concerns ahead of EPA’s decision, noting their engagement was vital to preserving the promise of the record-setting RVOs finalized earlier this year.

“Our position hasn’t changed — SREs should only be granted when refiners can prove disproportionate economic hardship,” Growth Energy wrote.

“It’s difficult to see how these refiners have met this threshold when they’re simultaneously reporting sky-high and, in some cases, record-setting earnings.”

text:
Thirty-nine opportunities on the Agriculture, Climate, Environment, Energy and Food page this cycle, twenty-two closing before the end of September.

Five conservation funders here write the check to a person. The International Iguana Foundation, the Whitley Fund for Nature, The Explorers Club through both the Kensington Conservation Grant and the Stephenson Exploration Advancement Program, the Neotropical Grassland Conservancy, and the Jean Sainsbury Animal Welfare Trust. Five distinct funders writing checks to named individuals, several of them preferring nationals of the country where the work happens. No institution, no host, no fiscal sponsor, and several of them prefer nationals of the country where the work happens. On a page whose largest calls need three partners in three countries, these five are the most reachable things on it.

The entries are concentrated in the Global South and the money is not. The volume of entries on this page is in Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and almost all of it is under USD $25,000: the Kenyan youth track on a fifty-fifty community match, agroforestry in Karamoja, climate-resilient energy access in Ethiopia, an agriculture fellowship in Maharashtra, the Pulitzer Center’s Global South civil society microgrants. Every award above USD $200,000 belongs to a European, North American or multilateral funder. And the most open-looking multilateral vehicles are the most gated of all: the Kunming Biodiversity Fund disburses only to UN Participating Organizations, so nationals of the countries it serves enter as sub-partners, and the European Partnership for Agriculture of Data favors continuation by the incumbent consortium. The practical version: the total at the top of this page overstates what a Southern applicant can actually reach, and the two most open-looking multilateral vehicles turn out to be the most gated of all. Sort this page by eligibility rather than by envelope.

The circular economy calls here are run by industry bodies and innovation agencies. Vinnova funds circular solutions for forest-based industries, plastics and textiles. Ecoembes runs a circular packaging challenge where the real prize is a pilot inside the company that finances Spain’s recycling system. The Raw Materials Partnership pools roughly €41 million across the raw materials value chain. The Research Fund for Coal and Steel funds the social and economic transition of coal regions, and specifies dissemination of what is known rather than new studies. The Department of Energy pays for storage design that eases production. The ask in each is supply chain capability rather than an environmental outcome, which means the proposal that wins describes a manufacturing problem being solved. Come at these from an environmental framing and you will be answering a question they did not ask.

This post is for paid subscribers. This helps support the time and effort it takes to curate and organize these opportunities.

To keep this accessible to everyone who needs it, we’re happy to offer pay what you can rates. You can find more details here.

New opportunities:

Sustainable Circular Solutions for Forest-Based Industries, Plastics and Textiles, Vinnova. *New!* *Closing soon!*

Vinnova, Sweden’s innovation agency, is opening a call under its Sustainable Value Chains programme for circular solutions across forest-based industries, plastics, and textiles. The agency wants materials kept in use rather than discarded, funding work that designs out waste, substitutes virgin inputs with secondary raw materials, and builds business models around reuse. It looks for solutions that can be implemented, not merely described, which is why the call asks each consortium to combine a solution provider, an implementer, and a customer for recycled or reused material. Requiring at least three organizations and a Swedish coordinating entity signals an agency funding delivery chains rather than isolated research. The strongest fits are Swedish-anchored consortia that pair technical capability with a partner ready to put the result into production.

Geographies: Sweden, in northern Europe, with foreign organizations able to join as unfunded partners or to receive funding only through a registered Swedish branch.

Who can apply: Collaborative projects of at least three participating legal entities, including companies of any size, public actors, research institutes, universities, and other relevant organizations, where the constellation covers at least two of three roles, a potential solution provider, a participant who intends to implement the solution, and a customer using secondary or sustainable raw materials or reuse-based products and services, and where the coordinating party is a Swedish legal entity conducting activities in Sweden; sole proprietors and individuals are not eligible.

Funding amount: Up to SEK 5,000,000 (SEK 5 million, roughly USD 481,000) per project, with no stated minimum, and aid intensity varying by organization type from 25 to 60 percent for companies and up to 100 percent for universities and non-economic public organizations.

Targeted Sectors / SDGs: Climate & Environment; Agriculture & Food Systems; Innovation & Technology; SDGs 9, 12. Focus: circular economy, secondary raw materials, forest-based industries, plastics and textiles, reuse business models.

Deadline: September 4, 2026.

Learn more and apply here.

Global South Civil Society Microgrants, Pulitzer Center. *New!* *Closing soon!*

The Pulitzer Center is inviting applications for its Global South Civil Society Microgrants, funding civic engagement projects that put its supported journalism to work in communities across Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. The Center is using these grants to carry reporting on rainforests, oceans, and the intersection of climate and labor beyond publication and into dialogue, education, and creative expression. What it wants to back is not more journalism but the moment a community turns a story into shared understanding and action, centering the people who protect and depend on these ecosystems. Requiring at least one Pulitzer Center story and a defined audience signals that reach and impact matter more than scale. The strongest fits are grassroots collectives, youth movements, and civil society coalitions rooted in these regions.

Geographies: The Global South, particularly Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia.

Who can apply: Grassroots organizations, community educators, civil society organizations and coalitions, youth movements, and other groups working at the intersection of journalism, civic rights, and active citizenship, which must have past experience developing and implementing civic engagement activities in the Global South, proven experience on the identified topics, and the operational capacity to manage microgrant resources from an international organization.

Funding amount: USD $2,000 to $4,000 per microgrant, with applicants specifying the amount requested alongside a draft budget; the total programme envelope is not disclosed.

Targeted Sectors / SDGs: Climate & Environment; Arts, Culture & Media; Philanthropy & Civil Society; SDGs 5, 13, 14, 15. Focus: rainforest degradation, indigenous rights, ocean governance, marine conservation, climate and labor, civic engagement, public dialogue.

Deadline: September 6, 2026.

Learn more and apply here.

Transforming Whole-Farm Systems through Regenerative Agriculture in Extremadura, Spain, EIT Food. *New!* *Closing soon!*

EIT Food is inviting agronomic consultancies, training organizations, and monitoring specialists to apply to deliver a regenerative agriculture program for corn and tomato growers across the Extremadura landscape in Spain. The organization pairs its own catalytic funding with contributions from three global food and consumer goods companies, using their sourcing relationships to move whole farm systems toward regenerative practice at scale. What it wants to back is measurable, verifiable change in soil health, water use, and emissions, not one-off training events, which is why the call bundles coordination, farmer advisory, and a rigorous verification system into a single mandate. Requiring local presence and Spanish fluency signals that EIT Food expects trusted, field-level delivery. The strongest fits are Spain-based teams that combine agronomic depth with credible measurement capability.

Geographies: Spain, specifically the corn and tomato production areas of the Extremadura region, with consortium members drawn from EU or Horizon Europe eligible countries.

Who can apply: Monitoring, reporting and verification providers, agronomic consultancies, training organisations, or related entities, applying as a single entity or as a consortium of at most three entities addressing all three work packages, where each participant has been a legally incorporated entity in an EU or Horizon Europe eligible country for at least three years, holds a PIC number, and can demonstrate organisational capacity and local presence in Spain while operating in Spanish and English.

Funding amount: Up to €820,000 (EUR 820,000, roughly USD 885,600), which is both the total available funding and the maximum per application, with a single winner receiving the full envelope on an actual-costs basis.

Targeted Sectors / SDGs: Agriculture & Food Systems; Climate & Environment; Innovation & Technology; SDGs 2, 12, 13, 15. Focus: regenerative agriculture, agronomic advisory, farmer training, monitoring reporting and verification, soil carbon, landscape-scale transition.

Deadline: September 10, 2026.

Learn more and apply here.

Charity Entrepreneurship Incubation Program: Animal Welfare Round (2027), Ambitious Impact (AIM). *New!* *Closing soon!*

Ambitious Impact, running its Charity Entrepreneurship program, opens an incubation round dedicated entirely to farmed animal welfare, recruiting people to found new charities that take on factory farming. For this round the organization rebuilt its research process around frontier problems rather than pre-scoped solutions, inviting founders to develop their own approaches to big, tractable questions in welfare technology, primary research, humane breeding, and neglected populations. It pairs each participant with a co-founder, funds a training phase and a longer exploration phase, and backs the strongest projects with seed capital to launch. The design signals a belief that talent and mid-stage funding, not ideas, are the real bottleneck. The strongest fits are analytical career switchers, industry insiders, veterinarians, and researchers willing to build something new for animals.

Geographies: Global, open to applicants from any country, with in-person components of two weeks in London plus an optional two weeks in San Francisco, travel fully covered and visa support available.

Who can apply: Individuals from any country and background who want to found a high-impact animal welfare charity, with no nonprofit, animal welfare, or founding experience required because the program provides the training; particularly good fits include farm, supply chain and ESG professionals, veterinarians, engineers and product builders, scientists and researchers, recruiters and people leaders, and consultants, lawyers and other career switchers, with founders ranging in age from 20 to over 50 and no vegan, vegetarian, or activist background needed.

Funding amount: USD $150,000 to $190,000 in seed funding per project, reaching roughly 95 percent of projects, plus a needs-based monthly living stipend of USD $2,000 to $5,000, capped at $10,000, during the training and exploration phases.

Targeted Sectors / SDGs: Agriculture & Food Systems; Climate & Environment; Governance, Policy & Advocacy; SDGs 2, 12. Focus: farmed animal welfare, factory farming reform, welfare technology, humane breeding, neglected animal populations, charity incubation.

Deadline: September 13, 2026.

Learn more and apply here.

text:
Donaldsonville, LA - As impacted residents provide public testimony later today on Hyundai Steel’s air permit for its proposed steel plant, Sierra Club is urging significant permit changes and pollution reductions. The hearing is part of a too-brief public comment period that will now end on September 15th after the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) granted a short 13-day extension following requests from multiple local groups and individuals, including Sierra Club.

***Sierra Club is working to finalize its written comments ahead of the newly extended deadline for written comments. A preview of the comments is available under embargo, upon request. ***

Despite a legal obligation to the people of Louisiana, LDEQ has fast-tracked the flawed permit, giving the public an insufficient amount of time for to review and comment on the 2,100-plus pages of proposed permitting materials for this complex project that will bring thousands of tons of pollution to an area of Cancer Alley that is already overburdened with pollution.

While Hyundai Steel does not have a final air permit, the company is planning a groundbreaking ceremony on Friday, September 4th.

Throughout 2026, Sierra Club, working with experts and local groups, submitted a series of pre-comments to LDEQ in an effort to bring to light the errors, miscalculations, and omissions in the permit application. Hyundai Steel made some changes to its permit application as a result of those comments, updating plans to electrify some components of the facility, which will lower levels of pollution from the facility.

However, as the draft permit currently stands, more electrification is necessary and the company also must make plans to reduce emissions of toxic dust. Further, Hyundai Steel completely removed the environmental justice analysis from the permit application, so the draft permit likewise omits this critical information. LDEQ did not do any analysis of alternative sites to determine if there is a location that would be less harmful to surrounding communities. LDEQ also did not conduct a proper jobs analysis or complete any of its other public trust duties, including impacts on drinking water and public health.

In response, Sierra Club Industrial Transformation Campaign Director Matthew Miles Goodrich issued the following statement:

“Residents of Donaldsonville and Modeste must have a meaningful opportunity to weigh in on a project that would fundamentally reshape the health, environment, and economy of their community for generations. Instead, LDEQ is rushing Hyundai Steel’s air permit through an inadequate public process while failing to do the basic analysis required to protect the public. Though we are glad Hyundai has made some improvements to its plans, this proposed permit still falls far short of what people there deserve. LDEQ must slow down, fully evaluate the project’s impacts and alternative locations, and put the health and well-being of Cancer Alley residents first for a change.”

text:
Why It Matters

The Corporate Energy Buyers Association amended its second quarter lobbying disclosure on August 31. The group represents corporate buyers who use contracts like virtual power purchase agreements to stabilize renewable energy projects. That strategy matters as Congress grapples with competing demands: decarbonization commitments, energy security priorities, investor appetite for returns, and surging electricity demand from data centers.

The amendment comes after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act reshaped the clean energy tax credit landscape established by the Inflation Reduction Act.

By the Numbers

CEBA reported $200,000 in lobbying expenses for the second quarter amendment, matching its first quarter spending. The organization operates as an in-house operation, with four registered in-house lobbyists: Rich England, Josh St. Pierre, Ian Harrison, and Tomas Green.

The group spent $370,000 in third quarter 2025, dropped to $210,000 in the fourth quarter, then stabilized at $200,000 for the first quarter of 2026 before the amended second quarter filing showed $200,000 again.

Cassidy & Associates Inc. filed reports for each quarter from third quarter 2025 through first quarter 2026, charging $90,000 per quarter for work on electric grid reliability.

The Bottom Line

CEBA's amended filing provides no detail on specific issues or legislation pursued in the second quarter, departing from its practice in prior quarters when it disclosed extensive activity across dozens of bills. The group has maintained consistent spending levels in recent months while continuing to work through both in-house and external lobbying channels on energy policy matters.

title: Environmental groups call for Detroit data center moratorium as city develops ordinance
description:

text:
Detroit’s City Planning Commission is developing recommendations for a data center ordinance after several working groups met in the spring and early summer.

Nine environmental justice and community groups and three elected officials signed a July 15 letter to Mayor Mary Sheffield that calls for a moratorium to provide more time to develop a protective data center policy.

The signatories on the call for a moratorium include Great Lakes Environmental Law Center (GLELC), Detroit Future City, Eastside Community Network, the Sierra Club Michigan Chapter, U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib, state Sen. Stephanie Chang and Detroit City Council Member Gabriela Santiago-Romero.

Without a moratorium in place, City Council Member Scott Benson, who convened the data center working groups, said he’s working quickly to create a “community-informed” ordinance that puts health, environmental, and financial protections in place by the end of the year.

The Detroit City Council recommended a two-year data center moratorium in March. Sheffield has not adopted the recommendation.

Sheffield’s administration “has effectively paused the permitting of new principal use data centers while the issue is being considered” by the planning commission and council, City Planner Eric Fazzini said in an Aug. 5 report.

The planning commission is drafting a data center ordinance and will release the language in the coming weeks, Benson told Planet Detroit Aug. 26.

Planning Commission Director Marcell Todd said data centers already operate in Detroit, but hyperscale data centers are creating controversy and concerning impacts nationwide.

“This is not just about permitting a use; this is actually more importantly about regulating a use,” Todd said during an Aug. 6 meeting.

Packard Plant, Shoemaker Street sites were eyed for data centers

Michiganders have frequently expressed concern over data center projects they fear could pass on costs to utility ratepayers or undermine Michigan’s climate law. Data center developers and public officials in other communities have said the projects could bring thousands of temporary construction jobs and millions in local tax benefits.

Hundreds of Detroiters stated their opposition to data centers in Sheffield’s Rise Higher survey, which Sheffield said is intended to help the city shape its priorities.

A data center was proposed for an east side industrial site on Shoemaker Street, near Conner Street and I-94, but the proposal was dropped, Erin Stanley, a policy analyst in Detroit City Council Member Latisha Johnson’s office, told Planet Detroit in July.

A city request for proposals for the site outlines technology and artificial intelligence as a possible use for the 14.4-acre, city-owned property.

Google evaluated the sprawling former Packard Plant for a 1-gigawatt data center that is now proposed for a site in Van Buren Township, the tech giant told state environmental regulators in a filing.

The 38-acre Packard Plant site is not large enough to accommodate the infrastructure and buildings needed for the data center, according to Google.

In December, former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan announced a plan to redevelop 28 acres of the Packard site with an indoor skate park, affordable housing, and a large industrial building.

This plan was terminated by Sheffield’s administration in February, Crain’s Detroit Business reported.

Some of the parcels at the Packard site were tax foreclosed by Wayne County in 2022. These parcels did not sell at auction and were transferred to the city, said city spokesperson John Roach.

Hyperscale data centers are large facilities like the Oracle and OpenAI facility under construction in Saline Township and Google’s proposed Van Buren Township development.

Data centers of this size can use over 1 gigawatt of energy, or as much power as a large city.

DTE Energy indicated that Detroit lacks the 345-kilovolt high power transmission lines needed to power hyperscale data centers, the Aug. 5 planning commission report said.

“Hypothetically, it may be possible to develop a hyperscale data center if it had an independent power source, such as a nuclear power plant or a new natural gas plant,” the report said.

City council approved a resolution July 21 in opposition to the unmitigated use of Detroit water resources to cool artificial intelligence data centers, noting the vast amounts of water consumed by some facilities.

This water usage could overtax local infrastructure, according to the resolution.

“The cumulative impact of these facilities is unknown as they continue to expand, and the Great Lakes Region lacks a consistent and adequate regulatory framework to ensure the protection of precious freshwater supplies,” the resolution states.

City needs data center ordinance to protect residents: Benson

Many data centers proposed across the country use on-site power generation, which could bring more pollution to Detroit, said Eden Bloom, an environmental advocate affiliated with the Detroit People’s Platform, a social justice organization.

The Detroit People’s Platform withdrew from the health and environmental working group because of the difficulty in reaching a consensus with other members and the short time given to develop recommendations, Bloom said.

Michelle Martinez, director of the University of Michigan’s Tishman Center for Social Justice and the Environment, also participated in the environmental working group. It lacked a process for public input on the ordinance, she said.

The subcommittee began meeting in June, while the main working group had been meeting since April, she said.

“It was pretty frustrating to be brought into a process ostensibly after the ink had dried,” she said.

The Data Center Zoning & Policy Working Group, the primary working group, included six representatives from DTE Energy, two from the Detroit Economic Growth Corp., two from labor unions involved in data center construction, and one environmental advocate among 33 people who were invited.

That’s according to an agenda from the group’s April 10 meeting obtained by the Detroit People’s Platform from Benson’s office.

Benson previously told Planet Detroit that he disagrees with allegations there wasn’t enough time for subcommittees to develop recommendations. It’s important to put an ordinance in place to protect Detroiters, he said.

“What I am going to do is make sure that the city of Detroit has regulations, which we do not have now,” Benson said in a July 6 phone interview.

Data center report plagiarizes material, uses industry sources: Environmental advocates

On July 30, GLELC attorney Andrew Bashi sent a letter to Detroit City Council that criticizes a July 22 data center report from the City Council’s Legislative Policy Division (LPD) for relying on industry-friendly sources, and accuses city staff of plagiarizing material.

The council report estimates the city could generate $107 million in property tax revenue over a 20-year period from a 1-gigawatt data center project.

The LPD analysis plagiarizes portions of other reports and relies heavily on industry-friendly sources, the GLELC letter says.

The sources include an Anderson Consulting Group study commissioned by Consumers Energy and a Public Sector Consultants report commissioned by the Michigan Chamber Foundation and Detroit Regional Chamber.

The Michigan Chamber helped launch a pro-data center group, Michigan for Responsible Data Centers, in March. The Detroit Regional Chamber is a member of the group.

The first three paragraphs from LPD’s conclusion are identical to text in the Citizens Research Council of Michigan (CRC) report: “Data Centers in Michigan: Evaluation of Policy Controversies Regarding Hyperscale Data Center Development.”

This text constitutes the bulk of the conclusion and is not in quotation marks. A footnote at the end of the third paragraph references the CRC’s report.

The LPD report’s community benefits section and jobs analysis also partially copy the CRC report.

The GLELC letter said this is significant because a reader would not know the report is not LPD’s analysis, but rather a “private organization’s conclusions relabeled as LPD’s own.”

LPD Director David Whitaker told Planet Detroit by email the report isn’t intended to be an exhaustive study of data centers’ potential financial impacts in Detroit.

“LPD does not have the expertise in-house to conduct the detailed analysis that GLELC suggests,” Whitaker said.

The department used sources like the CRC that are familiar with obtaining and analyzing municipal impacts, he said.

While it would have been correct to quote certain passages, LPD acknowledged where the statement came from and directed readers to the source with footnotes, he said.

CRC President Eric Lupher told Planet Detroit the group gives permission to reprint its work, provided it’s properly cited. For the most part, the LPD cites the research council’s work, he said.

“LPD might have headed this off by acknowledging in their introduction that what follows is a compilation of several recent reports on data centers,” Lupher said in an email.

Lupher agrees with GLELC’s criticism that the LPD report presents only the positive framing from the CRC’s construction jobs analysis, “while dropping CRC’s counterbalancing caveats, without any indication that material was omitted,” he said.

This frequently occurs when information is gleaned from larger reports, Lupher said.

In addition to these issues, the LPD’s footnotes cite “AI internet” as a source three times, with the caveat: “LPD cautions that the AI internet is subject to omissions and errors.”

Whitaker said the “AI Internet” sourcing was used “as it often provides a summary of various sources of information on a topic.

“As indicated in the report, that information is subject to omissions and errors.”

The issues the GLELC letter raised with the council report are unsurprising, and underscore the need for Detroit to take its time in developing a data center ordinance, said U of M’s Martinez.

A moratorium is needed until the rules are in place, she said.

text:
In a move that has been under close scrutiny from farm and fuel groups, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced decisions on Monday for 34 small refinery exemption (SRE) petitions, granting exemptions to 29 refineries.

According to the National Corn Growers Association (NCGA), the exemptions equate to almost 1.8 billion credits known as Renewable Identification Numbers, or RINs, to small petroleum refineries.

The decision exempts dozens of refineries from blending renewable fuels as required by the Renewable Fuels Standard (RFS), but EPA said it will reallocate 100% of the difference between projected and actual exempted volumes for 2025 SREs into the blending requirements for 2026 and 2027.

That reallocation was met with sighs of relief from major commodity and biofuels organizations, who all noted their disdain for SREs in general, but were largely complimentary of the decision to reallocate the exempted fuel volumes.

The American Soybean Association had estimated that biomass-based diesel demand would drop by 500 million gallons, and soybean farmers would suffer almost a $1 billion loss in revenue without a 100% reallocation in the current period.

READ NEXT: WHY SMALL REFINERY EXEMPTIONS COULD DELIVER A BIG BLOW TO FARMERS

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin called the SREs a “massive win-win for America’s farmers and small refineries” and Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins said the 100% reallocation’s impact for farmers and rural America “cannot be overstated.”

Ag groups weigh in

American Farm Bureau Federation President Zippy Duvall touted renewable fuels as a “tremendous success story” for the U.S. and rural economy, noting how the fuels reduce dependence on foreign oil, lower prices at the pump, support farm income, and provide good-paying jobs.

“While we have concerns about granting any small refinery exemptions that undercut a strong domestic biofuels market for farmers, we are pleased to see EPA’s commitment to 100% reallocation of exempted volumes before the end of October,” Duvall said.

“Reallocation is necessary to maintain robust demand for American grown crops. We called on the president to carefully consider the impact of changes to the Renewable Fuel Standard that would destabilize this important market, and we’re pleased that our concerns were heard.”

ASA also urged EPA to include 100% reallocation of updated expected SRE levels for 2026 and 2027.

“EPA proactively accounted for expected exemptions in setting those volumes, but SRE levels are now expected to be higher if new assessment methodology does not change,” the group wrote.

“Addressing updated 2025–2027 SRE levels together would protect the integrity of the RFS and avoid the need for annual supplemental rulemakings.”

NCGA President Jed Bower said his organization was disheartened by the high number of SREs, but thankful for the reallocations.

“We need vibrant markets for our products, particularly when it comes to corn ethanol, and the nation's drivers need affordable fuel,” Bower noted.

“Biofuels are a homegrown solution for increasing our country’s energy supply and reducing fuel costs. Recent history has shown that issuing SREs at this volume does nothing to reduce the price of gas.”

Biofuels group says SRE program is ‘broken’

Renewable Fuels Association President and CEO Geoff Cooper said unwarranted SREs continue to plague the RFS with uncertainty and instability, noting that reform of the “broken SRE program” is needed.

“While we continue to believe most of the SREs issued today are completely unjustified, we are somewhat encouraged that EPA is taking steps to minimize the damage through reallocation,” Cooper added.

“The proposed plan laid out by EPA today creates a pathway for ensuring no net loss in renewable fuel demand, and it is crucially important that the agency moves quickly to faithfully implement this approach.”

June polling for the Renewable Fuel Association found that more than 75% of respondents with an opinion want oil companies to be required to meet their renewable fuel blending requirements. Less than a quarter want oil companies to be allowed to avoid them.

Biofuels trade association Growth Energy thanked lawmakers who stepped up to voice concerns ahead of EPA’s decision, noting their engagement was vital to preserving the promise of the record-setting RVOs finalized earlier this year.

“Our position hasn’t changed — SREs should only be granted when refiners can prove disproportionate economic hardship,” Growth Energy wrote.

“It’s difficult to see how these refiners have met this threshold when they’re simultaneously reporting sky-high and, in some cases, record-setting earnings.”

text:
BMW does not build battery cells in series production. It never has, and – on current plans – it does not intend to start. Yet the company has spent years investing money, capacity and engineering talent into developing its own cells, running its own pilot production line, and now applying artificial intelligence across nearly every stage of the process. There is a strong case being made for this approach.

BMW's iFactory: the blueprint behind the new X5

Five drivetrains, humanoid robots and AI quality checks at Plant Spartanburg all trace back to one framework. AMS examines how BMW's iFactory concept, tested end to end on the new X5, is reshaping what a modern assembly line is built to do.

According to Christian Siedelhofer, Group Lead Technology Development, Battery Cells at BMW, the rationale comes down to control over knowledge rather than control over output. BMW's approach rests on three internal competence centres: The Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich, which handles research and development from material characterisation through to future cell concepts; the Cell Manufacturing Competence Center (CMCC) in Parsdorf, which industrialises that R&D at pilot scale; and a Cell Recycling Competence Center (CRCC), operational for a little over six months, which brings direct recycling from theory into practice.

Building and operating this infrastructure – without ever scaling up to a gigafactory – Has provided BMW with a wealth of knowledge and leverage it would not otherwise have. It allows the company to set specifications for external cell suppliers without dictating exactly how those specifications should be met. BMW defines a specification sheet, and suppliers must hit certain performance results, but the route they take to get there is their own. That structure, in turn, creates a feedback loop – BMW's expertise can, in turn, support suppliers in troubleshooting their own production issues, and BMW gains insight it could not generate without running cells of its own.

Advertisement

Cutting setup times with predictive models

The headline figure attached to BMW's AI collaboration with the University of Zagreb is a 50% reduction in material and time during individual process steps. Siedelhofer is careful to frame what that number actually represents. "The number is an example of what is possible in optimising a single process step out of many," he explains, and the results are currently being transferred from BMW's prototype build facility onto the pilot line — it has not yet been rolled out across the board.

Rather than a single AI system governing the entire battery cell production process, BMW is deploying multiple, discrete prediction models, each targeted at specific steps and trained on process and product parameters pulled directly from live operations.

The clearest example is the very first stage of cell production; mixing powders and liquids into a slurry. Because BMW frequently changes materials, solvents and active materials at its prototype build stage, the process parameters must be reset each time. "In the past, this was done by experience of operators to set the right process parameters," Siedelhofer says. Historically, if BMW had run an identical combination before, replicating past settings was straightforward. But new combinations are the norm, not the exception, and that is precisely where the AI models come in.

"If you change component A to B, then change the pump speed RPM or another, more deeply hidden machine parameter," he explains. "It's a very complex environment and the AI helps in these specific steps to find new starting points which are closer to the optimum of our existing process parameters" — covering variables such as mixing speed and temperature. Crucially, the AI doesn't eliminate physical testing; it shortens the distance between a cold start and an optimised process window, cutting the setup time needed whenever materials change.

That sensitivity to small variation doesn't disappear once a product reaches stable series production, either. Even when a supplier commits to one product long-term, "stable is not an absolute value," Siedelhofer notes. Materials carry tolerances — humidity levels included — and exterior conditions remain uncontrollable. "This is why we really set up this live data support to our operators, so they can use the data they're getting from the machine, from process, and from product to optimise and to keep the process in a stable process window."

BMW's Spartanburg line masters five-drivetrain X5 build

BMW Group has completed its $1.7 billion South Carolina expansion, unveiling the new X5 as the first vehicle assembled with five drivetrain technologies on one line, with the electric iX5 to follow by year-end.

Building a cell validation framework from scratch

BMW's decades of experience validating vehicles doesn't translate automatically to battery cells – a technology the company has only been working with intensively for a fraction of that time. Siedelhofer confirms that the cell validation framework is effectively being built from the ground up.

Advertisement

That gap is part of the justification for BMW's continued investment in cell development despite not manufacturing cells in series. Understanding the technology deeply enough to build a validation framework – and to specify supplier requirements with precision — requires the kind of data most vehicle manufacturers simply haven't needed to collect before. "It is important to get as much data out of your production and product as possible," he says, adding that BMW built this thinking into its prototype and pilot line from the outset, "so that we can make decisions that are data driven."

That matters more, he argues, is because battery cells aren't a technology BMW has worked with for a century, unlike combustion engines and vehicle assembly. "We have to catch up, and I think we are really on a good path because we are very data focused." But gathering that data is genuinely difficult. Cell production moves from powders and liquids, through a roll-to-roll electrode process, before converging into a one-piece flow only at the very end. Aligning data across that entire chain — tracing which batch of active material powder ended up in a specific finished cell — is significantly more complex than tracking a process with a single continuous flow from start to finish.

Extending AI beyond the cell

BMW's use of AI in battery development isn't confined to individual cells. It extends into high-voltage battery assembly, where roughly 960 individual cells are combined into a single pack. BMW is establishing five new plants worldwide, one in each major region, and – according to feedback from partners relayed during the conversation – the company collects more production data than any other manufacturer in this space, using AI agents and assistants to refine processes across the board.

Detecting the "worst enemy" of a battery cell

Quality inspection is where BMW's AI ambitions meet their hardest technical test. Towards the end of the production process, BMW uses computer tomography (CT) to assess finished cells – a well-established imaging technology in general terms, but one Siedelhofer describes as genuinely progressive when applied to battery cell production at this level of detail. The target is what he calls "the worst enemy of a battery cell" – a particle inside it, small and difficult to detect.

The challenge is that this isn't a simple pass/fail judgement. Siedelhofer draws a contrast with older manufacturing checks – inspecting whether a cable is properly clicked into place on a combustion engine assembly line, for instance, where a small window simply shows white or black, correct or incorrect. Identifying a particle inside a battery cell is far less binary. CT scans also introduce their own visual artefacts from the imaging process itself, which the AI must learn to distinguish from genuine defects.

Advertisement

Training a model to make that distinction reliably would, in an ideal world, require examples from millions of produced cells containing millions of real defects. BMW doesn't have anywhere near that volume at pilot scale, and buying in external data isn't a viable shortcut – different cell chemistries and designs would simply teach the AI to detect the wrong thing. Instead, BMW deliberately creates validation samples containing controlled defects for AI training purposes.

In some cases, this means physically implanting particles into cells before scanning them; in others, it means generating defects virtually within CT images. "You need one AI to virtually implement defects into your CT images, to then train the other AI to detect those defects," Siedelhofer explains.

Replacing – eventually – the voltage-hold test

The industry's current benchmark for a final "OK" verdict on a battery cell is the voltage hold method; measuring a cell's voltage, holding it in quarantine for a set period, measuring again, and checking whether it falls within the correct process window. BMW's AI-supported quality processes are being measured directly against that standard, and the bar is deliberately conservative.

"The threshold for replacing an established quality gate is intentionally high. Any new technology must outperform the state-of-the-art in at least one aspect while matching it in all others,” Siedelhofer says of any new method intended to succeed an established one.

So far, BMW's AI-based approach identifies every error the existing voltage-hold method finds – the minimum threshold for consideration. That doesn't mean an imminent changeover, however. Siedelhofer is candid that a wider dataset is still required before BMW would trust the new method to run alone, even at series-production scale. The likely path, in his view, is not a hard switch but a period of running in parallel; both methods operating side by side until production reaches a genuinely stable phase, at which point BMW could transition over.

BMW's Woodruff plant readies AI-led battery assembly

Ahead of December's series launch, BMW Group's new Woodruff facility in South Carolina pairs artificial intelligence with virtual reality training to deliver zero-defect Gen6 batteries for the fully-electric BMW iX5.

There's a tangible payoff even before full replacement happens. Conventional quality gates, Siedelhofer notes, often carry a high false "not OK" rate because they judge a cell on a single measured value rather than the fuller picture of how it was actually produced. By incorporating more process history into its assessment, BMW's AI-supported quality gates can reduce that false rejection rate – meaning less unnecessary scrap.

Working at pilot rather than gigafactory scale also gives BMW options that large-volume cell manufacturers don't prioritise. Because BMW isn't producing at true mass-market volumes, the company has the bandwidth to think carefully about what happens to any scrap it does generate – one of the drivers behind establishing its direct recycling competence centre in the first place.

Scaling: The "plumbing" problem, not the models

Asked where the biggest technical obstacle lies in scaling these AI models from prototype into series production, Siedelhofer is unambiguous; it isn't the models themselves. "The challenge in scaling is before you do analytics and predictions – the plumbing of the data," he says. Connecting robots and equipment to a usable data lake is, in his view, the real prerequisite for any analytics model to function – and that infrastructure work looks different at every scale and in every application.

That principle extends across technologies as well as production volumes. AI models BMW has developed for improving laser weld quality in battery cells, for example, can be adapted for use in high-voltage battery production, since welding also occurs there. The underlying model doesn't need reinventing – only the data feeding it needs to be reconnected, or "plumbed," differently.

The Parsdorf facility is designed with that scalability in mind. Rather than running cheaper, non-representative equipment, BMW has installed genuine, series-like machinery at every process step – for instance, the winder used at Parsdorf is the same type used in true series production, just deployed in smaller numbers. That design choice gives BMW clear visibility into how each individual process step would behave at full scale, even though total cell output at Parsdorf remains far below gigafactory volumes – volumes, Siedelhofer stresses, are the only way battery cell production becomes genuinely economic.

Towards a manufacturing copilot

The University of Zagreb collaboration was, in Siedelhofer 's view, never intended to stay confined to battery cells. From the outset, the ambition was for the AI tools developed through the project to extend well beyond battery production and into a broader concept — "some call it really a manufacturing copilot," he says, drawing a comparison to familiar office productivity copilots, but built for a production line instead.

Battery cell manufacturing remains, in his words, "special and a challenge" in its own right. But the AI capability built to solve its specific problems is explicitly designed to be portable to other production lines across BMW – one reason, he notes, that his team stays closely connected to colleagues working on high-voltage batteries and vehicle assembly more broadly. For BMW, the payoff of investing in cells it will never build at scale may ultimately extend well beyond the battery itself.

text:
Environmental groups have sued the Trump administration, alleging the Environmental Protection Agency approved a potentially cancer-causing "forever chemical" for use as an herbicide without fully assessing the risk.

The petition was filed Friday in the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit by the Center for Food Safety, the Center for Biological Diversity, and Pesticide Action & Agroecology Network North America, who asked the court to throw out the EPA's June 30 approval of trifludimoxazin and six products containing it for use on a wide range of crops including corn, wheat, soybeans, and apples.

Trifludimoxazin is part of the family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, synthetic chemicals with strong carbon-fluorine bonds that can take years to fully break down, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals."

The trifludimoxazin was initially approved in 2021 during the Biden administration. But the company agreed to stop selling the product the following year after environmental groups sued, citing its potential to cause cancer and harm to threatened and endangered fish. But the Trump EPA last year proposed registering it again for widespread use and issued a final approval in June.

The groups argue that the EPA approved the use of trifludimoxazin without accounting for evidence that the pesticide could cause cancer and harm wildlife and ecosystems.

The EPA itself has acknowledged that the chemical could harm many endangered and threatened species, including posing chronic risks to bees and other invertebrates. Meanwhile, rodent studies have found that at high doses, the chemical can cause thyroid tumors and adverse effects on the liver and reproductive systems.

The chemical, which blocks an enzyme in plants needed for growth, has been described as 10 times as potent as dicamba, another weedkiller used on soybeans and cotton, whose products have caused millions of acres of unintended crop damage since its approval in 2017.

But though the EPA's own guidance states that carcinogenic effects in animals could point to human risk, the agency stated that its final risk assessment found “no human health risks of concern."

The plaintiffs argue that the EPA did not take all the proper steps to reach this conclusion, having failed to quantify the chemical's danger, especially when combined with exposure to other approved chemicals.

“Trifludimoxazin is a likely human carcinogen that belongs to a family of weedkillers that also causes reproductive harm, birth defects, and neurological deficits in animal studies,” said Bill Freese, science director at the Center for Food Safety. “As if the health threats weren’t enough, this incredibly potent herbicide can drift to stunt crops and wild plants hundreds of yards from a sprayed field, while runoff threatens wetland plants. Potent biocides like this have no business on the American landscape.”

The lawsuit also notes that two of the approved trifludimoxazin products combine it with another toxic herbicide called saflufenacil, meaning that farmworkers who apply the chemicals could be exposed to the effects of both at once. The plaintiffs said the EPA did not evaluate the risk that would be posed to farmworkers who are exposed to these chemicals.

name: Clean Energy
title: Bioenergy is a Climate Problem We Can Only Solve Together - Earthjustice
authors: Peter Lehner, Carrie Apfel, Amy Yoon
description:
Today, advocates for truly clean renewable energy, forest protections, and clean communities are fighting these industries in their own separate silos.
The bioenergy industries benefit from government subsidies and mandates, but the costs fall on everyone else.
Together For Better Solutions Bioenergy is a climate problem hiding behind the guise of ‘renewable energy,’ but we have far better clean energy solutions that actually work for our climate, land, and communities.
With a unified voice, we can call for the government to strip mandates and subsidies.
Without that government guarantee, the industry pressure driving all three will reveal that this never had much to do with clean energy, but everything to do with land values and income.
text:
In Washington, D.C. and state capitals across the U.S., three powerful fuel industries have spent the last decades lobbying for versions of the same demand: require or subsidize sales of bio-based fuels. Corn and soy growers want ethanol and bio-based diesel mandates. Timberland owners and pellet manufacturers want tax credits and price supports for wood-fired electricity. Industrial feedlot and dairy operators want above-market payments for the methane gas their livestock produce.

This lobbying has paid off in the form of mandates in the Renewable Fuel Standard, subsidies in the Rural Energy for America Program, incentives in California’s Low Carbon Fuel Standard, and countless other subsidies, incentives, credits, and mandates scattered across federal and state programs. The industries benefit, but communities, consumers, taxpayers, and the climate pay the price.

These three industries win over public and government support through claims that their bio-energy source is cheaper, clean, and a solution for our climate than other energy sources. The truth, however, is the opposite: whole wood and pellet biomass, manure biogas, and crop-based biofuels are dirty, expensive, and only harm our climate, environment, and communities.

Today, advocates for truly clean renewable energy, forest protections, and clean communities are fighting these industries in their own separate silos. But while the debates about these three bio-energy sources occur in different contexts – forest management, meat production, or transportation fuels – they are largely the same. And if advocates recognize the commonalities in these fights, we can come together to help end wasteful subsidies, support healthier and more sustainable farming systems, accelerate truly clean energy and net-zero technologies, and hold corporate polluters accountable across the supply chain.

The Bioenergy Playbook

The industry’s success relies on a deceptively simple equation: “renewable” = “green.” The pitch is compelling because it begins with a genuine fact: carbon in trees, corn, and cow manure originally came from the atmosphere. And it’s logical to think: burn that material, and you’re just returning carbon to where it came from—making it carbon-neutral. What’s hidden is everything else—the land cleared, water consumed, chemicals applied, emissions from processing and transport, and the opportunity cost of using land for truly efficient renewable energy instead.

Each industry relies on the same playbook of accounting tricks to hide the real climate impacts:

For wood pellets, the “carbon debt” from logging – the impact of burning all the carbon in the wood – can take decades to repay through regrowth. And even then, the regrowth never fully catches up. The energy used to harvest timber and manufacture pellets produces carbon. Soil erosion releases more. And some forests don’t regrow at all. The math doesn’t work.

Growing corn and soy for biofuels releases high levels of greenhouse gases—especially from fertilizer manufacture and use. Using tens of millions of acres for fuel also pushes food production onto forests and grasslands, releasing the carbon they stored. Studies show the result: these biofuels are worse for the climate than gasoline.

Manure digesters used to produce biogas have a fundamental flaw. They capture a methane from manure pits, but they miss the significant amounts of methane belched by cattle. The issues don’t stop there: digesters regularly leak, and they create a powerful incentive for animal feeding operations to manage their manure to generate extra methane so they can get more subsidies. The system rewards unnecessary emissions.

Bad Economics and Bad for Communities

The math doesn’t just fail on emissions—it fails on economics. Biomass electricity needs government mandates and subsidies. Biofuels cost more than gasoline—and the EPA itself estimates the biofuel mandate will increase food and fuel costs by almost $10 billion per year. Manure digesters are the worst deal: they cost roughly ten times what the natural gas they produce is worth. The industry is government-dependent, not market-driven.

Landowner and agribusiness lobbies sell these programs to legislators on the promise of rural jobs. But that claim does not hold for any of these energy forms. Wood pellet plants create fewer and more hazardous jobs than often claimed; ethanol production has created few jobs, and those at a high cost; biogas production depends on infrastructure and generates few jobs.

The bioenergy industries benefit from government subsidies and mandates, but the costs fall on everyone else. Communities suffer from air and water pollutants, leading to severe impacts on health and quality of life.

In addition to the erosion and water pollution from timber harvesting, wood pellet production is severely polluting, harming communities, and largely unregulated. Near Gloster, Mississippi, a wood pellet plant exceeded its permitted pollution limit by three to four times while underreporting its true emissions by more than 25-fold.

Ethanol refineries emit significantly greater amounts of certain hazardous air pollutants than oil refineries do. In Iowa and Illinois, ethanol plants account for roughly 70% of all reported hazardous air pollution, while corn production is fouling drinking water supplies.

Communities near manure digesters and the feedlots that feed them, from California’s San Joaquin Valley to the rural South, suffer extreme air and water pollution, that is ignored by regulators.

And all of these bioenergy sources are devastating for wildlife and biodiversity, driving the conversion of native lands to crops, accelerating unsustainable logging, and polluting the clean water and ecosystems that wildlife needs.

Together For Better Solutions

Bioenergy is a climate problem hiding behind the guise of ‘renewable energy,’ but we have far better clean energy solutions that actually work for our climate, land, and communities.

Solar and wind power can produce gas and electricity far less expensively than manure biogas or wood pellet electricity. A hectare of solar panels charging electric vehicles delivers roughly 200 to 300 times as much mobility as a hectare of corn grown for ethanol. Even a conservative estimate still finds solar roughly 70 times more land-efficient than growing crops for biofuels, with none of the toxic pollution. Proven manure management techniques will reduce the methane generated and eliminate the need to capture it.

The farmland, woodland, and feedlot interests don’t coordinate with each other. They don’t need to. They’re running the same “renewable is green” playbook three times over, and they win because advocates are tackling each fight alone. They turn public subsidies into private land value, while our climate, environment, health, and quality of life suffer.

Here’s what breaks the cycle: Recognizing it’s one fight, not three. With a unified voice, we can call for the government to strip mandates and subsidies. Let these industries operate on their real merits—or lack thereof. Without that government guarantee, the industry pressure driving all three will reveal that this never had much to do with clean energy, but everything to do with land values and income.

text:
Palm oil and palm kernel oil are versatile oleochemical feedstocks widely used in food and personal care products and can be converted into industrial products such as biolubricants and bio-based plasticizers.

Despite its ubiquity, though, there are serious problems with palm oil. Palm oil production has led to deforestation and biodiversity loss, as well as unjust labor practices in Southeast Asia, where the majority of the world’s palm oil supply is produced.

Because it is derived from a tropical plant, the United States currently relies on imports to meet 100% of its demand for this critical platform chemical across the food, cosmetics, industrial lubricants, and plasticizer sectors creating significant supply chain vulnerabilities.

Mingyu Qiao, assistant professor of innovation and entrepreneurship in the Department of Nutritional Sciences (CAHNR), has received a $1.875 million grant from the Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office to turn seaweed into a replacement for palm oil and other medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) like coconut oil.

Seaweed farming has already established a foothold in Connecticut and New England as a sustainable and easy-to-grow crop.

Not only doesn’t seaweed consume fertilizers, water, or pesticides, as other crops do, but it also acts as a natural filter to clean the water in which it grows. Seaweed can be produced rapidly and on a large scale without competing for space with land-based crops.

“With seaweed, you can just put it in the ocean, and it’ll grow itself,” Qiao says. “You don’t need to apply any pesticides or fertilizers because the ocean has all the nutrients it needs.”

Qiao is using sugar kelp, a popular edible seaweed that is native to and already produced in Connecticut’s waters, for his research.

Qiao is using a biological process known as arrested anaerobic digestion to transform seaweed into MCFAs. Anaerobic digestion is a natural process through which bacteria break down organic matter in the absence of oxygen.

Normally this process produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. However, the natural salinity of seaweed inhibits methane-producing microorganisms, redirecting the process toward volatile fatty acid production. These acids can then be separated and upgraded into medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs), creating a more sustainable pathway.

This project is a collaboration with the Idaho National Laboratory, the recipient of $200,000 of the grant. The Laboratory will develop a method for preserving seaweed biomass long enough for it to be processed. Normally, seaweed rots within a few days of being out of the water. By adding lactic acid bacteria – the same bacteria found in yogurt – the researchers can stabilize and store the seaweed for months.

“That is the biggest problem for seaweed compared with something like corn or soybeans,” Qiao says. “This will solve that problem.”

Because the MCFAs Qiao’s team will produce are derived from seaweed, they can be used in all industries, like food and personal care, that require additives to be all-natural.

“For anything that comes into contact with the body, consumers increasingly prefer natural or bio-based materials because petroleum-derived products may contain trace impurities, some of which could pose toxicological or carcinogenic risks,” Qiao says.

This work will help support the U.S.’s supply chain resilience of critical chemicals and materials.

“For critical materials, [it’s important to be able to] produce them domestically,” Qiao says. “Even if it’s a little bit more expensive, those companies are willing to pay for that because it’s more secure. You can fully control that.”

text:
A federal judge ruled Monday that New York cannot enforce its landmark “climate Superfund” law, a measure that sought to charge fossil fuel companies $75 billion over 25 years to help the state deal with the costs of climate change.

While the legal battle is far from over, the ruling could give pause to lawmakers in many other states who have been considering similar legislation.

Chief Judge Brenda Sannes of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York ruled that New York’s 2024 law is preempted by the federal Clean Air Act, calling the measure “simply beyond the limits of state law.” Fossil fuel companies have long argued that federal regulations governing emissions supersede states’ authority to punish companies for their role in causing climate change.

“It is precisely because the (state) Climate Act operates within an area of law ‘in which the federal interest is so dominant’ that it cannot be enforced,” Sannes wrote in her ruling.

The case against New York’s law was brought by fossil fuel companies and the attorneys general of 22 Republican-led states.

“This is a major victory in the fight against liberal states, trying to balance their budgets on the backs of our hard-working men and women in the coal, oil and gas industries,” West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said in a statement.

Climate disasters are on the rise. These states want to make oil companies pay.

Environmental advocates called on New York Attorney General Letitia James to appeal the ruling.

“The fossil fuel industry would like nothing more than for one district court ruling in New York to scare lawmakers across the country into backing down, but this decision doesn’t bind other states or stop them from passing their own laws,” Cassidy DiPaola, communications director for Make Polluters Pay, an advocacy campaign supporting climate Superfund bills and lawsuits against fossil fuel companies.

“New York should fight this ruling, and every other state should keep moving until we make polluters pay their fair share.”

New York was the second state to pass a climate Superfund law, following a measure in Vermont. A lawsuit against Vermont’s law is still pending.

The laws are modeled on the federal Superfund program, which requires polluters to pay for the cleanup of toxic waste sites.

Lawmakers in at least 12 other states have proposed similar bills this session, although none has advanced so far. While the policy has gained significant attention and support in recent years, experts said that some legislators were likely waiting to see how the legal battles over the New York and Vermont laws would play out.

text:
The 2026 Report Card for Virginia's Infrastructure, released by the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE), gave the state's energy system a D, the lowest of its 13 graded categories and below the national D+ average for energy. It is the first time ASCE has included energy in its Virginia assessment, and the grade reflects a widening gap between electricity demand and the pace at which new generation, transmission and distribution capacity can be added. Dominion Energy CEO Robert Blue has said the utility expects power demand in its Virginia territory to double by 2039, driven in large part by the state's concentration of data centers.

Commercial Electricity Sales in Virginia Grew Nearly 30 Million MWh Since 2019

Federal data back up ASCE's concern. Commercial electricity sales in Virginia increased by nearly 30 million megawatt-hours between 2019 and 2025, faster growth than in any state except Texas, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), which credits much of the increase to the state's data center concentration, building electrification and electric vehicle adoption. Peak demand is climbing just as fast. Summer peak load in PJM Interconnection's Dominion zone reached 23,905 MW in 2025, 23% higher than in 2019, while winter peak load hit 25,413 MW in the 2025-26 season, up 45% from 2019-20. PJM now projects summer peak demand in the Dominion zone will grow by an average of 5.4% annually over the next decade, and expects the zone to see the largest absolute increase in summer peak demand of any PJM territory through 2030.

Virginia Remains the Nation's Largest Net Importer of Electricity

Virginia's ability to meet that demand also depends heavily on power generated elsewhere. The state remains the nation's largest net importer of electricity, with roughly a third of its demand brought in from outside its borders, according to figures cited by ASCE Virginia leadership. ASCE highlighted that reliance in assigning the D grade, while also noting that utilities are planning additional generation, transmission and distribution assets; its core concern is that anticipated demand is growing faster than currently planned expansion. Virginia is adding resources: state reporting shows utilities placed roughly 2,340 MW of solar and wind capacity into service between July 2018 and June 2025, and state policymakers have already begun adjusting how data center electricity costs get allocated as the buildout accelerates.

Bridges and Broadband Led the Rest of Virginia's Report Card

Virginia's overall C grade was unchanged from 2022, and several other categories improved. Bridges and broadband earned the state's highest marks at B+, solid waste received a B, drinking water and rail came in at C+, and roads, public parks and stormwater held at C. Dams and transit received C-, while schools and wastewater were graded D+. ASCE said categories receiving consistent funding have generally shown stronger improvement, though it warned that momentum could become harder to sustain as Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act funding winds down.

text:
Illinois Tech students spent the last four years re-engineering a stock 2023 Cadillac Lyric into an award-winning, next-generation electric vehicle as part of the EcoCAR EV Challenge.

More than 200 Illinois Tech students participated in the four-year challenge through the Interprofessional Projects (IPRO) Program or independent study. Working directly with engineers from General Motors, the students engineered advanced propulsion controls, connected and automated vehicle features, and vehicle-to-everything connectivity, all while improving energy efficiency and meeting real automotive industry standards.

The challenge culminated by taking the car to GM’s testing facility in Milford, Michigan, for two weeks of evaluation and then driving it to GM headquarters in downtown Detroit.

“EcoCAR allowed me to find a career path I’m passionate in and develop specialized skills that are difficult to teach in a classroom setting,” says Martin Harmon (ECE, M.S. 5th Year). “What intrigued me about the project was that it was one of the few organizations on campus that I felt allowed me to both reinforce my skills learned in the classroom and develop new skills. Designing and testing features on a real vehicle is an opportunity that most schools don’t have, and I didn’t want to pass it up.”

The Illinois Tech team was one of 13 teams of university students that were selected by GM and its co-sponsors, the United States Department of Energy and MathWorks. The team earned the Best Final Vehicle Integration Award and finished sixth in the overall competition.

“Our vehicle safety, robustness, and energy efficiency was comparable to the vehicle that finished first and second, and we were among the five cars of 13 that participated in the over-the-road events,” says Rashad Hossain (MAE 2nd Year). “This experience has helped me enter the automotive world and helped me secure an internship at Argonne National Laboratory.”

Illinois Tech Professor of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering Carrie Hall says that she was impressed by how well the students responded to the demands of GM engineers, who held the students to highest industry standards.

“Students were expected to maintain high standards by the GM engineers and maintain the quality expected of young engineers in the GM workplace,” Hall says. “It was a great opportunity to teach industry standards by working together with GM engineers. It was a great challenge to the students, and they were able to get a solid foundation for a professional career. Seeing the training ground was especially helpful.”

Hall and Professor of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering Matthew Spenko help lead the team, and she says seeing the car on the road after four years of work was particularly satisfying

Hall says students from academic backgrounds across campus participated in the EcoCAR EV Challenge, as it required knowledge in engineering, computer science, architecture, business, and even psychology to rebuild the car to the standards that were set.

“I was on the team for three years, and being able to see the project through to completion left a big impact on me,” Harmon says. “It was my first experience of seeing what a long-term engineering project is like and the amount of work and manpower that goes into something like that. I think the thing that left the biggest impression on me was the people in the team. Even if we were working on different aspects of the vehicle, people frequently would help others with their tasks when help was needed. There was mutual respect for others and the work they were doing.”
