text:
(TestMiles) – The electric Genesis flagship pairs a pillarless entrance and lounge-like cabin with 657 hp, but its biggest tests are still ahead.

Genesis spent its first decade proving that a Korean luxury brand could compete with familiar German and Japanese names. The 2028 GV90 begins a more difficult assignment. This time, the company is presenting its first full-size flagship SUV as an alternative to the grandest vehicles from Range Rover, Bentley and Rolls-Royce.

That intention becomes clear before anyone sits down. The GV90 Neolun uses rear-hinged coach doors and hides the center pillar inside the door structure, creating an uninterrupted opening when both doors are wide. The standard GV90 keeps conventional doors and a more familiar three-row layout. Both are electric, both sit above the GV80, and both are expected in the United States in early 2027.

It would be easy to treat the unusual doors as the entire story. They photograph beautifully, and the visual association with Rolls-Royce requires no explanation. Yet the more consequential idea is that Genesis has developed a flagship around Korean hospitality instead of reproducing a British club room or a German technology showroom. The result combines real wood, leather, stone and available wool cashmere with conveniences intended to change how occupants use a parked vehicle.

The specifications are substantial. Two motors provide a combined maximum of 657 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque. The 123.5-kilowatt-hour battery is the largest installed in a Hyundai Motor Group electric vehicle. Genesis estimates about 310 miles for the seven-seat version, although that figure comes from the company’s internal testing and is not an EPA rating.

For all the confirmed hardware, several buying questions remain unanswered. Genesis has not announced a U.S. price, EPA-certified range, cargo volume or towing capacity. No independent crash-test result or road test can yet establish whether the flagship drives, charges and operates as serenely as its presentation suggests. The GV90 has made a dramatic entrance. Its next job is to prove that the spectacle works in ordinary ownership.

Coach doors are the headline, not the whole story

Genesis calls the Neolun’s opening the Neolun Arch Gate. The rear door first moves slightly outward and then rotates toward the back of the vehicle, allowing it to operate without waiting for the front door. When both sides are open, there is no fixed pillar dividing the entrance. The arrangement should make access easier for second-row passengers, older family members and parents helping children into seats.

Eliminating a fixed center pillar creates engineering obligations as well as visual drama. Genesis says it replaced the usual structure with dual high-strength steel beams in the doors, reinforced the passenger compartment with integrated steel tubes and structural foam, and created a concealed roll cage. The company describes part of that frame as 1.5 times thicker than conventional construction. Those are manufacturer claims awaiting independent validation, but they show how much work was required to turn a concept-car gesture into production hardware.

Once parked, the Neolun can become a face-to-face room. Its front seats rotate 180 degrees at the press of a button, giving passengers a place to talk or work while the vehicle is stationary. The available four-seat Executive Suite adds folding tables, a refrigerator, privacy blinds and a partition between the second row and cargo area.

The cabin’s cultural reference is more interesting than its equipment count. A real-wood second-row floor uses radiant heat inspired by ondol, the traditional Korean practice of warming a room from below. A six-zone glass roof can vary its transparency, while radiant panels warm armrests, side panels and door trim. These choices turn warmth, calm and privacy into part of the design language rather than treating luxury as a list of screens.

Why Genesis is reaching above the usual luxury class

The standard GV90 and the Neolun serve related but different customers. A six- or seven-seat conventional-door model is the practical flagship for families who need three rows. Neolun supplies the theatrical entrance, more elaborate materials and a rear-passenger emphasis. The limited First Edition sits at the top with the most exclusive finishes and the full four-seat treatment.

That separation matters because shoppers will encounter images of the open coach doors and Executive Suite long before they see a price sheet. Not every GV90 will contain every headline feature. Genesis will need unusually clear trim explanations so that the showroom vehicle does not feel less special than the launch photography.

Range Rover Electric is the closest conceptual rival because it combines a full-size SUV body, electric propulsion and an established luxury identity. Rolls-Royce provides the obvious door comparison, although its electric Spectre is a coupe and the Cullinan SUV still uses an internal-combustion engine. Bentley and Mercedes-Maybach also compete for buyers who regard the passenger experience as seriously as performance.

Genesis enters that group without a century of inherited status. Its advantage is freedom from old expectations. The body takes inspiration from the clean volume of Korean moon jars, and the interior is organized around the brand’s idea of treating a customer as an honored guest. Its disadvantage is that ultra-luxury buyers expect the retailer, software, service and personalization process to feel as considered as the vehicle. A beautiful cabin cannot compensate for a difficult charging stop or an unresolved electronic fault.

An electric flagship with serious hardware

The two-motor system sends power to all four wheels through electronic limited-slip differentials at the front and rear, a first for Hyundai Motor Group. Genesis says the arrangement can reduce slip on wet, snowy or uneven surfaces and manage power during faster cornering. It sounds promising for a vehicle this large, although no one outside the development team has yet established its real-world behavior.

Rear-wheel steering can turn the back wheels by as much as five degrees. At parking speeds, that should reduce the space required for a U-turn and help the 208.1-inch SUV behave more like a smaller vehicle. At higher speeds, the same system is intended to improve stability. A multi-chamber air suspension changes ride height and spring stiffness, while electronically controlled dampers use separate responses for sharp impacts and larger body movements.

Quietness is another part of the flagship brief. Genesis says every window uses acoustic glass more than five millimeters thick, including the windshield, roof and tailgate glass. Soundproofing material fills cavities in the main structure, and additional absorbers and seals target noise entering through the body. Electric propulsion removes engine sound, but that can expose tire, wind and suspension noise that a combustion engine once masked.

The 123.5-kWh battery supports a claimed 10-to-80-percent charge in 22 minutes when connected to a compatible 350-kW DC fast charger. That is a laboratory-style best case, not a promise for every stop. Charger capability, battery temperature, starting charge, weather and the vehicle’s charging curve all affect the result.

The estimated 310-mile range is similarly provisional. It applies to the seven-seat GV90 under Genesis internal testing, not an official U.S. certification cycle. The EPA label will allow shoppers to compare versions on the same basis and will add efficiency information that a single range number cannot provide. A very large battery can produce a useful distance while still consuming more energy per mile than a lighter electric SUV.

Safety engineering carries unusual responsibility

The wildest feature is above the passengers. Genesis describes the GV90’s roof airbag as a production world first. During a severe rollover, it is designed to deploy beneath the panoramic glass, reduce contact with the roof and help prevent an occupant from being ejected through the opening. It is one of 12 airbags in the vehicle.

The concept has a history. Hyundai Mobis showed a panoramic-roof airbag in 2017 after identifying ejection through sunroofs as a rollover concern. Putting the idea into a production flagship is a meaningful step, but a manufacturer’s description is not the same as a crash-test result. The GV90’s unusual door construction makes independent side-impact, rollover and roof-strength evaluations especially valuable.

Genesis also says seat-mounted airbags can deploy at different depths according to occupant posture, cushion airbags are intended to limit submarining beneath a belt, and third-row curtain coverage has been extended. An in-cabin monitoring system evaluates occupant type, belt use and sitting position so the restraint system can respond accordingly.

Battery protection receives similar attention. Individual cells are separated to slow heat propagation, the pack is designed to shed heat, and a cloud-connected management system looks for abnormalities before they become emergencies. Structural measures are intended to direct major components underneath the vehicle during a frontal collision rather than into the battery. Again, these are engineering descriptions that need to be judged alongside regulatory compliance, recall history and independent testing.

The missing numbers will decide the verdict

The technology inside the GV90 extends beyond the safety system. A 23.6-inch OLED display rises by 90 millimeters when parked and becomes a 24.6-inch entertainment screen. The driver uses a 25-inch head-up display instead of a conventional instrument cluster. Pleos Connect is based on Android Automotive, while Gleo AI is intended to answer conversational requests.

Remote Smart Parking Assist 3 can handle selected parking maneuvers from outside the SUV. Memory Reversing Assist records a path and can retrace it backward, a potentially helpful feature when the vehicle has entered a narrow driveway or alley. A 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen system supports Dolby Atmos and can imitate the acoustics of Boston Symphony Hall or Wembley Stadium. Fifteen air cells in each massage seat complete a list that makes some private aircraft appear under-equipped.

What is missing is more important than another surprise. Buyers need U.S. pricing for all three expressions, final standard and optional equipment, EPA range, energy efficiency, charging performance in cold and hot weather, usable cargo dimensions, payload and towing figures. They also need to know how the four-seat partition affects luggage carrying and whether the huge Neolun doors are convenient in a tight garage.

Genesis deserves credit for avoiding a timid flagship. The GV90 is visually restrained but conceptually bold, and it gives Korean ideas of hospitality a physical form. It may suit a family seeking a serene three-row EV, an executive who works from the rear seat or an established luxury owner ready to consider a younger badge.

The final judgment cannot be made from an opening ceremony. Luxury at this level is measured in the quality of every routine interaction, from the first door movement to the third winter charging stop. Genesis has shown that it understands occasion. Pricing, road behavior, safety results and ownership support will reveal whether it has also mastered confidence.

text:
A federal court on Monday struck down a New York law that sought to hold fossil fuel companies accountable for climate change.

Brenda Sannes, an appointee of former President Obama, ruled that New York’s “Climate Superfund” law is preempted by federal statutes.

“The Climate Act is an unusual and sweeping statute, designed to address the effects of climate change — a ‘uniquely international problem of national concern,’” Sannes wrote.

She added that the act is “beyond the limits of state law” and added “it is precisely because the Climate Act operates within an area of law ‘in which the federal interest is so dominant’ that it cannot be enforced.”

In 2024, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) signed a bill that would hold the companies that have been responsible for the most planet-warming emissions to pay a total of $3 billion a year for 25 years.

The law is modeled after federal Superfund laws, which put companies on the hook to pay for the pollution that they cause.

Republican-led states and fossil fuel trade associations challenged the New York law in court, characterizing it as an attempt to reshape the entire country’s energy industry.

New York has argued that its law seeks to hold companies accountable for harm the state has incurred due to climate change’s impacts on rising temperatures and extreme weather.

The Trump administration has also sued New York to try to block the law. It has also sued Vermont, which has a similar one on the books.

“Taxpayers shouldn’t have to foot the bill for damages caused by polluters,” said Ken Lovett, senior communications adviser on energy and environment for Hochul, in an email.

“We are reviewing the decision to determine possible next steps,” he added.

Red states and the Trump administration celebrated the ruling.

“New York’s law would have expropriated $75 billion from energy companies around the world during an energy emergency and in direct defiance of American foreign policy and federal law,” Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson said in a statement.

“This is a major victory in the fight against liberal states, trying to balance their budgets on the backs of our hard-working men and women in the coal, oil and gas industries,” West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey (R) said in a statement. “West Virginians can’t afford more liberal policies that jack up electricity and transportation costs. Thankfully, New York politicians can’t put their hands in West Virginia families’ pocketbooks now.”

title: Koch Data-Center Push Draws Subsidy Scrutiny - Uprise RI
description:
Koch says Edged has built or developed projects for major hyperscale technology companies, a term for operators requiring unusually large computing facilities.
The projects include 96 megawatts in Chicago, 24 megawatts in Kansas City and 168 megawatts in Atlanta, according to the company.

text:
A privately held multinational conglomerate has expanded into the electricity-intensive data-center business through a developer reporting more than 388 megawatts of delivered capacity, a move that has drawn scrutiny from watchdogs over the company’s broader subsidy record and its political network’s campaign to accelerate energy permitting.

Koch Inc. created Edged in 2024 through Koch Real Estate Investments and entrepreneur Jakob Carnemark, positioning the company to develop, build and operate facilities for large technology customers as artificial intelligence and cloud computing increase demand for computing capacity.

A report published August 25 by the Center for Media and Democracy and republished by Good Jobs First connected that expansion to Koch’s use of public incentives across its broader business portfolio and to energy policies promoted by Koch-backed Americans for Prosperity.

The available subsidy data cover Koch Industries and affiliated companies across multiple industries and decades, rather than Edged or data centers specifically. The report therefore places Koch’s data-center expansion against the conglomerate’s subsidy history without establishing that Edged has received a particular public award.

Koch says Edged has built or developed projects for major hyperscale technology companies, a term for operators requiring unusually large computing facilities. The projects include 96 megawatts in Chicago, 24 megawatts in Kansas City and 168 megawatts in Atlanta, according to the company.

Edged lists facilities in Atlanta, Chicago, Columbus, Dallas, Des Moines, Kansas City and Phoenix. The company says its platform has delivered more than 388 megawatts of critical capacity, the power available to operate computing equipment.

The business extends beyond real estate. Koch says Edged acquires land, organizes construction and negotiates utility power agreements, while other Koch companies can provide expertise in engineering, cooling, solar power, battery storage and natural-gas generation.

Koch also says Edged can use behind-the-meter power, meaning generation or storage installed on the customer’s side of a utility connection, to supplement electricity from the grid. Those options include on-site solar, batteries and natural-gas generation.

Edged markets a closed-loop cooling system called ThermalWorks that Koch says consumes zero water and can support computing racks using as much as 200 kilowatts. The zero-water figure is a company performance claim.

The developer’s growth has also attracted potential buyers. Bloomberg reported on July 28 that Koch was exploring a sale of Edged and had received multiple bids that could value the company above $15 billion, though no transaction was final at that time.

That figure represents a possible enterprise valuation, not the amount Koch invested in Edged or proceeds from a completed sale.

Good Jobs First’s Subsidy Tracker lists $795,989,211 in state and local subsidies across 396 awards for Koch Industries and affiliated companies. It also lists $3,607,560 in federal grants and allocated tax credits.

The state and local records begin in 1977, with most listings dating from 2014 onward, and span Koch businesses in chemicals, manufacturing, fertilizer, pulp and paper, glass and electronics, among other industries. The database excludes awards for which dollar values were not disclosed.

Americans for Prosperity has separately backed federal permitting changes that it says would speed project approvals, expand energy supplies and lower costs. In a July statement, the Koch-backed organization explicitly cited growing energy demand from data centers, manufacturing and technology as a reason for changing the permitting process.

The policy campaign addresses a central constraint on data-center growth: electricity. The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects that annual electricity use by data-center servers could reach between 446 billion and 818 billion kilowatt-hours by 2050, depending on assumptions.

The Congressional Research Service summarized an estimate that data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023, equal to 4.4% of total U.S. consumption. Rapid growth has fueled disputes over who should pay for power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure required to serve large facilities.

Georgia Power says its revised rules require large data-center customers to pay infrastructure costs upfront, accept long-term contracts and cover their full cost of service without shifting expenses to residential customers. Rhode Island lawmakers have taken a more precautionary approach, proposing rules intended to prevent electricity infrastructure costs from being passed to households and small businesses.

House Speaker Pro Tempore Brian Kennedy announced legislation on January 29 that would have required annual water-use reports, allowed water-efficiency plans and required financial assurance for restoring data-center sites. The proposal also addressed how utilities allocate infrastructure costs associated with serving the facilities.

Rhode Island lawmakers separately considered a data-center tax incentive for qualifying projects investing at least $200 million in an enterprise or opportunity zone, or $400 million elsewhere. The proposal included labor requirements and conditions involving renewable energy or energy storage.

The Rhode Island measures concerned the industry broadly rather than Koch or Edged. The incentive bills were held for further study and died when the regular legislative session ended June 11.

title: Homegrown home battery upstart shares in $1.7 million of funding to boost local manufacturing
description:

First announced in November of last year, the Local Battery Manufacturing Program will provide up to $30 million in grants and $20 million in low-interest loans to support the local manufacture of residential, commercial and industrial batteries and battery components – and bolster local supply chains.
“The Local Battery Manufacturing Program is about building local manufacturing capability and keeping more value in our state,” said Amber-Jade Sanderson, state minister for energy and decarbonisation.

text:
Perth-based home battery market newcomer Magellan Power has been named as one of three Western Australian businesses to be awarded a total of $1.7 million in state government funding towards five projects designed to help grow the state’s battery manufacturing sector.

The funding, from WA Labor’s Local Battery Manufacturing Program, will help the three companies – including Adarsh Investments and ProtoLab Manufacturing – to develop and test prototypes, buy advanced equipment, and “significantly expand” their production capacity.

First announced in November of last year, the Local Battery Manufacturing Program will provide up to $30 million in grants and $20 million in low-interest loans to support the local manufacture of residential, commercial and industrial batteries and battery components – and bolster local supply chains.

Magellan, which was had its start back in 1991 designing and supplying uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems has since branched into energy storage, including the local manufacture and recycling of mostly commercial, industrial and community-scale, or stand-alone, battery energy storage systems.

In May of 2025 Magellan launched its first residential energy storage offering, Karri, just ahead of the July 2025 launch of the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries scheme.

There are no details on the five projects that will share in the funding, but in the case of Magellan, the company has several irons in the fire. It has been gearing up to manufacture the Karri battery, locally, and also aims to start production of modular community batteries that range between 100 kW to 1 MW.

Magellan is also in the process of establishing a new 15,000-square-metre headquarters at Trident Estate, Hope Valley, in Perth, which began construction last year.

Adarsh Investments is a manufacturer, fabricator and importer of component parts with – its website says – “a strong history of designing and manufacturing equipment and parts for the renewable energy industry.”

Protolab, meanwhile, describes itself as an electronics manufacturing company specialising in circuit board assembly and small-to-medium production runs.

“The Local Battery Manufacturing Program is about building local manufacturing capability and keeping more value in our state,” said Amber-Jade Sanderson, state minister for energy and decarbonisation.

“These projects will support the development of innovative battery technologies, increase production capacity, and help businesses manufacture components that would otherwise be sourced from interstate or overseas.

“By supporting local battery manufacturing, we’re helping build resilient supply chains, creating highly skilled jobs, and supporting Australia’s transition to a cleaner energy future.”

The program will now reopen for applications. Funding is available through two separate streams – the Production-Ready Stream, which provides up to $100,000 in matched funding to businesses for projects in three categories of pre-production activities; and the Production Scale-Up Stream, which provides up to $5 million in matched funding to existing battery manufacturers for projects that scale-up their operations.

More information about the Local Battery Manufacturing Program can be found here.

title: Matt Lanza: I'm a meteorologist who left Houston. Here's why.
description:

text:
When the news came out this spring that I was leaving Houston, I thought it was interesting that some media reports framed it as a meteorologist fleeing climate change. That led people to ask, “If a meteorologist is leaving Houston because of climate change, what should I be doing?” It also produced humorous social media fodder. Everyone believes what they believe.

But here’s the reality: Though I didn’t leave Houston because of climate change, it’s a reality that we need to build more resiliency in this city to manage the impacts.

If anything, I’m bullish on Houston’s future more than most other Texas cities. Why? Houston works. It’s functional, and it has an attitude and culture to match. When I’m asked what I’ll miss most about Houston, I answer, “The people and the food.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The people speak for themselves. Houstonians are some of the nicest, most charitable, coolest people in the country. Sadly, it often takes disasters for the world to see that. But living here, you get it.

As for the food? I don’t care what magazine or website rankings say, Houston has the best food culture in America. I’ve gotten to know folks in the food and beverage industry in Houston, and I cannot profess my admiration for them enough. And when I think about the consequences of extreme weather, I think about the people who work in that industry, where margins matter so much. One storm can end it for them.

Houston Chronicle Logo

Want more Houston Chronicle?

Make us a Preferred Source on Google to see more of us when you search.

Add Preferred Source

When I write for Space City Weather, I think of a restaurant owner as my audience. They care deeply about weather impacts, and they just want to know what everything means to their business, employees and livelihood.

When thinking about climate change and extreme weather, I don’t think of the politics or even the causes. What I think about is the impact. And outside of maybe Florida, Louisiana and California, I don’t think any place in the U.S. has seen more impact than Houston in the last 10 to 15 years.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

When we think about solutions, we need to think about mitigation and resilience. And yes, that stuff costs money. But you know what else costs money? People fleeing to other cities because they’ve flooded repeatedly. Amazing restaurateurs could well decide that though they love Houston, in order to function with fewer flood risks or power outages due to storms, they need to take their business to Austin or San Antonio or elsewhere. Maybe even a top-tier energy company could decide that to keep their operations functioning with fewer risks of disruption, they should set up shop in Austin or Dallas.

These aren’t far-fetched scenarios. These are plausible, and Houston and the state and the country, for that matter, need to think of them as such.

So what do we do? First off, accept that we’re going to have flooding. Flooding is a part of Houston. Honestly, it’s part of our culture at this point. “H-Town till I drown” should be a rallying cry, not a reluctant acceptance. We are a city that floods.

That said, we should be doing all we can to mitigate flooding. “Mitigate” doesn’t mean “prevent.” It means “reduce impacts.” Much of that work is underway, but as the Houston Chronicle has frequently reported, some of those projects are at risk, there’s political drama, and everyone has their hands in the pot. Some elected officials treat flood mitigation like a political football instead of focusing on getting to the finish line.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It’s long past time to stop playing games with this stuff. Sort out the timing and funding maturely. Work with the state of Texas. Get the projects done.

When it comes to politics, Houston residents have a degree of apathy. I blame no one for that in 2026. But the least we should demand of our elected officials is that they work aggressively together on flood mitigation. And we should all speak up about that.

Not only is Houston flood-prone, we’re also hurricane-prone. Hurricane Ike hit in 2008, but the Ike Dike is mostly still a plan on paper. Stories about Texas, and specifically about Houston’s hurricane risk, have been written multiple times since then. Since 2017, when Hurricane Harvey walloped Houston, we’ve seen numerous Category 4 and 5 hurricanes devastate parts of the Gulf Coast.

Work on the Ike Dike needs to speed up. Processes have to be done, and boxes need to be checked. But we need to cut the red tape or accelerate these reviews and get the project moving. The congressional delegation from Texas has done what they can so far. Let’s move faster.

We also make it extremely difficult for people to know their true risk when trying to decide on a home or rental. While embracing flooding as part of Houston’s fabric and doing what we can to minimize the impacts, we must think about ways we can make it easier for people to identify whether a home or apartment is in a flood zone. What is the true risk to a property?

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Though people complain that physical signs related to flooding hurt property values, we at least need to make it less confusing for home buyers and renters to access something beyond the 100 and 500 year floodplain maps and the “it can flood anywhere” mantra to assess their true flooding risk.

No one gets a “Welcome to Houston” packet that gives you the truth — good and challenging — about life here. Maybe someone needs to develop that.

I am grateful to Houston for providing me 14 years of memories. I am grateful to the people who trust Eric Berger and myself with Space City Weather and The Eyewall, our hurricane-coverage site. And though the only constant in life is change, I will hold this city close and root for it from a distance. And I’ll continue to advocate for its future whenever I can.

Matt Lanza is editor of The Eyewall and managing editor of Space City Weather. He now lives in Connecticut.

Climate change activists urged Hochul's administration to appeal. A spokesperson for Hochul's administration said “taxpayers shouldn’t have to foot the bill for damages caused by polluters” and that the administration was reviewing the decision to determine its next steps.

President Donald Trump's administration previously challenged Michigan, Hawaii and Vermont over similar laws after he declared a “ national energy emergency ″ and ordered his attorney general to take action against states that may be illegally overreaching their authority in how they regulate energy.

In a statement, the Department of Justice said it is “delivering on President Trump’s order to protect American energy from state overreach.”

“New York’s law would have expropriated $75 billion from energy companies around the world during an energy emergency and in direct defiance of American foreign policy and federal law,” Adam Gustafson, a principal deputy assistant attorney general, said in a statement.

New York's law had required companies responsible for substantial greenhouse gas emissions to collectively pay $3 billion a year over 25 years into a fund for infrastructure projects meant to repair or avoid future damage from climate change.

Lawmakers approved the bill to force big oil and gas companies to contribute to the cost of repairs inflicted by extreme weather events and to underwrite resiliency projects such as coastal wetland restoration and upgrades to roads, bridges and water drainage systems.

The biggest emitters of greenhouse gases between 2000 and 2018 were to be subjected to the fines.

text:
Over 190,000 Pennsylvanians have dropped their healthcare coverage through Pennie, the commonwealth’s healthcare marketplace, after Republicans in Congress refused to extend Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax credits that expired at the end of last year.

“It’s catastrophic, and I don’t use that word lightly,” State Rep. Arvind Venkat (D-Allegheny) said in an interview.

Venkat, who was first elected to the Pennsylvania House in 2022, sits on Pennie’s Board of Directors, and is the General Assembly’s only practicing emergency room physician.

“Individuals who have dropped their health insurance coverage are a time bomb waiting to happen,” he said.

He added, “we don’t know when we might get sick and when we might need care, and what we’re seeing is a rapid increase in the number of our fellow Pennsylvanians who are very vulnerable to falling into medical debt, to experiencing bankruptcy, and having severe medical consequences.”

Republicans allowed the ACA tax credits, which were part of the Inflation Reduction Act, to expire at the end of last year, and Pennie officials at the time warned that as many as 200,000 customers dropped their coverage.

Venkat pointed to House Bill 2550, which passed out of the Pennsylvania House by a 200 to 2 vote earlier this year, as a potential solution to ease rising costs, but it has sat in the state Senate since June.

The bill would establish a tax credit for small businesses with 50 or fewer employees who contribute to their employees’ health insurance premiums through an arrangement with Pennie. Other states that have enacted similar proposals or are considering them include Indiana, Mississippi, Ohio, Connecticut, and Arizona.

“If we continue on this trajectory over the next two to three years, we could end up falling from a high of almost 500,000 Pennsylvanians who are insured on Pennie to closer to 300,000 or even less,” Venkat said.

Nationally, a survey from the Kaiser Family Foundation released earlier this year found that over 80% of Americans enrolled in an ACA marketplace plan saw their healthcare costs increase and 55% cut spending on food and other expenses to remain covered.

Pennie customers saw their average premiums increase by 102% after the ACA tax credits expired with rural counties seeing the largest increase in premiums, and according to Venkat, the increase in healthcare costs is becoming an issue while talking to constituents.

“I door knock constantly…, and I have heard story after story from my constituents who are trying to stay insured, had good health insurance through Pennie, and now they have been forced to drop their health insurance coverage,” Venkat said.

“The issue of affordability in healthcare is significant and one that may be the most important issue in this election, and one that I hear always when I’m speaking with my constituents.”

text:
WADENA — House District 5A candidates made their case to voters at a candidate's forum Thursday, Aug. 27, in Wadena, hosted by the Todd-Wadena Electric Cooperative.

Dan Mitchell of rural Pequot Lakes is the DFL candidate for Minnesota House District 5A. He is running against Republican incumbent Krista Knudsen of Lake Shore.

Mitchell, a cybersecurity engineer, is married with two boys — the youngest in the Air Force. Mitchell has 20 years of experience in emergency services work, including EMS and firefighting.

He said that at some point, the political parties quit working together and now they just play politics. “I don’t think the middle class is being represented anymore,” he said. “I would like to defend the middle class. The American middle class is the most powerful force in the world, but it’s being hollowed out.”

Knudsen is a former city council member and mayor of Lake Shore, where she lives with her husband and four children. She said that when she first ran for Minnesota House in 2022, ”I felt something was wrong with our state. We ran a restaurant in Lake Shore and had just survived COVID (shutdowns). We could go back to church again. Children were back in school again. We should never go back (to those mandatory shutdowns) again.” She said she has learned a lot in her first term in the Minnesota House.

Renewable energy was raised in the forum, especially regarding a 2023 DFL-passed law that requires electric utilities to provide 100% carbon-free electricity by 2040.

Under the law, investor-owned electric utilities are required to be 80% carbon-free by 2030. That requirement is 60% for other electric utilities – like Todd-Wadena Electric Cooperative. However, all electric utilities must be 90% carbon-free by 2035, and 100% carbon-free by 2040.

Mitchell said that he has written about green energy from a national security standpoint, and that the current war in shows the need for America to hedge its bets with wind, solar and nuclear energy, which he supports. “We need to recycle the spent (radioactive fuel) rods. Other countries do it,” he said.

When it comes to climate change deniers, Mitchell said they are going off incorrect information. “There are all kinds of facts out there," he said. "Just saying it’s true doesn’t make it true. We should (have) green energy on our grid.”

Mitchell also spoke strongly against data centers, which he said are costly in various ways to locals who live near them, and exist to make the tech billionaires even richer. The public should not fund data centers, he said. “The people making the most money should pay the most money,” he said.

Knudsen said that “renewable energy is a hot topic in the (Minnesota) House,” adding that there may be room in the mix for renewable energy, but it can’t be the only solution. “We can’t depend on solar or wind in Minnesota — it (electricity) must be affordable and reliable.” Consumers should quit subsiding green energy, she added, and the state has to seriously consider generating more nuclear power.

The current requirement for 100% renewable power in Minnesota by 2040 is unworkable, she said. “It will bankrupt our state to do that.”

Fraud is a big issue in Minnesota, and could end up being as much as $9 billion, then-First Assistant U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson said in a news conference in December. Or not. As of Aug. 25, documented cases being prosecuted total less than $500 million, which includes the $250-$300 million in the Feeding Our Future case.

Asked about fraud in Minnesota, Mitchell said “fraud is a big issue. It’s unacceptable that you lost track of millions. All that money was sent out for COVID (relief) — it was the wild, wild West. They should have known it was ripe for fraud.”

But two wrongs don't make a right, and “the people of Minnesota are being punished,” he said, for ideological reasons by the federal government. To take legitimate federal food benefits and social services funding away from honest Minnesotans under the guise of fighting fraud “is unacceptable,” he said.

He also attempted to turn the tables on Republicans at the forum, noting that many of them were in office at the time and also failed to notice or stop the fraud. “Why,” he asked, “aren't we pointing the finger at them?”

Knudsen said that “fraud is rampant in the state,” she said. “We have to clean house in our agencies — there’s no way anyone can tell me they didn't know what was happening."

Safeguards must be put in place to prevent fraud, she said. “Money is being thrown at nonprofits with zero results, zero accountability," she said. “Fraud is a huge concern, and it will take a long time to address it adequately."

Asked how to stabilize the farm economy, Knudsen said that “agriculture is the backbone of rural Minnesota,” and she advocated reducing property taxes, including on agricultural property, making energy “affordable for all of us,” and lowering input costs, like fertilizer, for ag. “We need government to get out of the way — one-size fits all mandates hurt rural Minnesota the most.”

Mitchell said, “how do we save the small farm and the farm-to-table operations? The connection (in the public mind) between farmers and food is almost gone. We’re losing that. How do we fix that? It’s not easy.”

At Farmfest, there were representatives from drone companies, banks, giant tractor manufacturers and others who serve large farm operations. “I will fight for the small farm,” he said.

text:
Maxion Structural Components and Novelis have jointly developed Maxion InVolt, a battery housing for electric commercial vehicles stamped from rolled aluminum using a new alloy created for the application.

The companies say the InVolt housing is about 35% lighter than an extruded aluminum housing built to the same technical requirements. The design can be adapted to different vehicle sizes, from light to heavy commercial vehicles, and the companies are aiming it at global markets.

Weight is a central constraint for battery-electric buses and trucks. Stamped aluminum is already widely used across the automotive industry, and Maxion says that, compared with current processes, the stamped approach is more cost-effective and allows easier access to internal components for maintenance.

Aluminum’s combination of low weight and impact absorption suits the safety and performance demands of electric commercial vehicles, according to Novelis, which supplied the raw-material expertise. Aluminum is repeatedly recyclable without loss of properties, and Novelis says that recyclability can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 95%.

“With over 40 years of experience in the automotive sector, Novelis is focused on co-creating innovative and customized solutions to meet the demand for more sustainable mobility,” said Daniele Albagli, Vice President of Sales for Novelis South America.

“The development of this solution represents a crucial step in our strategy to reduce the weight of electric commercial vehicles and, consequently, contribute to reducing CO₂ emissions without compromising vehicle load capacity,” said Marco Tulio Ricci, Global Director of Innovation and Engineering at Maxion Structural Components.

title: Why Power Now Leads the Manufacturing Growth Plan - Bloom Energy
description:
The companies manufacturing the servers, chips, cooling systems, electrical equipment and other infrastructure behind that growth need electricity to power their growth.
A production line can’t wait for power For manufacturers, electricity is part of the production environment.
For executives, the practical implication is to evaluate power needs alongside production requirements – before site, capital plan, and operating timelines are set.
But their assumptions that electricity will be available whenever the growth plan requires it no longer hold.
Companies that address power early will be best positioned to turn demand into production and gain a competitive advantage.
text:
Power access and reliability have always been critical considerations for manufacturers. They affect operating costs, consistency, and the economics of every facility.

In my conversations with industrial customers, I’m hearing that electricity is becoming an earlier priority in expansion decisions. AI data center growth is a big factor in this shift. The companies manufacturing the servers, chips, cooling systems, electrical equipment and other infrastructure behind that growth need electricity to power their growth.

Manufacturers still focus on customer demand, workforce, and supply chain in these decisions. But more than ever before, they are asking how much power they can secure, whether it will be ready in time, and how that impacts their schedules and outcomes.

A production line can’t wait for power

For manufacturers, electricity is part of the production environment. An interruption can stop a line, disrupt a controlled process, damage material, or affect quality.

Growth creates a different version of the same problem. Most manufacturers do not expand by building a new facility every time demand rises. They add a line, expand a clean room, install more automation, or bring additional equipment onto an existing campus. The site, workforce and customers may already be in place – but sometimes, the power is not.

When the timing of new power capacity does not match the production plan, a growth opportunity can become a scheduling problem, then a customer problem and eventually an investment problem.

Powering the AI supply chain

Every AI deployment has a physical supply chain behind it. As investment in AI infrastructure grows, manufacturers are increasing outputs. Servers have to be assembled and semiconductors fabricated. Networking equipment, cooling systems, and electrical infrastructure must be produced at scale.

With that come decisions about equipment, facilities, capital, and power. Availability of power now matters at many points in the value chain.

MiTAC Computing is a clear example. The company manufactures AI servers, and rising demand for AI infrastructure requires it to support current operations while preparing for additional production. At MiTAC’s Fremont, California, manufacturing campus, Bloom Energy is deploying fuel cell systems for an islanded microgrid, building on an existing deployment at their San Jose facility. Onsite power generation, via fuel cells, helps the company bring new capacity online at AI speed.

The cost of waiting on power

Energy cost remains a real challenge where a relatively small difference in electricity prices can affect the economics of an energy-intensive operation. But manufacturers now also have to account for the cost of waiting. A company may have customer demand, approved capital, equipment on order and a production target, but the business case changes if power won’t be available for several years.

Delayed revenue, customer commitments at risk, or a competitor capturing a market opportunity first are commercial questions. That means power belongs in the same conversation as operations, capital allocation, site selection, and expansion.

For executives, the practical implication is to evaluate power needs alongside production requirements – before site, capital plan, and operating timelines are set. Utility service remains critical, but when utility timelines don’t match business timelines, manufacturers can evaluate fuel cells as a source of reliable, onsite power generation. The goal is not to replace the grid, but to expand companies’ growth options.

The same principle applies to resilience. Reliable power protects against outages and lost production, but it also supports the upside. It can determine whether a company can increase output when customers need it.

Power as a competitive advantage

Manufacturers will continue to compete on product quality, cost, talent, technology, and execution. But their assumptions that electricity will be available whenever the growth plan requires it no longer hold.

When a manufacturer cannot add capacity on schedule, the effect can move quickly through customer commitments, supply chains, and future investment decisions. A power constraint at one facility becomes a production constraint somewhere else.

Companies that address power early will be best positioned to turn demand into production and gain a competitive advantage.

text:
Every year, hundreds of millions are spent on subsidies to help people in low- and middle-income countries use better stoves that emit less climate-warming carbon dioxide. But questions remain about whether that money is well spent, especially after a 2024 study estimated that clean cookstove projects were wildly overstating their environmental benefits.

A new paper from Wharton business economics and public policy professor Susanna Berkouwer sets the record straight. Their study with co-author Joshua Dean, professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, finds that high-quality clean cookstove subsidies can be far more cost-effective at reducing carbon emissions than subsidies for electric vehicles or rooftop solar panels.

The study of more than 1,000 households in Nairobi, Kenya, calculated that cookstove subsidies for the ECOA Char stove abate carbon dioxide at $7 per ton. For comparison, it costs $1,356 in electric vehicle subsidies or $237 in rooftop solar subsidies to abate 1 ton of CO2e (carbon dioxide equivalent).

Berkouwer hopes the study will spur investment in clean cookstove subsidies by settling the question about whether the improved appliances really can make a difference in the fight against climate change. More than 200 million people around the world cook with charcoal because it’s cheaper and easier to obtain than electricity or other cleaner fuels.

“There’s so much money going into green innovation and technologies in higher-income countries, and we’re leaving a lot of opportunities on the table to invest more effectively in slowing climate change,” Berkouwer said. “A small change can have a much bigger impact than we realize.”

“A small change can have a much bigger impact than we realize.”— Susanna Berkouwer

How Cookstove Subsidies Compare to Others

The study relies on precise and independently collected data. Berkouwer and Dean used a randomized controlled trial — the gold standard in research — and measured charcoal consumption four different ways to ensure accuracy.

They also adjusted for additionality and impact, two features that can skew the results if not accounted for. Additionality is whether the subsidy actually increases sales, and impact is whether increased sales actually reduce emissions. Impact can be eroded by poor durability of the appliance, low use, or households stacking them alongside their old stoves. And additionality can be thrown off by the number of people who were planning to buy the improved stove regardless of the financial incentive.

Berkouwer uses the example of electric vehicles to explain additionality. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 offered a tax credit of $7,500 for the purchase of a new EV. The money certainly incentivized new buyers, but there were also buyers who planned to buy an EV anyway and just pocketed the savings.

“One of the criticisms about a lot of subsidy programs is that the money is going to people who were doing it anyway, so you’re not really changing behavior. But you can quantify that and take it into account,” Berkouwer said.

In their study, the professors determined nonadditionality was 16%. Even factoring that in, the total cost of subsidizing one additional cookstove was $32. More importantly, each dollar of the cookstove subsidy abated around 200 times more CO2e than an EV subsidy.

“When you think about it that way, cookstove subsidies have a negative cost of abatement: Every ton of CO2 abated saves us money.”— Susanna Berkouwer

Convincing a Skeptical Market

Berkouwer, whose research focuses on environmental and developmental economics, said the rigorous study methods can be applied to other carbon financing projects. The professor wants to see more empirical research that can drive better policies and greater investment in climate solutions, especially in the developing world.

“Every ton of CO2 is a ton of CO2, regardless of where it came from. What does the evidence say about how we should spend the money to reduce the most amount of CO2?” Berkouwer said. “Our research shows that subsidies for clean cookstoves can be among the most effective.”

Berkouwer also stressed the quality-of-life benefits that come along with the subsidies. The International Energy Agency estimates that 1.5 billion people will still be cooking with charcoal, wood, or kerosene by 2030. Improved cookstoves reduce the amount of money spent on fuel by households living in severe poverty. The study determined that the average household saves $284 over three years of ownership of an improved cookstove, money that can be spent on food, school, or medical expenses. They can also generate reductions in indoor air pollution, and reduce the time burden on women who collect firewood.

“When you think about it that way, cookstove subsidies have a negative cost of abatement: Every ton of CO2 abated saves us money,” Berkouwer said.

text:
Dive Brief:

The U.S. battery energy storage sector faces more near-term risk than other industries from President Donald Trump’s executive order last week restricting foreign-produced bulk power components, BloombergNEF analysts said in a note Friday.

Deployment delays are likely for many grid-scale battery projects as developers await additional guidance from the administration, seek alternative suppliers or redesign projects, according to the BNEF note.

Battery project developers and operators should map existing and planned assets that may be affected by the order, assess regulatory risk allocation in supply contracts, consider expanding supply chain diligence and prepare to mitigate or replace affected equipment that has already been installed, lawyers with Morgan Lewis’s energy practice said in a separate post Friday.

Dive Insight:

Trump’s executive order seeks to prevent certain foreign-made batteries, transformers, inverters and related digital products from connecting to the U.S. power grid after its Aug. 26 effective date.

It also gives Energy Secretary Chris Wright discretion to impose conditions on “the continued use, operation, maintenance, servicing, or updating” of equipment procured or installed before Aug. 26.

Trump’s order follows a narrower order Trump signed during his first term that blocked installations of bulk power system equipment with ties to a “foreign adversary.” China, which both Trump and former President Joe Biden have described as a U.S. adversary, accounts for 80% of global lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, according to the International Energy Agency.

And many U.S. battery deployments rely on inverters manufactured by Chinese companies, which in 2025 supplied about 40% of U.S. inverter volumes from production hubs in India and Southeast Asia, according to the BNEF note.

The Aug. 26 order compounds challenges faced by users of imported battery systems and inverters from the Foreign Entity of Concern rules finalized by the U.S. Treasury Department in February, BNEF trade and supply chains analyst Zoe Zakrzewska told Utility Dive in an email. Authorized by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, those rules restrict how reliant U.S. equipment producers’ and energy project developers’ supply chains can be on Chinese-tied firms while still qualifying for federal manufacturing and investment tax credits.

“Battery energy storage systems and inverters are the two technologies that are clearly subject to both of these sets of rules … [but] the new EO has the potential to be far more punishing,” Zakrzewska said.

It “could likely be the nail in the coffin for Chinese battery and inverter manufacturers selling in the US market: while the FEOC rules allowed some room for Chinese firms to adapt, the [bulk power system] EO can easily shut out these firms for good,” she added.

The risk is greater for project developers as well because last week’s executive order may affect projects that began construction before the January 1, 2026, deadline to avoid Foreign Entity of Concern compliance but have not yet begun operations, Zakrzewska said.

Electrical equipment manufacturers reacted cautiously to last week’s executive order. Bridget Bartol, the head of industry and regulatory affairs at the National Electric Manufacturers Association, told Utility Dive on Thursday that “there’s a need for a lot more clarity,” particularly with regard to the order’s impact on software products.

“I think there’s going to be a lot of dialog between the industry and the administration,” Bartol said.

In the meantime, the BNEF note said developers that have procured but not yet installed battery system equipment may wait to move forward until the administration clarifies how the order applies, which Zakrzewska said should happen at some point.

Developers are likely to cancel altogether some projects made uneconomical by the prohibition on lower-cost Chinese imports, BNEF added.

The longer-term impact of last week’s executive order may be lessened by new manufacturing capacity coming online in the United States and in countries not covered by the executive order, Zakrzewska said.

text:
Donald Trump this month announced plans to rescind a landmark rule that has protected old-growth forests in the US for 25 years. If finalized, the rollback is expected to benefit the companies that Tom Schultz, chief of the US Forest Service, represented in his previous roles as a timber industry lobbyist and executive, according to research by consumer advocacy non-profit Public Citizen.

The Roadless Area Conservation Rule, more commonly known as the “roadless rule”, was adopted in 2001 to limit development in roughly 45m acres of national forest. Industry interests and Republican representatives have long lobbied for the rule’s rescission, which would open up those swaths of untouched land to road construction, drilling and logging.

In a statement, Schultz described the move as “the best way to restore the balance, reduce wildfire risk, and secure the long-term health of our forests and neighboring communities”. But studies suggest it could put 400 threatened and endangered species at risk and imperil ecosystems.

Industry interests will be the main beneficiaries of the change, advocates fear.

In an emailed statement, a Forest Service spokesperson, who did not provide their name, noted that Schultz had also held positions in Idaho and Montana government.

“Chief Schultz’s appointment reflects the administration’s recognition that the Forest Service’s current challenges require leadership with broad federal land management experience, not just internal tenure,” the person said.

Schultz is the first-ever Forest Service chief who did not previously work within the agency itself. Before Trump tapped him for the job, he served as president of the Federal Forest Resource Coalition, a trade association representing companies that purchase timber from the federal government, and was also vice-president of resources and government affairs at Idaho Forest Group, a major lumber manufacturer.

He is one of dozens of former extractive industry insiders Trump has placed in key environmental positions. Energy secretary Chris Wright was CEO of fracking company Liberty Energy, while interior official Tyler Hassen was an oil executive. Forty-three former fossil-fuel employees and 29 former corporate executives held administration positions, an October analysis from Public Citizen and corporate watchdog Revolving Door Project found.

Schultz has long been critical of the roadless rule. As it was being considered in 2000, he said: “It’s going to be very difficult to actually generate revenue from state trust lands that could be encompassed within a roadless designation.”

The American Forest Resource Council (AFRC), a timber industry trade association on the west coast that includes the Idaho Forest Group, has recently directly advocated for the rescission of the roadless rule. In comments to the federal government last year, the lobbying group said the “one-size-fits-all” policy unnecessarily prevents “active forest management” – intentionally thinning forests through practices including logging – which it says is the best way to mitigate wildfire risk.

Since his appointment, Schultz has echoed these calls. “Active forest management is not an option. It’s essential,” he said in the announcement of the proposal to rescind the roadless rule, which also referred to the policy as “one-size-fits-all”.

“Active forest management is central to the Forest Service’s multi-use mission – not an industry agenda,” the Forest Service spokesperson said.

In a statement, Nick Smith, spokesperson for the AFRC, said: “There is broad bipartisan support for increasing forest health treatments – thinning, prescribed fire, and even logging – to reduce the size and severity of wildfires and make forests more resilient to climate change.”

A recent analysis of the Forest Service’s own data found that wildfires were nearly three times as likely to start near roads, raising questions about the administration’s claim that expanding road access will reduce wildfire risk, said Lois Parshley, climate research director at Public Citizen.

“But from the industry’s perspective, it will also open up new possibilities for logging,” she said.

Asked about Parshley’s concern, the Forest Service spokesperson said that repealing the roadless rule “allows safer use and maintenance of existing roads that first responders have long said they need to reach fires quickly”.

“Forest‑treatment science is clear: thinning plus prescribed fire reduces wildfire severity by more than 60% – and up to 72% compared to untreated areas,” they said. “Access enables treatment; without access, prevention and response suffer. Gates and seasonal closures can be used to manage public traffic while preserving routes that firefighters and forest managers may need.”

The AFRC’s comments say that “strategically placed and maintained roads are essential for safe and effective wildfire response”, and that in “nearly every major wildfire over the past 15–20 years”, the Forest Service has identified a lack of road access as a key barrier to effective response, Parshley said. That argument also appears in Schultz’s rationale for repealing the rule, she noted. In the administration’s announcement, he said the roadless rule “has frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to action – prohibiting road construction, which has limited wildfire suppression and active forest management”.

Smith of the AFRC said that “millions of roadless acres have burned across the west since the rule’s adoption in 2001.”

“Federal lands are far more likely to burn than private lands, which typically have far more roads,” he said. “According to the congressional budget office, a wildfire on federal land is on average five times the size of one on nonfederal land nearby.”

Critics dispute the logic that the roadless rule is good for wildfire management, arguing that roads can increase the risk of human-caused fires.

Since Schultz came into the Forest Service in February 2025, the American Forest Resource Council has spent more than $210,000 advocating to expand harvesting in national forests, lobbying records show. Meanwhile, the Idaho Forest Group increased its spending on lobbying in 2026 and reported advocating to support “efforts to advance forest management”, including with the agency now run by its former executive, Parshley found.

Smith of the AFRC claimed that “the amount of money AFRC spends lobbying Congress and federal agencies in support of policies to improve the health of federal forests and nearby rural communities is dwarfed in comparison to the many anti-forestry NGOs.”

Idaho is exempt from the roadless rule; it has its own regulations on roadless areas developed with the federal government. But the proposal to kill the roadless rule is just one industry-backed change to forestry that the Trump administration has put forth. As the head of the Federal Forest Resource Coalition, Schultz in July 2022 delivered testimony before Congress in which he suggested roadless areas were limiting the industry, saying: “nearly half of the National Forest System [is] off limits to management.”

Though he did not call to overturn the policy specifically, he advocated allowing states to manage more Forest Service timber sales, expanding exemptions from environmental review processes, and changing stewardship contracting rules to support logging and wood-processing infrastructure.

The Trump administration has since adopted or advanced each of those proposals, Parshley found in a report earlier this year. And Schultz has directly helped implement them, she found. For instance, in December 2025 he personally signed an agreement with Idaho’s governor to double federal timber sales from the state’s national forests.

“That directly benefits his former employer the Idaho Forest Group”, she said.

Idaho Forest Group has been contacted for comment.

Under Schultz, the Forest Service has ramped up timber sales. In June, he told senators that the agency had exceeded its timber-sale target. He has also overseen a historic and widely criticized structural reorganization of his agency, moving the agency’s headquarters from the nation’s capital to Salt Lake City, eliminating regional offices and staff and shifting authority over forests to states.

Schultz has made it clear that he aims to weaken regulations. In April, he told Congress that he is “trying to cut through regulation”.

In a company earnings call after Schultz was confirmed, lumber company PotlatchDeltic CEO Eric Cremers confirmed that industry executives maintain direct familiarity with Schultz in his new role, saying: “We know the new Forest Service chief.”

“It’s pretty clear that the industry was excited by their reactions to Schultz’s nomination and then confirmation,” said Parshley.

title: Why EPA's SRE Decision Is Good News for Biofuels: Scott Irwin Breaks Down the RFS Reallocation
description:
In an interview with Gleason, University of Illinois Agricultural Economist Scott Irwin explained that the broader policy framework offsets the immediate volume hit.
Full Reallocation Offsets Exemption Numbers The key takeaway highlighted by Gleason and Irwin is the EPA’s upcoming supplemental rulemaking scheduled by the end of October.
Commodity and Biofuel Market Impacts Irwin told Gleason that the decision carries minimal implications for the corn market, noting that ethanol remains largely neutral to SRE shifts.
With full reallocation secured for 2026 and 2027, the biomass-based diesel sector gains a constructive, positive trend moving forward.
Scott Irwin is an agricultural economist on the Urbana-Champaign campus of the University of Illinois and member of the farmdoc team.
text:
Reporting from Todd Gleason features analysis from University of Illinois Agricultural Economist Scott Irwin on how the EPA’s 100% reallocation of Small Refinery Exemptions turns a large exemption headline into a net-neutral wash that supports biomass-based diesel.

Gleason reports that while the Environmental Protection Agency recently ruled on 34 petitions for Small Refinery Exemptions (SREs)—totaling nearly 1.8 billion gallons in exemptions at 50% or 100% levels for the 2025 Renewable Fuel Standard compliance year—the move is actually unvarnished good news for agriculture and biofuels. In an interview with Gleason, University of Illinois Agricultural Economist Scott Irwin explained that the broader policy framework offsets the immediate volume hit.

Full Reallocation Offsets Exemption Numbers

The key takeaway highlighted by Gleason and Irwin is the EPA’s upcoming supplemental rulemaking scheduled by the end of October. Through this rule, the agency plans to reallocate 100% of the extra Renewable Identification Number (RIN) volumes from these 2025 SREs into the 2026 and 2027 compliance obligations.

Irwin pointed out to Gleason that this 100% reallocation is both critical and surprising:

Under the previous “set rule” for 2026 and 2027, the EPA had only reallocated 70% of projected SRE volumes.

Restoring 100% of the extra 2025 volumes into 2026 and 2027 obligations makes the total volume impact essentially a wash rather than a reduction in biofuel demand.

The recaptured volume guarantees the demand remains intact across upcoming compliance years.

Commodity and Biofuel Market Impacts

Irwin told Gleason that the decision carries minimal implications for the corn market, noting that ethanol remains largely neutral to SRE shifts.

The clear beneficiaries of the EPA’s decision are biodiesel, renewable diesel, and soybean oil. With full reallocation secured for 2026 and 2027, the biomass-based diesel sector gains a constructive, positive trend moving forward.

Scott Irwin is an agricultural economist on the Urbana-Champaign campus of the University of Illinois and member of the farmdoc team. The Environmental Protection Agency yesterday announced a decision on 34 petitions from small refineries seeking exemptions, or SREs, from compliance with the 2025 Renewable Fuel Standard obligations. The agency expects the exemptions to be reallocated into 2026 and 2027. Audio and story courtesy of Todd Gleason at the University of Illinois.

name: Texas American Energy
title: 3 principles to make AI data centers good grid citizens - Utility Dive
authors: Robert Walton, Drew Baglino, Vlad Troy, Michael Polsky, Herman K. Trabish, Ethan Howland, Varun Sivaram
description:
But within seconds, roughly 3,100 MW of demand vanished as data centers switched to backup power.
But the technology now exists for AI facilities to be good grid citizens — advancing energy affordability and grid reliability.
Do no harm Today’s data centers fall short of this foundational standard in two ways.
Read More in Transmission & Distribution AI data centers need power faster than the grid usually moves.
There’s a chance the AI data centers may strain the grid leaving communities to bear the brunt.
text:
Drew Baglino is founder and CEO of Heron Power; Vlad Troy is vice president of AI infrastructure at NVIDIA; Michael Polsky is founder and executive chairman of Invenergy; and Varun Sivaram is founder and CEO of Emerald AI.

On July 22, a transmission line failed in Northern Virginia. The fault was routine, the kind of disturbance the grid shrugs off constantly. But within seconds, roughly 3,100 MW of demand vanished as data centers switched to backup power. The voltage disturbance was felt from Washington to Chicago, though PJM reported no impact to bulk-system reliability. This follows an incident two years earlier, also in Northern Virginia, when roughly 60 data centers disconnected from the grid and transferred to backup power.

Events like these and others such as in Texas are why the North American Electric Reliability Corp. issued its highest-level alert in May, a measure reserved for urgent threats to the power system. Federal regulators have issued new directives for connecting large loads to the grid, and communities are asking whether the AI buildout will come at their expense.

We represent companies that build four layers of AI infrastructure: the power to supply AI; the computing systems that produce intelligence; the power electronics that connect facilities to the grid; and the software that orchestrates computation in response to grid conditions. We understand the anxiety that communities feel about the growth of specialized AI computing facilities, whether related to rising energy bills or less reliable power.

But the technology now exists for AI facilities to be good grid citizens — advancing energy affordability and grid reliability. We propose defining that good citizenship by three obligations of ascending ambition. First, an AI factory should do no harm to the grid. Second, it should offer flexibility when the system is stressed. And third, it should add to the grid: helping bring new generation, storage and transmission into service in ways that strengthen the system. All three can be met with commercially available technologies today, and for the first time they come together within a single architecture that our four companies can offer together.

Do no harm

Today’s data centers fall short of this foundational standard in two ways. When grid voltage dips even briefly, backup systems disconnect the whole facility, which is how one Virginia fault became a 3,000-MW shock. Compounding this, the workload is rapidly changing: a facility’s power draw can now swing by 10s of megawatts in seconds, fast and large power swings that can stress the surrounding grid.

During voltage disturbances, batteries at data centers can provide backup power to the GPUs and export power to maintain grid stability, carrying the facility through rather than abandoning the system at the first sign of trouble.

Facilities that disconnect during a grid disturbance can amplify that disturbance; every facility that rides through makes the system more resilient. Do no harm is the floor — but built into the AI data center rather than promised by its operator, it becomes something the grid can actually rely on.

Flex when the grid needs it

For a century, the power system has run on a one-way assumption: demand does what it wants, and supply must chase it. Utilities build for the hottest afternoon of the year, which is why the grid runs far below capacity nearly all the time — on average, barely above half.

An AI facility can break that assumption: by flexibly controlling its power use when the grid is strained, it can operate within local and global capacity constraints, connect faster and push local community power bills down rather than up. According to Duke University, if large new loads trim consumption for less than half a percent of their hours each year — a heat wave here, a cold snap there — the existing grid could absorb roughly 100 gigawatts of new demand, years sooner than interconnection queues allow. The Brattle Group estimates that a 10% improvement in grid utilization would cut average retail rates by nearly 4%.

Add to the grid

The third obligation is not just to use power carefully. It is to make sure the energy built for an AI factory becomes part of the system around it, contributing to reliable and affordable energy supply for all ratepayers.

Read More in Transmission & Distribution

AI data centers need power faster than the grid usually moves. Many projects will therefore begin with co-located generation and storage. Used well, those resources are bridge power: they bring AI capacity online quickly while a fuller grid connection is completed. Used poorly, they become permanent islands: assets sized for one customer, walled off from the grid, and unavailable when neighboring homes and businesses need them most.

In areas where high-priority interregional transmission needs exist, like those recently studied by the Department of Energy, an AI facility can also catalyze the infrastructure investments needed to realize the identified reliability and affordability benefits. For example, high-accredited capacity, customer-funded interregional transmission projects like the Grain Belt Express can directly serve AI demand while also delivering these benefits to millions of ratepayers.

That is the difference between building around the grid and adding to it. While speed to power is paramount in today’s environment, the end goal is not a private power plant next to a private computer forever. The goal is to use AI demand to pull new energy infrastructure into service faster, then operate that infrastructure as part of the shared system.

Citizenship by design

Regulators and utilities can accelerate all of this with performance-based rules that reward behavior rather than mandate equipment. A facility that demonstrably rides through disturbances, smooths its draw, supports the grid, and delivers verified flexibility at its interconnection point should connect faster and on better terms. Silicon Valley Power and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas have begun to show what such frameworks look like, though the Texas rules are still being settled. FERC’s June 18 orders directing all six regional grid operators to justify or reform their large-load tariffs put this framework on a national timeline. The orders explicitly reward the behaviors we describe — ride-through, flexibility, grid enhancement — making good citizenship not just good policy but good interconnection strategy.

Read More in Transmission & Distribution

America is in the middle of one of the largest infrastructure buildout programs in its history. There’s a chance the AI data centers may strain the grid leaving communities to bear the brunt. But built as we describe, the same buildings can steady the voltage in their neighborhoods, absorb available capacity in their regions, and lower the bills of families and businesses who share their wires. The buildout can leave the grid stronger than it found it. That is what good citizens do, and it happens to be very good business.

text:
—

A group of environmental and scientific organizations, represented by Earthjustice, filed comments today calling on the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to reject the agency’s proposal to waive all major environmental protection requirements for commercial space launches and other activities. The group warned that the sweeping waiver would violate federal law and have negative impacts on public health, wildlife, and the safety of the communities living near rocket launch and reentry sites.

Companies across the space industry have in recent months ramped up plans to increase space launches. SpaceX just announced plans to build a $100 billion rocket launch complex in Louisiana, which would enable thousands of launches a year. The site SpaceX selected is a sensitive coastal marsh more than eight times the size of Manhattan. The area presently protects Louisianans from storm surges and is a key wintering site for migratory birds.

“This proposed rule is outrageous, unwise, and illegal. Instead of catering to the for-profit space industry, the FAA needs to do its job and properly oversee commercial space activities to protect our communities and our environment,” said Ruskin Hartley, executive director of Dark Sky International.

“A 21st century gold rush to extract profits from space is arriving at the same time as an all-of-government deregulatory program,” said Tim Whitehouse, Executive Director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “We will continue to insist that the government fulfills its obligations to protect our people, our communities, and our wildlife, and to comply with anti-pollution and wildlife protection laws.”

“The environmental laws on the books are there for a reason: to ensure companies remain responsible for and accountable to the frontline communities in which they are operating,” said Scott W. Stern, Senior Associate Attorney, Earthjustice. “We will not stand idly by if the federal government refuses to do its job.”

Commercial space activities are known to have numerous environmental impacts, including emissions from rocket launches, falling debris, and light and noise pollution that would disrupt and harm wildlife.
